title: ‘I want to own a grocery store & café with my friends’: Food co-op initiative launches in downtown Newport
description:
Vermont has a long tradition of food cooperatives, currently boasting 15 of the member-owned stores. The most recent addition, the Caledonia Food Co-op in St. Johnsbury, opened last month after eight years of fundraising and organizing.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  ‘I want to own a grocery store & café with my friends’: Food co-op initiative launches i[...]
text:
Erica Wilson, founding president of the Kingdom Co-op, and Thomas Goodwin, general manager of Green Mountain Natural Foods and a member of the Kingdom Co-op board, in the store in Newport on July 1, 2026. Photo by K. Fiegenbaum/VTDigger
Newport-area residents have launched an effort to transform their Main Street grocery store and cafe into a member-owned food cooperative in hopes of ensuring its sustainability.
“What we want to do is bring a business to the community that is going to support the local producers and serve the community members that are here,” Erica Wilson, founding board president of the Kingdom Co-op, said in early July. A food co-op is run by a board of directors elected by its members, each of whom owns a small portion of the business.
The effort began when local businessman Rick Woodward stepped in to purchase Green Mountain Natural Foods in early 2024. Woodward has owned the three-story historic building in which the store is located for nearly a quarter-century and has stepped in as owner or co-owner several times when the natural food business has been put up for sale.
While owning the store was “never part of his career plan,” Woodward wants to ensure that it remains a natural foods store and a downtown staple, he said in an interview last week. After purchasing the business a year and a half ago, he immediately started talking to community members and other local food businesses about the possibility of a co-op model.
Wilson heard about the idea through her position as general manager of a local dairy, Butterworks Farm. She was excited to get involved, she said, to connect with another piece of the local food economy.

The Montgomery Ward building in Newport on July 1, 2026. Photo by K. Fiegenbaum/VTDigger

In the time since, some of the community members Woodward connected with, including two store employees, have stepped up to form a five-member founding board. The group has surveyed residents, held events to educate locals about the co-op model and, last month, began selling memberships.
The change would be a return to roots for the store, which was initially founded as a co-op in West Glover in 1971. It later moved to Barton, Orleans and then finally to Newport in 1977. In the early 1980s, however, a member of the co-op purchased it and converted it into a private business.
Green Mountain Natural Foods currently occupies the first floor and basement of the Montgomery Ward building downtown, located directly across the street from ‘the pit,’ the vacant, fenced-off block of land in the center of town abandoned over a decade ago during a failed redevelopment project as part of the EB-5 investor fraud scandal.
The natural foods store is filled with local produce, breads, cheeses, bulk foods, health supplements and wine. A cafe making smoothies, coffee, sandwiches and soups occupies a little less than half the space, with airy indoor seating.
Woodward, who owns multiple properties in town, said that his vision for the Montgomery Ward building since purchasing it in 2002 has always included shared spaces of some kind with a wellness component. The second floor has long been occupied by small offices with shared amenities, and in 2018, Woodward and his daughter opened a co-working space called The Work Commons on the third floor.
“It’s a really great ecosystem here and a model in a town that isn’t doing super great economically,” he said. According to recent U.S. Census Bureau data, an estimated 23% of Newport residents are below the poverty line, well above the state’s overall poverty rate of 9%.
Woodward noted that visitors and tenants can find everything in the building from yoga classes to massages to an accountant for hire and, of course, groceries and coffee. 
While Green Mountain Natural Foods already sources much of its produce locally as many co-ops aim to, Woodward said he wants the community to feel — and be — a part of the store: “I want to own a grocery store & café with my friends,” reads the effort’s motto. Woodward plans to continue to own the building itself.
Vermont’s co-op tradition
Vermont has a long history of food co-ops: the Adamant Co-op north of Montpelier opened in 1935 and is the longest continuously operating food co-op in the country. There were 15 food co-ops in the state as of 2025 with 58,000 member-owners, according to Erbin Crowell, executive director of the Neighboring Food Co-op Association. These co-ops employ around 950 people, which, together, makes them among the top employers in the state.
The state’s newest food co-op, the Caledonia Food Co-op in St. Johnsbury, opened its doors July 8 after approximately eight years of organizing and fundraising.
“Once they are established, food co-ops tend to be anchors of their communities and the local economy, with an average of 30% of sales being local products, compared to 2-5% in supermarkets,” Crowell said in an email. “They are also more sustainable and resilient … in Vermont alone, 8 food co-ops have served their communities for 50 or more years.”
Woodward said that while many residents currently shop at Green Mountain Natural Foods, he believes that people will be more likely to shop there more often if it is run as a co-op: if they are a member and have a real stake in the business.
In addition to cooperatively-owned grocery stores, there is also a parallel movement of “community supported enterprises” in the state, which are owned by a town or local nonprofit, Jake Claro, Farm to Plate director at the Vermont Sustainable Jobs Fund, said in an email. These include enterprises such as the Peacham Cafe, which is rented by a subsidiary of a local nonprofit housing provider to a cafe manager for the benefit of the community, and the Main Street Market in Richford, which was purchased by a local primary care practice in 2020 after its announced closure would have left residents without a nearby grocery store.
Prepared meals have been a particularly fast-growing portion of grocery store sales nationally and in Vermont, such as at the Hunger Mountain Co-op in Montpelier, Claro said. This is something Wilson also envisions being a potential growth area for the Kingdom Co-op — offering prepared meals and meal kits, and also making sure much of those offerings and what is served in the store’s cafe is sourced locally.

The Caledonia Food Co-op in St. Johnsbury opened on July 8, 2026. Photo by K. Fiegenbaum/VTDigger

“Local food is not just more expensive, it’s harder to source from smaller producers,” she said. “But if we make it our initiative as a community, it’s totally doable.”
So far, Wilson said, many community members she has spoken with support the idea of Newport having its very own food co-op.
Along with beginning to sell memberships, the Kingdom Co-op board is working through the myriad of steps needed to make the co-op a reality, including vetting financial projections and creating a business plan. Early technical and advisory support has come from the Center for an Agricultural Economy in Hardwick, which works to build a more interconnected local food system, and Newport’s downtown development group.
“Whatever plan comes together, it needs to support the community as a whole,” Wilson said.

title: What’s a farmers market in Vermont without the farmers?
description:
Farmers are turning a corner in Vermont, with more looking to community supported agriculture and direct-to-farm stands as more financially viable options.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  What’s a farmers market in Vermont without the farmers?.
text:
The Old North End Farmers Market in Burlington on Tuesday, August 4, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Vermont boasts more farmers markets per resident than any state in the nation, according to data from the U.S. Department of Agriculture, yet almost all of them say they are in search of one common thing — the farmers.   
For generations, growers have leaned on farmers markets as a critical sales channel. Now, most of the state’s markets — 34 of 58 — say their single biggest concern is attracting more farm vendors to survive, according to the Northeast Organic Farming Association of Vermont. 
The reason, survey data suggests, is blunt: Farmers at the markets aren’t making the money they used to. 
Average agricultural sales at each of the ubiquitous markets that the organic farming group tracks have fallen by nearly 60%, from $158,296 in 2022 to $91,790 in 2025 — even as the number of markets statewide kept climbing.
With more markets, fewer farmers and thinner returns, growers are being pushed toward community supported agriculture shares and direct-to-farm stands as options that offer steadier money and less dependence on a sunny Saturday. 
The result is a quiet reordering of how Vermonters buy local food, and a hard question for the longtime staples in the Green Mountain state: What is a farmers market without the farmers?
“Markets close for many reasons, but a major reason that they close is that there just aren’t enough vendors, specifically agriculture vendors, to keep the market viable,” said Andrew Graham, the farmers market specialist at Vermont’s organic farming group.
The biggest culprits for the plunge in sales over the three years, the data suggests, are the larger farmers markets, although it does not specify which ones. 
While the number of these particular markets has stayed relatively the same, with four or five each year, the average agriculture sales dipped by more than half from $493,676 in 2022 to $213,234 in 2025. 
For Gus Griffin, a farmer who co-owns Glinnis Hill Farm in Northfield, farmers markets can be a useful sales channel when partnered with other sales models, like CSAs and farm stands. 
Participating in the Capitol City Farmers Market in Montpelier every Saturday, along with offering both market-style, where customers can visit a farm stand to choose their own produce, and traditional boxed CSAs, Griffin said farmers markets are seeing a new wave of farmers who might be more business-driven than older farmers. 
Farmers markets help new farmers build a customer base, he said, but this generation is more willing than the last to explore alternatives.
“We’re kind of selling a luxury product, and so when the economy is in trouble, we might also struggle,” Griffin said. “So, having those upfront sales, like a CSA, obviously makes your life feel a lot more secure.”
Dairy farmer Lyle Edwards, who formerly owned Spring Brook Farm, offered an alternative sentiment. 
Farmers markets never seemed like a viable option for him, he said, while he was running the farm. 
“Time is probably the biggest thing,” he said. “I mean it wasn’t going to do good on the scale. I think it’d be good for the guys that got eight or 10 cows to market raw milk, but we just like to sell milk wholesale.” 
While Edwards still helps in milking the cows on the farm, he sold his farm and explained that more and more farmers are simply aging out of Vermont, and the farmers market industry is likely feeling much of that shift.  
For many farmers, it also becomes economically harder for them to participate in the farmers markets when the vendor fees rise. This is a trend specifically seen from larger farmers markets across the four-year span of the state organic farmers group’s survey data. 
Hilary Martin, right, helps customers at the Diggers” Mirth Collective Farm stall at the Old North End Farmers Market in Burlington on Tuesday, August 4, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
The total average market revenue from vendor fees rose from $7,101 in 2022 to $11,898 in 2025, the data shows.
Farm Credit East, a financial cooperative that offers credit and services to farmers and producers in the Northeast, including those in Vermont, announced on Monday that they are awarding $92,000 in small grants to 175 farmers markets and farmers market organizations for National Farmers Market Week, which runs from Aug. 2-8. 
The grant funds will support more than 3,000 producers with marketing efforts. Markets can also use the funds to improve access to fresh produce for those in underserved communities and supplement funds from programs such as the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, according to the press release. 
The need for more financial support comes as farmers struggle to keep up with the rising costs of attending farmers markets.
As a result, farmers are more keen than ever on exploring alternative ways to sell their goods, said Abbey Willard, the agricultural development division director at the Vermont Agency of Agriculture, Food & Markets. 
“Farmers are choosing the options that make them money and that are most viable for their business,” Willard said. “So, if they’re choosing not to be at a farmers market, that may be because the other markets or other tasks that they’re otherwise attending to are more viable options for them.” 


Vermont is changing. So are the markets.
According to statutes set by the state, farmers markets part of the Vermont Farmers Market Association are required to have at least two agricultural vendors in order to even be recognized as a farmers market. 
The association has 61 known markets across the state — a number that has risen since 2022, when there were just 56 known markets. 
While the data might not be ironclad, Graham acknowledged, it has become increasingly evident to him that most markets are expressing a struggle to find farm vendors. 
The Winooski Farmers Market is one of them.  
“We sometimes have to make difficult decisions in order to maintain the focus on agriculture at the market, turning away some really talented chefs, artists or makers because we do want to make sure we’re not crossing the line into becoming a different kind of event,” Sarah Brunkhorst, the Winooski’s market manager, wrote in an email to VTDigger. 
Only 13 out of the 50 seasonal and half-season vendors at the Winooski Farmers Market sell grocery, produce and wellness, and only seven are exclusively grocery vendors, according to the vendor list on their website. 
“New farm recruitment has undoubtedly been a challenge for many of us,” Brunkhorst added. 
The farmers market consumer demographic is also changing, Willard, from the state’s agriculture agency, pointed out. That’s in large part due to the rise in tourists. 
As more of them herd in to see and experience what is considered by many to be a signature part of Vermont culture, she said, most of what they are looking for is not fresh produce but rather crafts and local hot food.   
Meanwhile, Willard added, Vermonters are not gravitating toward farmers markets as much as they used to despite the rise in the number of them. 
“I think it used to be that a farmers market was one of the only ways that you, as a Vermonter who was committed to buying local food, could access local food,” she said.
That is no longer the case for much of Vermont. 
According to poll data from Farm to Plate’s 2023 annual report, Vermonters are buying their local food from grocery and convenience stores more than ever before. 
For instance, in 2018, only 42% of Vermonters polled said that they purchased their local food from convenience stores. In 2023, the number has more than doubled to 87%. 
A customer walks out of the Old North End Farmers Market with a shopping bag full of produce in Burlington on Tuesday, August 4, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
For areas in the state that are not abundant with grocery stores, such as Winooski, farmers markets are there to help fill in the gaps. 
“Right now Winooski has some really amazing cultural markets and corner stores, but we don’t have a full-scale grocery store or supermarket,” Brunkhorst said. “So, our focus has been not just on farm products, but all kinds of foods and goods that the community might be missing easy access to.” 
While the Winooski Farmers Market has grown over the years, she said, it is seeing a much larger volume of applications from hot food and craft vendors than agricultural producers. 
However, Brunkhorst refused to define farmers markets as exclusively one thing, whether it be cultural events or direct-to-consumer agriculture distribution channels. 
Instead, she said she views them as a way for the community to have almost all of their needs met in one place, including the farmers who will often barter their left-over produce after a market. 
In addition to the bartering, Griffin, from Glinnis Hill Farms, also noted the positives for farmers attending farmers markets, such as face-to-face time with customers and brand recognition. 
What he’s also noticed, however, are the major uncertainties that come with it.  
“We want to farm, we want to do something that is good for the earth, and we also want to make a living, and so we’re coming at it from a pretty business-minded perspective,” Griffin said. “On a rainy day at the farmers market, we might make 1,000 less dollars than on a sunny day. And having a business that is so reliant on sunny Saturdays is kind of just not necessarily resilient.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Lynn Fitch hopes her campaign for governor exceeds previous best effort by woman, Evelyn Gandy in 1979
description: Attorney General Lynn Fitch is greeted by supporters shortly before discussing her 2027 campaign for governor during an event at the Mississippi Republican Party headquarters in Jackson on Wednesday, Aug. 5, 2026.
text:
Attorney General Lynn Fitch is vying to do what has never been done in Mississippi and in 16 other states – be elected governor as a woman.
The Republican attorney general completed a three-day tour of the state last week touting her qualifications after announcing she is joining what is expected to be a crowded field in 2027 to succeed Gov. Tate Reeves, who is term limited.
Fitch is in her second term as attorney general after serving two terms as treasurer. She has to be considered the most serious and formidable female candidate for governor in Mississippi since 1979. 
That year, then-Lt. Gov. Evelyn Gandy led the competitive field of six candidates in the Democratic primary. She was unable to garner a majority of the vote, prompting a runoff between her and former Lt. Gov. William Winter.
In the runoff, Winter won 57% of the vote to capture the Democratic nomination, which at the time was tantamount to winning the office of governor. In those days, the Republican nominee, if there was one, did not pose much of a threat in the November general election.
In 1979, both Gandy and Winter were veteran politicians who had held multiple statewide offices.
Winter had served in the Mississippi House and in the statewide posts of tax collector (now abolished), treasurer and lieutenant governor. He had waged two unsuccessful campaigns for governor before his 1979 victory.
Gandy, the first Mississippi woman elected to a statewide constitutional office, had served as treasurer, insurance commissioner and lieutenant governor before the 1979 campaign. Like Winter, she also got her start in the Mississippi Legislature.
While Winter and Gandy both were entrenched politicians, each had unique attributes. Winter is praised for his  work to improve public education at a time when anti-integration sentiment literally threatened the existence of public schools. His work on racial reconciliation after leaving public office was also notable.
Former Mississippi Lt. Gov. Evelyn Gandy. Credit: AP file photo
Gandy, of course, was a true trailblazer in terms of female involvement and success in Mississippi politics.
Fitch will be the first woman serving in a statewide office in Mississippi to run for governor since Gandy in 1979.
Many believed that Amy Tuck, who served as lieutenant governor from 2000 to 2008, would run for the office of governor and would be a strong candidate, thanks to her ability at retail politicking. But after finishing two terms as lieutenant governor, Tuck took an administrative job at Mississippi State University and has never ventured back into politics.
The political timing was bad for Tuck, who was first elected as a Democrat and switched to become a Republican. She was constitutionally prohibited from running for a third consecutive term as lieutenant governor, leaving her with the options to challenge Republican Gov. Haley Barbour, pursue a lesser office or step aside from politics.
Many believed after Barbour’s tenure ended, she eventually would pursue the office of governor, but she never did.
In more recent times, Cindy Hyde-Smith, who won the post of agriculture commissioner in 2011, might have been considered a strong candidate for governor. But she took a different path, becoming the first woman to serve Mississippi as a United States senator. Like Tuck, Hyde-Smith was first elected as a Democrat before becoming a Republican.
The timing was bad for Tuck in 2011. Fitch is hoping the timing is right for her now as she pursues the vacant office of governor.
And perhaps the timing seems right based on what has happened in surrounding states. Both Arkansas and Alabama currently have Republican female governors, and Republican U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, a native of Jones County in south Mississippi, is attempting to become the first female governor of Tennessee.
Women also are vying for the governorships of Georgia, Florida and Texas.
Could one of those Southern states become the 34th state to elect a woman governor and could that history maker be Fitch?

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas’ Medicaid expansion is endangered. Again.
description: Months before Arkansas lawmakers convened for their 2013 legislative session, the thought that the state would expand Medicaid was almost laughable. Republicans had just won a majority in both chambers of the Legislature, with many candidates winning what had once been localized races by running against President Barack Obama and his signature healthcare law[...]
text:
The Arkansas Department of Human Services building on Main Street in downtown Little Rock.(Photo by John Sykes for the Arkansas Advocate)Months before Arkansas lawmakers convened for their 2013 legislative session, the thought that the state would expand Medicaid was almost laughable.
Republicans had just won a majority in both chambers of the Legislature, with many candidates winning what had once been localized races by running against President Barack Obama and his signature healthcare law. 
The U.S. Supreme Court’s ruling that summer left up to states the decision on whether to expand Medicaid to more low-income people under the Affordable Care Act. And the decision faced an especially uphill climb in Arkansas, with a three-fourths vote needed to pass the budget bill for Medicaid.
It was a threshold that was difficult enough to get for “motherhood and apple pie,” as then-Gov. Mike Beebe often quipped. Clearing that hurdle and convincing Republicans to embrace a key part of Obamacare seemed improbable.
Yet that’s exactly what happened, with Arkansas becoming the first state in the South to expand Medicaid and the first in the nation to use private insurance to do so. 
A new decision by the Trump administration has injected more uncertainty for the program and the thousands of Arkansans who rely on it for health coverage.
Arkansas’ expansion has gone through multiple names and governors, but the recurring theme of its 13-year history is improbability. The program has repeatedly survived multiple attempts to kill it and has been credited with cutting the state’s uninsured rate and the costs hospitals pay for treating patients without coverage.



Let us know what you think...


 


There’s been no shortage of legislative drama surrounding the program over the years, including marathon voting sessions in each chamber. One year, the House speaker asked State Police to retrieve a member who wasn’t present to vote. Republican lawmakers who supported the program have been targeted in heated primaries by opponents on the right.
The expansion survived one year through a bizarre procedural move that required supporters of the program to back a bill calling for its end, a provision that then-Gov. Asa Hutchinson struck through a line-item veto. 
But the Trump administration’s decision not to renew the state’s premium-assistance approach has put the expansion — now called ARHOME — back in familiar, endangered territory. And supporters of the program face a tougher political climate as they hope to find a way to retain coverage for more than 200,000 low-income Arkansans. Health providers and experts already are warning of disastrous consequences if the coverage ends. 
Arkansas’ new work requirements come at a hard moment for state’s fragile healthcare system

It’s unclear what will happen to people using ARHOME when the expansion program expires at the end of the year. The state has requested a two-year temporary waiver, which would tee up a new debate over the future of Medicaid when the Legislature meets next year.
Arkansas policymakers are left with two primary options for replacing the hybrid model the state uses. They could move those on the program to fee-for-service Medicaid or could look at moving them to managed care.
Either approach faces its own political risks before a predominantly Republican Legislature that struggled at times to reauthorize Arkansas’ expansion. 
Moving enrollees to fee-for-service may face opposition from conservative Republicans who already worry Medicaid’s rolls are too large. Democrats and some Republicans may resist managed care because of the impact it could have on services for enrollees.
Health experts say the only option that shouldn’t be on the table is letting thousands go without any insurance coverage. Doing so would send shockwaves through a healthcare system that’s already under the strain of low reimbursement rates and rising costs that have prompted some hospitals to cut back services.
But finding a way out may be much more difficult than when Arkansas adopted expansion 13 years ago. The state has become even more polarized, with many Republicans aligned with Trump and his push to cut Medicaid.
Finding a way forward isn’t impossible, but the odds seem stacked against it. Another fight for survival is fitting for a program that few would have bet on in the first place.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Trinity Health CT hospitals cited for patient safety more than others
description: Saint Francis Hospital has received nine 'immediate jeopardy' violations since 2023, the most in CT, and Johnson Memorial ranks second.
text:
Two Connecticut hospitals owned by one of the largest nonprofit Catholic health systems in the country have struggled in recent years with serious shortcomings when it comes to patient care.
Since 2023, hospitals operated by Trinity Health of New England have received more “immediate jeopardy,” or “IJ,” citations than hospitals in any other Connecticut health system. An IJ is the most serious quality and safety finding the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, CMS, can issue to a hospital.
An immediate jeopardy violation indicates a situation in which CMS determines that the provider “has placed the health and safety of recipients in its care at risk for serious injury, serious harm, serious impairment, or death.”
Saint Francis Hospital in Hartford has been issued nine IJs since January 2023, the most of any hospital in the state, and Johnson Memorial in Stafford ranks second, with five IJs over the same period, according to Connecticut’s Department of Public Health. Both are owned and operated by Trinity Health of New England. (The noncompliance reports at Saint Francis were reported last month by the Hartford Courant.)
In a statement, Stephanie Valickis, a spokesperson for Trinity Health of New England, rejected the notion that the trend represents broad safety issues.
“The suggestion of systemic quality issues across our hospitals is inconsistent with the quality and safety outcomes we continue to achieve. Across our system, hospitals have earned national recognition for clinical excellence,” she stated.
But state elected officials say the system is falling short of its commitment to Connecticut.
“Trinity Health, as a national organization, has a lot of resources. And I don’t think they’re putting enough of those resources into the state of Connecticut,” Comptroller Sean Scanlon said. “I would like to see them do that.”
Valickis said in a statement that Johnson Memorial has made strides more recently to strengthen oversight and recruit additional staff. The facility earned a Leapfrog Hospital Safety Grade “A” rating in the last four reporting periods, Valickis said. And Johnson Memorial’s last IJ finding occurred in June 2025.
Leaders at the health system have acknowledged that there is still work to do at Saint Francis.
Valickis declined to make Steven Hanks, chief executive officer, and Robert Roose, president of acute care, available for interviews with The Connecticut Mirror. But on Thursday, Hanks and Roose invited state Sen. Saud Anwar, D-South Windsor, and reporters on a tour of Saint Francis, where they acknowledged the issues that plagued the hospital and showed some of the work that’s been done to improve patient care.
Anwar has for the last few years been sounding the alarm about the hospital’s issues and used the opportunity to ask about the kind of investments Saint Francis could expect from its national leaders.
Roose said Saint Francis has received $6 million in recent months from the parent organization and that it could expect to receive “tens of millions of dollars every year over the course of the next several years.”
“The commitments that we have been shown is that the capital that is needed for Saint Francis and for Trinity Health of New England will be provided,” Roose told Anwar during the tour.
In a statement, Gov. Ned Lamont said the state is working with Trinity leadership to monitor improvements at Saint Francis.
“Connecticut residents deserve accessible, affordable, high-quality healthcare. The Department of Public Health has been working cooperatively with Trinity to ensure they meet these expectations,” Lamont said.

The New England branch of Trinity Health runs Johnson Memorial Hospital in Stafford. Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

Trinity Health’s safety issues in CT
Trinity Health is a $25 billion Michigan-based health system that touts itself as “one of the largest not-for-profit, faith-based healthcare systems in the nation.” The organization operates in 23 states and includes more than 90 hospitals across the country.
The system has three short-term acute care hospitals in Connecticut — Saint Francis in Hartford, St. Mary’s in Waterbury and Johnson Memorial in Stafford — through its Trinity Health of New England subsidiary, which also includes a rehabilitation hospital in Hartford and Mercy Medical Center in Springfield, Mass. 
In April, Trinity Health of New England signed an agreement to sell Mercy Medical Center to Baystate Health for $293 million. The sale will take effect in November, pending regulatory approval.
A review of CMS reports going back to 2020 revealed that Trinity Health of New England was dealing with quality issues at both Saint Francis and Johnson Memorial Hospitals between 2023 and 2025. 

The Johnson Memorial Hospital campus in Stafford on Aug. 6, 2026. Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

Johnson Memorial
On April 10, 2023, a patient was admitted to Johnson Memorial’s emergency department with suicidal ideation, according to a CMS report published that month. 
“The patient was not provided a timely suicide risk screen, was not searched for contraband items, was not changed into hospital safe clothing prior to being unsupervised, and was allowed unsupervised in the bathroom prior to a contraband search, where he/she cut their wrist with a razor, resulting in a finding of Immediate Jeopardy,” the report stated.
In an interview with regulators that day, the hospital’s emergency department director said, “the hospital had a behavioral health unit within the ED, which was safe for patients, but it was closed due to a lack of staff. Additionally, the hospital did not have a policy or procedure on how to manage a patient with behavioral health needs in the main ED.” 
The report states that the hospital reviewed and revised its changing and search policies for patients, “educated staff, and initiated audits.”
The challenge of maintaining a safe environment for behavioral health patients in emergency departments is not unique to Johnson Memorial. A review of inspection reports for all hospitals going back to 2020 revealed that several have been cited for failing to adequately monitor people being treated for mental health crises in EDs.
The following year, 2024, Johnson Memorial got hit with two more Immediate Jeopardy findings, according to a CMS report, though neither was directly related to staffing. 
In January of that year, an Immediate Jeopardy finding was issued for failure to properly sterilize surgical instruments. That February, the hospital received another IJ for failing to properly observe a patient with suicidal ideation, though not as a result of inadequate staffing.
But staffing shortages resulted in at least one more Immediate Jeopardy finding at Johnson Memorial in 2025. On Jan. 3, a patient initially admitted to the medical / surgical unit of the hospital with shortness of breath was experiencing declining blood pressure and needed to be moved to an Intensive Care Unit, or ICU. But Johnson Memorial’s ICU was closed because of inadequate staffing, according to a CMS report. 
The patient had to wait nearly four hours before being transferred to an ICU at another hospital, where the medication the doctor had prescribed could be safely administered, resulting in an IJ finding. In an interview with regulators on Jan. 22 of last year, the hospital’s director of patient care services said the ICU was closed and had been since Dec. 20, 2024.
In response to CMS, hospital administrators said the ICU reopened on Feb. 3, 2025, and the facility had instituted protocols to guide nursing staff in how to adequately provide care during gaps in ICU coverage.
But when regulators returned for a visit in June 2025, the ICU was closed and, once again, a patient in need of intensive care didn’t receive it in a timely manner, according to a CMS report.
“Hospital staff failed to implement the protocol to open the ICU which resulted in a delay in care. The delay resulted in a finding of Immediate Jeopardy (IJ),” the report stated.
Valickis, the Trinity Health of New England spokesperson, said in her statement that hospital leadership has worked hard to address the issues at Johnson Memorial and to restore the quality of care it provides today.
“Johnson Memorial Hospital is a strong and stable healthcare facility, fully compliant with all regulatory requirements and deeply committed to serving our community,” Valickis stated.
Schaefer, the spokesperson for DPH, confirmed that on follow-up visits, Johnson Memorial was found to be in “substantial compliance” with CMS requirements.
Valickis said the behavioral health pod of the emergency department “has been continuously open” and the ICU “is open based on capacity and utilization, with clear protocols in place to respond to the critical needs of patients when they arise.”

The Saint Francis Hospital entryway in Hartford. Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

Saint Francis
Progress at Saint Francis isn’t as far along. Over the last several years, regulators have found quality and safety issues resulting in patient abuse, neglect and death.
In August 2023, staff failed to monitor a patient’s cardiac function in accordance with policy, and, according to a CMS report, “the patient’s change in condition was not identified in a timely manner when the patient was found pulseless and expired.”
The hospital entered into a consent order with the state in September 2024, committing to allow an independent consultant to assess its progress on staffing and safety. That consent order is still in effect, Schaefer confirmed.
But the issues continued, reports show.
In 2026, Saint Francis has received three immediate jeopardy citations — two in February and one in March. In one instance, staff failed to monitor and notify a physician when a patient’s condition worsened. The patient was found “unresponsive, cold to the touch with no palpable pulse.” Physicians attempted resuscitation, but the patient died.
The Department of Public Health entered into another consent order with Saint Francis just last month, which stated that it “remains concerned that prior remediation efforts have not resulted in sustained compliance across all cited areas.”
In recent months, Trinity Health of New England has acknowledged the problems at Saint Francis. In April, the health system replaced its president and CEO with Hanks. Roose was named interim president of Saint Francis Hospital and now serves as president of acute care for the system.
Hanks, who also leads Trinity Health New York, replaced former Trinity Health of New England president and CEO Montez Carter. Roose replaced Valerie Powell-Stafford at Saint Francis.
Both Hanks and Roose are physicians and longtime employees of Trinity Health. The pair signed a full-page ad that appeared in the Hartford Courant on a Sunday in July in which they acknowledged Saint Francis’ lagging performance and pledged to address the problems with safety and quality.
“Transparency requires us to acknowledge a simple truth: we have work to do,” the ad read. “We are not asking anyone to overlook the challenges of the past. We are saying clearly that a new direction is underway, guided by accountability, transparency and an unwavering commitment to excellence.”
During Thursday’s hospital tour, Roose and Hanks told Anwar that they’ve made progress. The system is deploying new capital investment, and over the last couple of months, voluntary turnover has fallen to its lowest level in several years.
Afterwards, Anwar said, there’s still a long way for the hospital to go. But he said he found the transparency from Roose and Hanks reassuring and a marked difference from previous leaders of the hospital system.
“It was a breath of fresh air,” Anwar said. “In the past I heard denials and rationale for [the] things happening.”
Scanlon, too, said he’s encouraged by Trinity’s recent efforts but said the state needs to ensure that momentum continues.
“It’s incumbent on all of us in the state to monitor their progress to make sure they’re actually making progress,” Scanlon said.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Clap during a city meeting in Emporia and you too might be hustled off to jail. Just ask Lux.
description: Lux Claridge isn’t who you’d expect to be busted for disorderly conduct. The 37-year-old high school physics teacher is soft spoken and has quick green eyes beneath a mop of brown hair. Wearing a yellow tee promoting a bicycle festival in northwest Arkansas, a pair of pale blue shorts, and with one blue sock and […]
text:
When high school physics teacher and data center opponent Lux Claridge, 37, was arrested for clapping during a city commission meeting last month, the video of their arrest made national news. Claridge — seen here Aug. 4, 2026, outside the Emporia city offices — was booked into jail on charges of disorderly conduct and interfering with law enforcement. (Photo by Max McCoy/Kansas Reflector)Lux Claridge isn’t who you’d expect to be busted for disorderly conduct. The 37-year-old high school physics teacher is soft spoken and has quick green eyes beneath a mop of brown hair. Wearing a yellow tee promoting a bicycle festival in northwest Arkansas, a pair of pale blue shorts, and with one blue sock and one orange sock stuffed into the tops of new generation Chuck Taylors, they exude a kind of natural calm.
But Claridge is Public Enemy No. 1 to the Emporia City Commission.
Claridge has become the face of data center resistance for my town of Emporia, in east-central Kansas, and much of the nation, because video of their arrest after clapping at a July 22 city commission meeting went hyperscale. Yes, clapping. There were at least three television stations on hand and dozens of smartphones in hand to capture Claridge being hauled by police out of the commission room at city hall, up the steps outside and into the back seat of a police car.
The video was carried by CNN and the arrest was reported in outlets as varied as the New York Post and 404 Media. As Wichita Eagle columnist Dion Lefler dryly noted, “this was not a good look for Emporia.”
But the optics have been painful ever since the data center proposal was unveiled June 2 and the city commission unanimously voted to annex 1,000 acres for the project on the west edge of town the very next day, despite heavy public opposition. Where was the fire? It was coming from inside the station all along. City leaders have been ignoring the public and committing civic arson ever since.
Then there is Gary Pinkston, the Chase County native and West Coast real estate developer who was introduced to the public as the folksy and benevolent developer of the Flint Hills Digital Campus project, but who is entangled in a messy personal and business Chapter 11 bankruptcy.
Pinkston’s credibility was shot when it was revealed he testified in a bankruptcy hearing in June that he had no personal interest in the project. He also swore he did not write “A Message to My Neighbors in the Flint Hills,” a column that identified him as the developer of the project. Pinkston is second in crowd unpopularity only to Garrett Nordstrom, the sharp-dressed Lawrence grant specialist and municipal consultant who has represented the project at various city meetings. Unsurprisingly, much of the Flint Hills Digital Campus website is no longer publicly accessible. It is password protected. Some of the information appears at another site, gosouthwind.com, but Pinkston’s name is absent
It’s been all smoke and mirrors since June 2.
Seven weeks in, the data center has fractured this community of about 25,000 on the edge of the Flint Hills, dividing those who are for it — the pooh-bahs at the local Regional Development Association, Emporia Main Street, and the local Chamber of Commerce — against a diverse swath of the public united in outrage over the secrecy of the project, the environmental effects that accompany data centers, and the existential question of whether data centers are good for humanity. What is happening in Emporia is similar to the push for data centers across rural Kansas, an economic development gold rush threatening to turn thousands of acres into a silicon prairie.
A resistance group, Emporia Neighbors United, has organized protests and mounted petition drives aimed at stopping the data center by resolution or referendum, recalling city commissioners, and seeking to change the structure of city government from a commission to a council. Commissioners are elected at large, Neighbors United founder Jay Vehige told me, which favors the wealthy and the well-connected. With a council, the city would be divided into wards, with some candidates being elected from poor and working-class neighborhoods.
While the petition to recall Commissioner Erren Harter, and another to reform the city government, are still being circulated, a petition asking for an ordinance to ban “high impact data centers” or to put the question to a citywide vote was verified by the county election official on July 21. The petition met the 805-signature threshold, which amounts to 25% of registered voters. The clock began ticking on the city’s 20-day deadline to adopt a resolution banning data centers or put the issue on the Nov. 3 ballot.
I ran into Vehige the other day, outside the city offices. He said he had been trying to visit the city clerk’s office to check on the status of some open records requests he’d filed, but found the outside doors were locked. He said he finally gained entry by going through the water department. The controversy over the data center has city officials so rattled they’re apparently afraid to answer the door.
The Claridge arrest drew national attention to Emporia at a time when anger over data centers has coalesced into a new grassroots political movement. Factions who traditionally disagree on immigration enforcement or gun rights are finding common ground in their opposition to data centers, with concerns ranging from environmental pollution and higher utility rates to what more artificial intelligence may do to us as a society. The opposition also stems from a feeling that we are losing agency in our own lives, that we’re being forced to accept big and faceless tech whether we like it or not, that our decisions are increasingly made for us wholesale.
The question in Emporia isn’t technical. It’s not about Luddites resisting progress, or civic leaders as Ayn Randian visionaries. It’s about who government ultimately serves. It’s about who you can trust.
Despite hours of public testimony at rezoning and other hearings that ran about 6-1 against the data center, city officials have plowed ahead, giving the project green lights at every step of the way.
It is clear they don’t a damn about how the public feels.
Watch the video stream from the July 22 commission meeting in which Claridge was arrested. The audience is warned not to applaud in support of those speaking during the public hearing and then is forbidden from snapping fingers or even silently waving hands. Such behavior was deemed “disruptive.” But Claridge continues to clap, and as their wife, Jessica Danford, approaches the lectern to give her two minutes of comment in opposition, Mayor Becky Smith, apparently prompted by another commissioner, instructs police to remove Claridge.
Claridge tells police they have a right to be there and a right to clap.
“Drag me out,” Claridge says resignedly.
Claridge then goes to the floor. Three police officers, including the chief, carry them out of the room.
The five commissioners look on without a word urging restraint. Harter puts his hands on top of his head, as if signaling internal distress. Smith attempts to calm Danford, telling her it’s “OK.” But the commotion caused by Claridge’s removal is by far the most disruptive thing to happen during the meeting, and it is self-inflicted.
A leader, at this point, might have calmly suggested that Claridge should stay. A leader might have urged compassion over cruel adherence to arbitrary rules. But there were no leaders in that moment. There were only tinpot tyrants who cared more about decorum, which always favors those in power, than the opinions of the public they are elected to serve.
Still waiting to speak, Danford begins to cry.
“Please don’t hurt them,” she pleads.
Then the video stream was paused as the commission took a 10-minute break. Meanwhile, Claridge was booked into the county jail, made to change into an orange jumpsuit, and informed they were facing two charges, of disorderly conduct and interference with law enforcement. They were given a summons with a court date of Sept. 10 and released after Emporia Neighbors United raised $385 for their bond.
When I asked Claridge why they didn’t leave when asked, they said it was improper for the commission to order no clapping in the first place. It was a First Amendment issue, they said. Claridge has retained an attorney and intends to fight the charges.
“The Emporia Police Department remains committed to ensuring public meetings are conducted safely and in an orderly manner,” the city declared in a statement, “while also respecting the rights of all citizens to participate in the civic process.”
Claridge was engaging in the kind of civil disobedience and passive resistance practiced by Henry David Thoreau and Martin Luther King Jr. There was nothing unsafe in what Claridge was doing, and any disorder was the result of overreaction by the commission and police.
On Aug. 5, the city commission met again, but this time the public had less of an opportunity to participate because the meeting was held virtually. The session was live streamed, but no public comment session was allowed. The reason for the virtual meeting, according to a press release, was “public safety.”
The next meeting, set for Aug. 19, also will be held remotely.
“I want everybody to know that these were real threats,” Smith said during the meeting. “Our security was upped. And it’s not necessarily the locals. There are threats from all over the world and all over the country, and all it takes is one. And I want everybody to be safe.”
She said the public comment session was scrubbed because there was no good way to handle it safely. Guess she didn’t know Zoom works both ways. Smith also said the situation had been rough for city staff and police and that the threats were continuing.
“If you don’t believe us, we’ve got a lot we could show you,” she said, “but we try not to give those people too much advertising.”
OK then, show us. Help us understand why you hid from the public during the most important city meeting since just about forever.
Later, the commission took up the issue of the Emporia Neighbors United petition. The city attorney questioned whether the action the petition sought was legislative or administrative in nature. If administrative, which requires specialized knowledge that city staff might possess for zoning or other requests, then it would be invalid. The commission voted unanimously (but of course!) to seek a “declaratory judgment.”
This was framed as impartially sending the matter to a judge to decide, as if the commission were simply asking for an opinion, but that’s not how such actions work. Such judgments are final, not advisory. There must be a dispute to be resolved. The city will go to court to block the petition and odds are that a judge will agree that it’s an administrative issue and that voters just aren’t as qualified as the zoning board and city staff in making decisions.
Cities seek declaratory judgments to avoid being forced to take action by petition. In 2020, Wichita challenged a petition by “Save Century II” that would have forced a binding public vote on the demolition, transfer or replacement of historic buildings owned by the city. A district court judge, and later the Kansas Court of Appeals, voided the petition because it was deemed to ask for administrative action.
Meanwhile, Kanza Park Place LLC, the official applicant for the Flint Hills Digital Campus, is now free to prepare the site and market the proposal to end users. City officials stress that any end user will have to agree to certain “nonnegotiables” yet to be worked out, but it’s clear that in Emporia money talks and the public walks.
I am reminded of historian Howard Zinn’s “A People’s History of the United States.” In the chapter explaining the rise of the robber barons in the last quarter of the 19th Century, Zinn noted the concentration of power and wealth among an elite few. At the top of the power pyramid were J.P. Morgan, of U.S. Steel, and John D. Rockefeller, of Standard Oil.
“Meanwhile, the government of the United States was behaving almost exactly as Karl Marx described a capitalist state: pretending neutrality to maintain order, but serving the interests of the rich. Not that the rich agreed among themselves; they had disputes over policies. But the purpose of the state was to settle upper-class disputes peacefully, control lower-class rebellion, and adopt policies that would further the long-range stability of the system,” he wrote.
What is happening in Emporia during the last seven weeks, and in rural communities across the country, has disrupted the local political system of the kind we haven’t seen in decades. Once small town governments could be relied upon to provide the necessary services of modern life, such as water and sewer and trash collection, schools for our children, and police to keep us safe on the streets. It typically did so with little fuss, through nonpartisan elections in which feelings might get hurt, but which were of little note to the rest of the country.
The existential question of our age, the proliferation of AI by a few tech oligarchs, is being taken up by towns across rural America unprepared to deal with the technical or philosophical questions before them. Add the threat of violence, and the anxiety for all sides becomes acute.
In Emporia, the division between city leaders and the public is now all but complete with the move — albeit temporary — to hold remote meetings. The city has broken no laws, as Kansas allows for remote meetings and doesn’t require a public comment period. The threats might be real, but the timing couldn’t be worse for public trust.
But the city never intended for the public to have a meaningful voice in this anyway. The last seven weeks have been about quashing a grassroots rebellion.
Violence, or threats of violence, must be discouraged. But putting the city into near lockdown and placing a screen between the commission and the public is not the answer. Let’s see some arrests for actual lawbreaking, and not merely for clapping, if the threats are credible. But allow the public to address their commissioners face-to-face, especially when action is being considered that will change the very character of the town.
“There’s a big disparity between we, the people, and the government in power,” Claridge told me. “Everywhere you look, communities are saying: ‘We don’t want this.’ But the government is working pretty hard to make it happen.”
Claridge remains committed to getting answers about the data center, and they intend to be professional about it.
“Being violent doesn’t help,” they said. “Disagreeing with someone is not an excuse for violence, or anything that puts someone in real danger.”
I asked if the socks had any personal or political meaning.
“Life is too short to match socks,” Claridge said.
Max McCoy is an award-winning author and journalist. Through its opinion section, the Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Is it time for CT to tax EVs?
description: Why do electric vehicle drivers pay much less toward the upkeep of our highways even though they contribute to their wear and tear?
text:
Why do electric vehicles get a free ride on our highways?
Why do traditional internal combustion engine car owners pay about 43 cents per gallon in gasoline taxes while EV owners pay nothing… and yet their cars are thought to cause more wear and tear on our highways because they’re so heavy (due to their batteries)?  Is that fair?



Those were the questions posed last spring when the legislature considered a bill to make EV (and hybrid) owners pay their fair share.  But HB 5568 never got out of the Finance, Revenue and Bonding Committee after a single public hearing brought unanimous, vocal opposition:  54 testified against, zero in favor…  not even close.
As of December 2025, there were more than 73,156 electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles registered in Connecticut, a 20% increase over the previous year.  But while those numbers are climbing, EVs and hybrids still represent less than three percent of all vehicles registered in the state.  Still, it seems that you see (but often don’t hear) them all the time, whooshing around almost silently, their drivers wearing that smile of money-saving satisfaction.
If you’re the hypothetical “average driver” in Connecticut and you drive about 12,000 miles a year, you’ll end up paying about $209 a year in gasoline tax.  Drive 15,000 miles and that number jumps to about $250 a year.  And that assumes your car gets about 24.5 mpg.
Those gasoline taxes flow into the Special Transportation Fund  paying for road repairs, the Division of Motor Vehicles, and mass transit that many drivers never ride but benefit from anyway.  (More people taking mass transit = fewer on the roads).
Opponents of a tax on EV’s and hybrids fear it would discourage their adoption, running counter to Connecticut’s state policy of reducing auto emissions.
Connecticut is one of only eight states that don’t tax EVs.  In Pennsylvania the fee is $250 a year for EV owners and $62.50 for plug-in hybrids.  In Vermont it’s $89 and $44.50, respectively.
The Connecticut bill, if it hadn’t died in committee, would have raised registration fees for battery electric vehicles to $345 every three years and for plug-in hybrids to $233 every three years, with standard gasoline vehicles remaining at $120.
Right now EV’s only pay $57 registration fees every three years, further incentivizing their adoption.
Lawmakers (and the Connecticut Department of Transportation) argue that the Special Transportation Fund is in trouble if EV adoption rates continue and gasoline tax revenues continue to fall.
Why did the bill die in committee?  Why didn’t it have the name of any lawmaker(s) as its sponsor?  Because it’s an election year and nobody wanted their fingerprints on a bill that hurts affluent EV drivers… or the environment. “Bad optics,” as they say.
Never mind that CDOT recently replaced new, electric trains on Shore Line East with diesel locomotives belching exhaust as they run between New London and New Haven.  I guess that saying you’re ‘green’ is easier when you ignore the obvious.
We used to think of the necessary reform of our Social Security system as the “third rail of politics.”   Maybe taxing electric vehicles is the same thing?  Or there’s always the idea of tolls.

title: ‘I hear you, I see you:’ Alabama Democrats elect Bobby Singleton as chair
description: Alabama Democrats on Saturday elected Senate Minority Leader Bobby Singleton party chair amid calls for the organization to take advantage of the most promising electoral landscape for state Democrats in years. Singleton got 165 votes (72.7%) over current Chair Randy Kelley, who got 62 votes (27.3%) in a vote in which the 200-plus members of […]
text:
Senate Minority Leader Bobby Singleton, D-Greensboro, watches as votes are counted during an election for Alabama Democratic Party chair at the Alabama State Democratic Executive Committee's on Saturday, Aug. 8, 2026 in Montgomery, Ala. Singleton won with 73% of the votes from about 220 SDEC members. (Stew Milne for Alabama Reflector)Alabama Democrats on Saturday elected Senate Minority Leader Bobby Singleton party chair amid calls for the organization to take advantage of the most promising electoral landscape for state Democrats in years.
Singleton got 165 votes (72.7%) over current Chair Randy Kelley, who got 62 votes (27.3%) in a vote in which the 200-plus members of the State Democratic Executive (SDEC) voted by holding up pieces of paper with “vote” printed on them while other members walked around to count. 
“I want you to know that I hear you, I see you,” Singleton said in a two-minute speech prior to the vote. “We need to make sure that we realize and listen to people. I’m gonna hold listening tours across all 67 counties because I want you to know: Women, I see you and I hear you. I want the LGBTQ to know that I hear you and I see you. We can no longer sit back and do things in an archaic way.”
The vote, coming amid a potentially promising year for the party, ended a tumultuous tenure for Alabama Democratic Party Chair Randy Kelley, an ally of Joe Reed, the vice chair for minority affairs for the party and a major force among state Democrats. In 2023, the SDEC passed bylaws that eliminated youth, LGBTQ+ and disabled caucuses and reduced the powers of affirmative action; Asian and Pacific Islander; Hispanic; and Native American caucuses “to monitor the affairs of the groups listed.” Most of the minority caucuses were restored in 2024 by order of the Democratic National Committee (DNC). 
The change in leadership also followed weeks of online discourse that ranged from complaints of a lack of election education to accusations of illegal campaign finance practices from former candidates. House Minority Leader Anthony Daniels, D-Huntsville, who nominated Singleton, said the party needed a chair that could raise money.
“This is no indictment on anyone, anywhere, because as we leave here today we have to be united no matter what and put our differences to the side as we move forward,” Daniels said. “We cannot let any election go unchallenged on the other side.”
Alabama Senate Minority Leader Bobby Singleton, D-Greensboro, hugs former Alabama Democratic Party Chair Randy Kelley after winning election as party chair at the Alabama State Democratic Executive Committee’s meeting on Saturday, Aug. 8, 2026 in Montgomery, Ala. (Stew Milne for Alabama Reflector)
Singleton said in an interview after the election that the change within the party demonstrates frustrations members, candidates and legislators have felt with party leadership.
“I know I was getting frustrated as a member of the legislature when I looked around, and we’re in the middle of battles. There was never the Democratic Party that supported us. I saw the Republican Party support their people,” he said. “I want to bring that same kind of energy and say that we’re at the table.”
Kelley touted the party’s progress during his first term in his opening statement, but said the party needs to expand its reach to churches. 
“If we realized how we had the Civil Rights Act, the Voting Rights Act, the Bus Boycott victory of Montgomery, Fair Housing Act, much of that came by social-conscious pastors, Black people and white folks of goodwill, and we’re all beneficiaries of it,” Kelley said. “We’re going to have to activate the churches if we even expect to win.”
He also mentioned the flipping of a Huntsville-area House seat by Rep. Marilyn Lands in a 2024 special election, and the election of U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Mobile, in 2024, during the chairman’s report. 
As soon as SDEC members raised their vote cards for Singleton, his voters and other non-voting Democrats in attendance cheered for the lawmaker. 
In Kelley’s chairman’s report he said the party should be united and shift away from toxicity.
“Together, we can make a better future for our children. Together, we can transform Alabama,” Kelley said. 
Singleton said he has a 90-day plan, but did not have time to go over it during his allotted time. He promised to visit Alabama’s 67 counties and bring government as close to the people as possible.
“We’re going to unite as one party, one future, and we will do it right here together. And in November, we’re going to win,” Singleton said.
Singleton said in an interview after the election that his 90-day plan includes visiting every county before the general election, which is in 87 days, fundraising events and supporting county chairs and candidates. 
“It’s robust, and there’s only 87 days until the election, and I’m talking about 90 days, but it goes beyond that,” Singleton said. “I’m really talking about the core of this party and how we’re gonna have to rebuild the core of this party, being able to be attentive and allow people to have a voice.”
He also plans to release a 90-Day Progress Report that includes three stages: listen, build and mobilize. He does not plan to step down as Minority Leader.
Singleton nominated Caroline Self, an elected member of SDEC in House District 2, who won by 139 votes (66.5%) over Tori Bailey, an elected member of the SDEC from House District 3.
“I want to work to win. We have opportunities this year that we have not seen since I was a child. I get out every day and I work countless hours because we can win in November,” Self said.
Doug Jones and Rep. Philip Ensler of Montgomery, the party’s nominees for governor and lieutenant governor, lingered at the meeting but did not speak.
The meeting had a slow start, with approval of November’s meeting minutes taking over an hour. Stan Glasscox, an elected SDEC member from House District 63, left the meeting briefly and returned with two bottles of beer for himself and Amber Buck, an SDEC representative from Tuscaloosa.
Stan Glasscox gestures to the audience as he is asked to leave for drinking alcohol during a meeting of the Alabama State Democratic Executive Committee hearing on Saturday, Aug. 8, 2026 in Montgomery, Ala. (Stew Milne for Alabama Reflector)
He was asked to leave the voting area of the meeting. He handed off one beverage to a guest, stood on the side of the guest area to finish his beverage and returned to vote. 
“Whether you’re black, white, straight, or gay, whatever your pronoun may be, whether you’re young or old, I want this party to be one Democrat,” Singleton said in an interview. “That’s all we want to do, is focus on being a Democrat so we can win in November.”
Although Democrats have the largest slate of candidates since 2018 and had increased primary turnout, they remain underdogs statewide. There are a few competitive legislative seats the party hopes to flip in November.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: UP Academy Holland’s turnaround success offers a nuanced lesson on receivership
description: If the goal is to improve outcomes for students attending chronically underperforming schools, the most important question is not whether receivership succeeded everywhere. It is whether it succeeded anywhere, and if so, why.
text:
THE MASSACHUSETTS Board of Elementary and Secondary Education recently voted to end state receivership of UP Academy Holland and return the school’s operation to Boston Public Schools. It was a significant moment for a school that, just over a decade ago, was among the lowest performing in the state. 
The vote should also prompt a broader conversation. 
For the past several years, the dominant narrative surrounding state receivership in Massachusetts has been that it did not work. There is evidence to support that view. Several state takeovers produced mixed results, and the outcomes often fell short of the ambitious promises that accompanied them. 
But if the goal is to improve outcomes for students attending chronically underperforming schools, the most important question is not whether receivership succeeded everywhere. It is whether it succeeded anywhere, and if so, why. 
UP Academy Holland, soon to return to its original name, John P. Holland Elementary School, deserves to be part of that conversation. 
When the school entered receivership, it ranked in the bottom 1 percent of public schools statewide. Today, it is one of the strongest-performing schools in Boston. It ranks second among Dorchester schools in English language arts growth and is among the top-performing Boston Public Schools in ELA and math growth overall. Third-grade students outperform district and state averages in math proficiency among comparable high-needs schools, and multilingual learners exceed district and state peers on ACCESS growth measures. 
Most importantly, the school is now positioned to return to district governance while preserving the systems, culture, and instructional practices that drove its improvement. 
That outcome matters. 
BPS still has more than 40 schools performing in the bottom decile statewide, although the district is implementing numerous strategies to improve performance. Across Massachusetts, educators and policymakers continue to wrestle with the challenge of helping chronically underperforming schools improve. Holland demonstrates that meaningful transformation is possible. The question is why. 
I have spent much of my career at Holland, first as a member of the founding leadership team, then as principal, later supporting the development of school leaders, and now as CEO of UP Education Network, the organization that partnered with BPS to manage the school during receivership. 
No single curriculum, training, or intervention transformed Holland. The theory of change was more fundamental, and frankly, isn’t glamorous nor particularly innovative: create clarity about excellence, build systems aligned to that vision, and develop the capacity of leaders to improve teacher practice through sustained coaching and feedback. We were steadfast in our belief in the power of these elements, and over time, those elements did in fact reinforce one another and produced improvement that could last beyond any one leader or organization.  
Looking back, three broader lessons stand out. 
First, school transformation takes time. 
One of the challenges in education policy is that improvement timelines are often measured in election cycles, contract terms, or leadership tenures. School transformation rarely operates on those timelines. 
Holland made significant gains early in its turnaround, but lasting improvement required years of refining and strengthening the practices behind those results. It required building the capacity of leaders and teachers, responding to new challenges, and sustaining a culture of improvement through leadership transitions, changing circumstances, and even a global pandemic. With stability, persistence, and a willingness to stay the course, these systems have thrived at Holland. 
Second, successful turnarounds require true partnership. 
Too often, conversations about receivership frame districts and external operators as competing interests. In practice, successful school improvement depends on the opposite. 
Throughout Holland’s transformation, BPS and UP maintained a shared commitment to the same outcome: ensuring students had access to an excellent school. That partnership required trust, flexibility, and an understanding that improvement efforts were being carried out on behalf of the district, not in opposition to it. 
The transition now underway reflects that same spirit. District leaders, union leaders, state officials, school leaders, and UP have spent the past year working together to identify what must be preserved for the school to continue thriving and maintain student outcomes. 
Third, and perhaps most importantly, struggling schools need the right partner. 
Not every organization is equipped to lead school transformation, which requires far more than good intentions. It requires the ability to establish a clear vision, translate that vision into coherent systems, develop strong leaders, and support educators through years of challenging work. It also requires the discipline to execute those practices consistently and the willingness to keep learning when something is not working. 
It requires humility as well. The most effective partners recognize that success is not measured by how long they remain in control. It is measured by whether the school can thrive after they leave. 
At Holland, the goal was never to create a permanent alternative to district leadership. The goal was to build a school strong enough to succeed within BPS. 
As Holland returns to district governance, that work is not ending. Through ongoing collaboration, both organizations are committed to ensuring continuity for students, families, and staff. Improvement is not sustained through abrupt transitions. It is sustained through thoughtful ones. 
The lesson of Holland is not that receivership is the answer to every struggling school. Nor is it an argument for a return to broad state takeovers. 
The lesson is that school transformation is possible. 
Massachusetts remains a national leader in education, but statewide success can obscure the reality facing students in schools that have struggled for years to deliver the outcomes they deserve. 
As the state formally closes the chapter on Holland’s receivership, we should resist the temptation to view the story solely through the lens of a broader debate about state intervention. Instead, we should study it carefully. 
Because if we are serious about improving outcomes for students in chronically underperforming schools, our responsibility is not to replicate a governance model. It is to study and replicate the practices that make lasting improvement possible. 
Holland offers one example. Students and families demand that we learn from it. 
Hillary Casson is the Chief Executive Officer of UP Education Network.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Montana Dem lawmakers call for Bankhead to drop out of U.S. Senate race
description: Twenty-two Democratic members of the Montana Legislature are officially asking Alani Bankhead, the Democratic nominee for the U.S. Senate race, to drop out and support the independent in the race, Seth Bodnar. In a letter dated Aug. 7, seven senators and 15 house members say they are “united in believing that Seth Bodnar is the […]
text:
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Alani Bankhead speaks during a Lewis and Clark County Democratic watch party for the primary at the Rialto in Helena, Montana, on Tuesday, June 2, 2026. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)Twenty-two Democratic members of the Montana Legislature are officially asking Alani Bankhead, the Democratic nominee for the U.S. Senate race, to drop out and support the independent in the race, Seth Bodnar.
In a letter dated Aug. 7, seven senators and 15 house members say they are “united in believing that Seth Bodnar is the candidate who shares our Democratic values and has the experience, knowledge, resources and capacity” to take on Republican Kurt Alme.
The letter was first reported by CNN’s Patrick Svitek.
A month ago, 17 lawmakers wrote a letter to both Bankhead and Bodnar, asking them to meet and discuss a way to unite voters against Alme. That letter did not explicitly ask either candidate to drop out, but highlighted that Bodnar appeared better positioned at the time to run the strongest general election campaign.
On Friday, Bodnar held a press conference assuring his supporters he would not drop out of the race, regardless of whom else was in it.
Bankhead told the Daily Montanan she is also committed to staying the course.
In their letter, the lawmakers argue the most important consideration for the U.S. Senate election is to elect someone “who will oppose the destructive policies of the Trump Administration, while advancing an agenda that benefits all Montanan.”
“It is this concern for our constituents, the direction of our country and our American Democracy that motivates our support for Seth at this time,” they wrote. “…A prolonged three-way contest — and the resulting divisions among voters, volunteers, donors, allied organizations and candidates — will weaken Democratic and allied campaigns across the ballot.”
The signatories represent more than a third of all elected Democrats in Montana.
Four representatives — Mike Fox, Shelly Fyant, Jennifer Lynch, Luke Muszkiewicz — signed the first letter asking the two candidates to discuss options, but not the latest one.
In reliably Republican states across the country, Democratic candidates dropping out of U.S. Senate races has become a trend, giving independent candidates a clearer path to head-to-head matchups with Republicans.
In recent polling, Bodnar has shown strength in a face-off with Alme, but the Republican easily wins a crowded field.
The idea is modeled on Dan Osborn in Nebraska, who ran as an independent in 2024 against a Republican incumbent without a Democrat in the field — coming within seven points of winning even as Trump carried the state by 21 points. Osborn is running again in 2026 and the state Democratic Party has supported not fielding a candidate.
Democratic candidates in Idaho, Alaska, and South Dakota have all dropped out of their respective races this cycle.
A Montana Democratic Party spokesperson told the Daily Montanan this week that the party supports Bankhead as the winner of the primary.
Bankhead won the Democratic primary by 12,000 votes more than her closest competitor, and was buoyed by more than $2.5 million in outside spending on her behalf.
As a general election candidate, she has failed to gain endorsements from traditionally left-aligned organizations and the state’s biggest Democratic players while fundraising just $60,000.
Meanwhile Bodnar outraised all federal candidates in each reporting period and has stacked up support from unions, environmental and veterans organizations, and former elected officials from both parties, including former Democratic U.S. Senators Jon Tester and Max Baucus, and former Republican Gov. Marc Racicot.
If Bankhead did drop out of the race, it is likely to spark a legal battle over whether the Montana Democratic Party is required in state law to name a replacement.
A group of Democratic lawyers wrote a memo to the state party last month laying out the legal framework behind not choosing a new candidate.
On the other side, Republicans, including Alme’s campaign, circulated a memo written by the state’s former solicitor general, arguing why Democrats would be required to name a successor.
The deadline to withdraw from November’s ballot is Monday at 5 p.m.
