New Mexico First Judicial District Judge Bryan Biedscheid late Thursday issued a 68-page rul[...]
text:
New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez on Friday lauded this week’s $567 million judgment against Meta Platforms Inc. as “historic” and wide-ranging, but also railed against decades-old laws that he said continue to limit his office’s ability to protect kids online.New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez on Friday lauded this week’s $567 million judgment against Meta Platforms Inc. as “historic” and wide-ranging, but also railed against decades-old laws that he said continue to limit his office’s ability to protect kids online.
New Mexico First Judicial District Judge Bryan Biedscheid late Thursday issued a 68-page ruling that ordered the social media giant to pay for an abatement fund to address the harms it has caused to the state’s youth through its online platforms, particularly Instagram. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In ordering the fund’s creation, Biedscheid agreed with plaintiffs that Meta was creating a “public nuisance” in the state by creating addictive algorithms and an online environment that facilitated connections between kids and child predators. Of the $567 million the judge ordered Meta to pay, $420 million is designated for “treatment” of harms the platform caused. 
A Meta spokesperson told Source NM that the company would appeal the ruling. Torrez said Friday that the appeal process could take “months, if not years” to play out. The attorney general said he will urge Biedscheid to order the company to pay the judgment while litigation resumes regarding other changes the judge ordered the company to make. 
The ruling marks the end of the second closely watched trial New Mexico brought against Meta. In March, a jury ordered Meta to pay $375 million after agreeing with Torrez’s office that the company had violated state consumer protection laws. 
Torrez, in a news conference Friday, said the combined $942 million in judgments against Meta should send a message to the world that “companies of this size and scale can actually be held accountable.”
But he also said laws his office sued under are woefully outdated in confronting the modern internet and a 2026 economy that is largely shaped by giant tech companies. For example, the state’s consumer protection act has not been updated since 1970, he said.
“Why does that matter? It matters because that statute was built for a totally different world,” he said. “It was built for a totally different economy, and it didn’t conceive of or understand or anticipate companies of this size and scale, or the business practices that they engage in.”
New Mexico Department of Justice rests case in second phase of Meta child safety lawsuit

Other laws that Torrez cited as antiquated include Section 230, a provision in a 1996 federal law that protects companies like Meta from being liable for content their users publish on their platforms and a 1998 law that prohibits platforms from collecting data on children under age 13 without their parents’ permission. 
The judge repeatedly cited Section 230 and the First Amendment as reasons he could not order Meta to make changes to its algorithm, as well as rein in potentially addictive features like “infinite scroll” and videos automatically playing when they arrive in users’ feeds. 
The judge also said the Child’s Online Privacy Act of 1998 — another law Torrez said was outdated — meant he could not legally order Meta to impose stricter age verification for young children seeking to use the platforms. 
The state’s lawsuit had urged the court to order Meta to greatly strengthen the steps it takes to verify users’ ages, including with the help of artificial intelligence and other tools. Biedscheid ruled that the state’s hopes rested on “unproven technology” and, if implemented, would unfairly disadvantage Meta versus other similar social media companies. 
Because of the 1998 law, he wrote, “It is the Court’s conclusion that it cannot order Meta to request children to submit personal data or be passively tracked online, even for age-verification purposes.”
Biedscheid further wrote that it is beyond his court’s jurisdiction to impose the age-verification requirements, writing that  “regulatory solutions to these problems lie in the executive and legislative branches and not with this Court.”
While Torrez said he believes the judge’s ruling on the matter was a “misapplication” of federal law, he agreed that the next steps required to protect children online lie outside of the courts.
The ruling marks “an opportunity to rely on and incorporate rapidly advancing and evolving technology into a proposed legislative solution, which my office will be presenting to the New Mexico Legislature in the coming weeks,” Torrez said. 
He also called on Congress to heed what he said is growing discontentment from social media users about the outsized role companies like Meta play in influencing policy and daily life. 
“If Congress woke up and did its job and passed and updated a refreshed version based on the world we live in now and not the world we had in the 1990s, we could address these issues,” he said. “We can’t address them as long as Congress and legislative bodies are sitting on the sidelines.”



In addition to imposing financial penalties, Biedscheid’s ruling ordered Meta to make some of the following changes to its platforms:

Impose stronger safeguards for minors and tougher enforcement against predatory adult accounts
Prevent minors from sending or receiving nude images that violate Meta’s policies
Eliminate push notifications for users under 18 during overnight hours and during schooldays 
Hide publicly visible counts showing how many users “liked” or “hearted” a particular young user’s post
Impose mandatory time-use limits for users under 18 of no more than 90 hours a month
Post monthly, prominent disclosures to New Mexico users about the risks associated with Meta’s platforms
Fund a statewide education and public awareness campaign in New Mexico
Provide specialized training and resources for local law enforcement investigating internet crimes against children
File semiannual public compliance reports with the court documenting its progress implementing every aspect of the order

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Judge declines to force Nebraska Democratic Party to replace former Senate candidate Burbank
description: A Lancaster County district judge declined to grant William Forbes a temporary injunction to force the Nebraska Democratic Party to replace U.S. Senate nominee Cindy Burbank after she dropped out of the race.
text:
Lancaster County District Judge Susan Strong listens as evidence is presented on the first day of the civil trial to determine the validity of the medical marijuana ballot measures at the Lancaster County Courthouse on Tuesday, Oct. 29, 2024, in Lincoln. (Kenneth Ferriera-Pool/Lincoln Journal Star)LINCOLN — A Lancaster County district judge declined to grant William Forbes a temporary injunction to force the Nebraska Democratic Party to replace U.S. Senate nominee Cindy Burbank after she dropped out of the race. 
In her ruling, Lancaster County District Court Judge Susan Strong said that Forbes’ arguments would raise “serious constitutional concerns” and that he was unlikely to succeed in forcing the party to replace Burbank. 
“The court is not convinced by Forbes’s counterargument, at least not yet. While the word ‘may’ can be used to express options or possibilities, the presumption under Nebraska law is that it expresses permissive or discretionary action,” Strong wrote. 
Nebraska Public Media reported on the ruling first. Forbes lost to Burbank in the Democratic Senate primary.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In his lawsuit, Forbes cited a state law that reads: “If a vacancy on the ballot arises for any partisan office except President and Vice President of the United States before a general election, the vacancy shall be filled by the majority vote of the proper committee of the same political party.”

His attorneys argued earlier this week that the law’s language requires a replacement. Nebraska Democrats said Forbes is misreading state law because the statute he cited addresses the process that must be followed if a party chooses to replace a nominee, whereas the law about a candidate declining the nomination says the party “may” replace the person and then points to the statute Williams is citing. 
Strong seems so far to agree with the party’s interpretation of the laws.
Williams’ attorneys have asked the court for an “expedited case progression order” — basically asking to speed up the legal process. Strong, in a different order, wrote that she will issue such an order “based on the parties’ written submissions.” 
This is just the latest drama in the Nebraska U.S. Senate race. In the Democratic primary, allegations were made that each candidate was a “plant” to help either incumbent Sen. Pete Ricketts or nonpartisan candidate Dan Osborn. Both Ricketts and Osborn have denied any involvement with Forbes or Burbank. 
Nebraska Democratic Party leaders have said that they will take the case to the state Supreme Court if the ruling doesn’t go their way.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri AG bars St. Louis company from kratom sales as federal 7-OH ban looms
description: An agreement with Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway will bar the owners of St. Louis-based Green Dragon from selling kratom products in the state, the latest development in her office’s crackdown on 7-OH and related substances. Under the agreement announced Thursday, Green Dragon and owners David and Matthew Jadwin cannot own, operate or hold a […]
text:
Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway announces the state's lawsuit against American Shaman in a press conference outside her office March 31, 2026 (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).An agreement with Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway will bar the owners of St. Louis-based Green Dragon from selling kratom products in the state, the latest development in her office’s crackdown on 7-OH and related substances.
Under the agreement announced Thursday, Green Dragon and owners David and Matthew Jadwin cannot own, operate or hold a financial interest in a Missouri business that markets, advertises or sells 7-OH or other kratom products to consumers or distributors.
The company must also remove the products from its Missouri stores and stop selling, distributing or advertising them in the state.
The Independent was unable to reach the Jadwins for comment.
7-OH, short for 7-hydroxymitragynine, is an opioid-like compound found naturally in trace amounts in kratom. Concentrated products containing much higher levels of the compound are commonly manufactured by chemically converting mitragynine, another kratom alkaloid.
The products are sold as gummies, liquid shots, tablets, powders and other forms in smoke shops, gas stations, convenience stores and online.
The agreement is similar to those Hanaway has made with other 7-OH distributors, including Kansas-City based companies American Shaman and Relax Relief Rejuvenate Trading LLC. 
“These unregulated, highly addictive drugs have taken lives and fueled addiction across our state. This resolution is another decisive step to protect Missouri families from the deadly impact of gas‑station opioids,” Hanaway said in a press release. “Our office will continue pursuing any distributor or retailer that puts Missourians in jeopardy.”
The Green Dragon agreement goes further than some of Hanaway’s previous settlements because it restricts the owners from having a financial interest in businesses selling kratom products in Missouri.
It comes as federal officials are moving toward temporarily placing concentrated 7-OH and three related substances in Schedule I of the Controlled Substances Act.
The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration announced July 1 that it intends to temporarily schedule 7-OH above specified concentration thresholds, along with mitragynine pseudoindoxyl, MGM-15 and MGM-16. The action would not apply to natural kratom containing only trace amounts of 7-OH.
Schedule I is the federal government’s most restrictive category for controlled substances and includes heroin.
The DEA proposal would generally cover processed or synthetic products containing more than 0.05% 7-OH or more than 1 milligram of the compound per article, along with botanical kratom containing more than 0.05% 7-OH by dry weight.
The Department of Health and Human Services separately sought public comment on the proposed threshold, with the comment period ending July 31. The more than 11,000 comments are to be provided to federal officials for consideration before the temporary scheduling order is issued.
The DEA was required to wait at least 30 days after publication of its July notices before issuing the order. The agency said it intended to act “as soon as possible” after that period expired. The temporary designation would last two years and could be extended for another year while federal officials consider permanent scheduling.
It is unclear when the DEA will issue the order.
The federal effort has also become entangled in a new congressional inquiry into the kratom industry’s ties to the Trump administration.
The U.S. Senate Committee on Finance’s ranking member, Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., has called for an investigation into an alleged conflict of interest related to Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin’s advocacy for restrictions on 7-OH. Wyden is requiring information be provided to the committee by the end of the month, related to Mullin allegedly holding a financial stake in Oklahoma-based Botanic Tonics — a competitor of 7-OH products — reportedly worth as much as $1 million.
If the DEA issues its temporary scheduling order, Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services spokeswoman Lisa Cox said the state would then file an emergency rule reflecting the order that would be effective in less than 10 days.
Hanaway applauded the proposed federal restrictions, saying Thursday that 7-OH products are “synthetic, addictive opioids that carry grave risks.” 
Her office has meanwhile pursued the products under existing Missouri consumer protection laws. 
Under the Green Dragon agreement, the company must remove the products subject to the agreement from its Missouri retail premises, and cease sales, distribution, offering, transfer, delivery, marketing and advertising to any consumer or distributor located in the State of Missouri. 
Additionally, Green Dragon agreed not to sell any dietary supplement without first obtaining a scientific analysis of its active ingredients to ensure that consumers are not exposed to dangerous substances like 7-OH without their knowledge.
The Green Dragon agreement, filed in Cole County Circuit Court as an assurance of voluntary compliance, ends the attorney general’s investigation of the company, which began in November. It does not include an admission of liability, and no court found Green Dragon or its owners liable.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Another 2 Utah Supreme Court seats need to be filled. Here’s who made the list
description: The Appellate Judicial Nominating Commission has selected 12 nominees — three women and nine men — that Utah Gov. Spencer Cox may choose from when deciding how to fill two vacancies on the newly expanded Utah Supreme Court.  The two open seats on the state’s highest court result from the sudden resignation of Justice Diana […]
text:
The entrance to the historic Supreme Court chambers in the Capitol in Salt Lake City is pictured on Wednesday, June 17, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)The Appellate Judicial Nominating Commission has selected 12 nominees — three women and nine men — that Utah Gov. Spencer Cox may choose from when deciding how to fill two vacancies on the newly expanded Utah Supreme Court. 
The two open seats on the state’s highest court result from the sudden resignation of Justice Diana Hagen in May and the upcoming retirement of longtime Chief Justice Matthew Durrant at the end of this month. 
Hagen’s resignation came after the Utah House, in response to a public records request from KSL, released a previously dismissed complaint alleging she had an extramarital affair with an attorney involved in the state’s redistricting case. The Judicial Conduct Commission dismissed the complaint as lacking evidence and credibility, but Cox and Utah’s top Republican legislative leaders called for an independent investigation into the claims. 
Amid affair allegations, Utah Supreme Court Justice Diana Hagen resigns

Hagen denied the allegations, but said in her resignation letter she decided to leave the Utah Supreme Court because she didn’t want her friends and family to be dragged into a public controversy. Had she not resigned, Hagen would have been up for a retention election this November. 
The latest list of nominees Cox will choose from to replace Hagen and Durrant comes during a time of extraordinary turnover and expansion of the Utah Supreme Court. Just two months ago, the governor filled two new seats on the Utah Supreme Court, after the Utah Legislature expanded it from five to seven members earlier this year. 
The Utah Senate confirmed his appointments of Stephen Dent, a federal prosecutor, and Jay Jorgensen — who most recently worked as an attorney for the state’s predominant faith, The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints — in June. 
Unlike the last list of all-male nominees for those two new seats (which drew some criticism), this time the Appellate Judicial Nominating Commission’s pool of candidates include three women. The list also includes three Utah Court of Appeals judges. 
Gov. Cox says his Utah Supreme Court picks were the most qualified. Critics disagree

Cox, in a June news conference, pushed back on criticisms that not enough women were being considered for the Utah Supreme Court, calling that an “insane narrative” while pointing out he appointed both current Associate Chief Justice Jill Pohlman and Hagen in 2022. 
“I don’t go into this looking at your chromosomes when I’m making an appointment,” Cox said at the time. “I’m trying to find the best legal minds who will represent the state of Utah. And I think that’s all that should matter.” 
Cox’s selections — subject to confirmation by the Utah Senate in coming weeks — could change the dynamics of the Utah Supreme Court, which up until recently was made up of a majority of women. Now, however, with Hagen gone and two new seats filled by Dent and Jorgensen, the scales have tipped — and could tip further depending on Cox’s upcoming picks. 
Pohlman and Justice Paige Petersen are currently outnumbered by men. Cox also appointed Justice John Nielsen in October to replace former Associate Chief Justice John Pearce who retired last June. 
The nominees to replace Hagen and Durrant are:

Cherise Bacalski, attorney and founder of The Appellate Group, a firm that specializes in appellate cases, and an adjunct professor of writing for Brigham Young University’s J. Reuben Clark Law School. 
Christopher Ballard, general counsel and chief of staff of the Utah County Attorney’s Office. 
Christopher Bates, shareholder of the law firm Kirton McConkie.
Matthew Bates, 3rd District Court judge, currently serving Salt Lake, Summit and Tooele counties. 
Matthew Bell, 5th District Court judge, currently serving Beaver, Iron and Washington counties 
Samuel Chiara, 8th District Court judge, currently serving in Daggett, Duchesne and Uintah counties. 
Michele Christiansen Forster, a Utah Court of Appeals judge. 
William Hains, deputy division director of criminal appeals in the Utah Attorney General’s Office.
Michael Menssen, a partner of the international law firm Mayer Brown. 
Amy Oliver, a Utah Court of Appeals judge. 
Stanford Purser, solicitor general in the Utah Attorney General’s Office.  
Ryan Tenney, a Utah Court of Appeals judge.


SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Utahns can weigh in on the list of nominees by submitting written comments to the Appellate Judicial Nominating Commission at judicialvacancies@utah.gov or by sending letters to the Commission on Criminal and Juvenile Justice, P.O. Box 142330, Salt Lake City, UT 84114-2330. 
The deadline for written comments is noon on Aug. 16. The Nominating Commission could request further information or conduct an investigation of the nominees after reviewing public comments.  
After the public comment period, the list of names will be sent to the governor, who will then have 30 days to choose appointees for each vacancy. Both will also be subject to confirmation by the Utah Senate.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Take two on RI cannabis licenses: Regulators restart application process
description: Rhode Island’s Cannabis Control Commission on Friday reopened the application process for prospective retailers after regulators’ first attempt to license more pot shops was halted by a federal court order and voided under a new state law. Gov. Dan McKee on June 10 signed a pair of bills that undo a provision in the original […]
text:
Buds of cannabis on display inside Mother Earth Wellness in Pawtucket, one of nine retailers licensed to sell recreational pot in Rhode Island. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)Rhode Island’s Cannabis Control Commission on Friday reopened the application process for prospective retailers after regulators’ first attempt to license more pot shops was halted by a federal court order and voided under a new state law.
Gov. Dan McKee on June 10 signed a pair of bills that undo a provision in the original 2022 Rhode Island Cannabis Act that required cannabis retailers be majority-owned by Rhode Island residents, along with kickstarting a new application process within 60 days. 
Federal judge poised to dissolve injunction that halted RI’s cannabis retail licenses

They’re changes the state made in order to resolve the trio of federal lawsuits that led to U.S. District Court Judge Melissa DuBose blocking the Cannabis Control Commission from holding the lottery it was planning to hold in May to award licenses.
DuBose also stopped regulators from continuing to screen and review any of the 97 retail license applications submitted by the original Dec. 29, 2025, deadline. 
“Our focus is to maintain that momentum by implementing the amended Cannabis Act as efficiently as possible,” Michelle Reddish, chairperson of the three-member regulatory panel, said in a statement Thursday.
Online submissions for the state’s three license types will be accepted through Monday, Nov. 23. Prospective retailers seeking a social equity license, reserved for those adversely affected by the war on drugs, must first receive certification by Sept. 11. 
The commission’s announcement did not include a timeline for regulators to review applicants nor say when licenses would be awarded.
The revised law requires social equity businesses to be majority owned by one or more people who can show they were disproportionately impacted by criminal enforcement of past prohibitions, including being arrested or having a family member who was.
Under the 2022 act that legalized recreational cannabis, the commission can offer 24 new licenses to retailers, with six reserved for social equity applicants and another six reserved for worker-owned cooperatives. But not every license type received an application in each of the six geographic zones during the first go, which left regulators with a maximum of 20 licenses to issue across the state.
As it stands, nine shops are selling recreational cannabis in Rhode Island under hybrid retail-medicinal licenses grandfathered in from the state’s medical marijuana program.
The halt in the state’s first application pool left many would-be business owners continuing to pay rent on storefronts they may not even be able to open. Though they can’t recoup their property costs, the new state law allows those initial applicants to be refunded any fees paid to the commission. 
All prospective retailers were required to pay an application fee of $7,500 and a yearly $30,000 licensing fee. Fees were waived for the first year for approved social equity applicants.
Over half of all applicants — 56 — sought general retail licenses. Another 19 were worker cooperatives while the remaining 23 were for social equity applicants.
Charon Rose, spokesperson for the Cannabis Control Commission, said in an email Friday that refund checks are expected to be issued on a rolling basis beginning next week. She did not state how many of the 75 applicants who paid the original application fee sought refunds.

outlet: News From The States - Fair. Fearless. Free.
title: US Senate confirms FEMA administrator alongside dozens of nominees
text: WASHINGTON — The U.S. Senate on Friday approved Cameron Hamilton to lead the Federal Emergency Management Agency, giving the agency its first administrator since President Donald Trump took office last year. The 51-47 vote confirmed more than 70 nominees as part of one package, including the administrator of the Transportation Security Administration, chairman of the Council of Economic Advisers and the director of the Indian Health Service. The rest of the batch contained a mix of deputy directors, under secretaries, assistant secretaries, ambassadors, U.S. attorneys and judges.Hamilton’s confirmation vote follows a bit of a rollercoaster for him at FEMA. He ran the agency in an acting capacity for the first few months of 2025 before being fired after testifying to Congress that he personally did “not believe it is in the best interest of the American people to eliminate the Federal Emergency Management Agency.”He then spent several months working as a senior adviser in the Education Department before being hired as the senior vice president of response and recovery at LTS, Inc., a consulting firm in Virginia. He stayed there until April, when he became a senior adviser/senior counselor at the Department of Homeland Security. ‘Fair and reasonable’Trump formally nominated Hamilton as his pick for FEMA administrator in May without the hype he’s doled out for some of his other picks.  Hamilton testified before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee in June that if confirmed to run the agency he wouldn’t provide more resources to Republican regions of the country over Americans who vote for Democrats. “What I can tell you is that if confirmed, my focus will be to ensure that FEMA is objective, is fair and reasonable, follows the law, and is consistent in the approach to how we adjudicate and process claims and requests for disasters,” he said. Shifting responsibilities to statesDuring his time away from the federal government, Hamilton spoke about his experiences running FEMA in an acting role on an episode of the “Disaster Tough” podcast released in September.“I was not hired to abolish FEMA. That was never a part of the conversation and that’s never something that I would have agreed with,” he said at the time. “And I was very clear, I wanted some reform. I wanted to cut wasteful spending. I wanted to downsize the agency. There's no denying that. And I think most of those things could be done wisely and properly.”Any offloading of responsibilities from the federal government to states, he said, would include “a gradual phasing out.”“We needed to give the states some time to see what that entails and to respond accordingly,” he said on the podcast. “Not just, 'Hey, the water is now shut off. You're on your own.' That's not wise. That's not being a good partner.”Trump has spoken throughout his second administration about shifting some of the responsibility for natural disaster preparedness and response to state governments. “We want to wean off of FEMA and we want to bring it down to the state level,” Trump said in June 2025. “We're moving it back to the states so the governors can handle it. That's why they're governors. Now, if they can't handle it, they shouldn't be governor.”Trump established a FEMA Review Council to propose changes, which it did in May, though neither the president nor Congress has taken significant steps in the months since to implement any of the suggestions.Funding debateCongress approved a budget of $32 billion for FEMA for the current fiscal year with $26.4 billion of that for the disaster relief fund. The Trump administration asked lawmakers to cut funding for non-disaster FEMA grants by $1.3 billion in the spending bill for the upcoming fiscal year, which is set to begin Oct. 1. The White House budget office wrote in its proposals that reduced funding for those programs would refocus “the agency on sound emergency management while encouraging States and communities to build resilience and use their unique local knowledge and resources in disaster response.”House Republicans proposed a total spending level of $34.1 billion for FEMA in fiscal 2027. Of that, $28.39 billion would be dedicated to the disaster relief fund. The Senate Appropriations Committee has yet to release its annual funding bill for the Department of Homeland Security, which includes FEMA.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Hillsborough Republicans vie to try to defeat Kathy Castor after 20 years in Congress
description: PLANT CITY — Among the congressional districts Florida Republicans most ardently hope to flip this year after they approved a highly partisan redistricting map is the 14th District, which Democrat Kathy Castor has held for two decades. Eight Republicans filed to run for the dramatically reconfigured seat in the Aug. 18 primary, including Mike Beltran, […]
text:
Former GOP state Rep. Mike Beltran speaking in Plant City on Aug. 4, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)PLANT CITY — Among the congressional districts Florida Republicans most ardently hope to flip this year after they approved a highly partisan redistricting map is the 14th District, which Democrat Kathy Castor has held for two decades.
Eight Republicans filed to run for the dramatically reconfigured seat in the Aug. 18 primary, including Mike Beltran, who represented parts of the district in the Florida House from 2018-2024, and Kevin Steele, who has represented a state House district in Pasco County since 2022.
Castor won the seat by 15 points in 2024. As redrawn by Gov. Ron DeSantis this spring, its population voted by more than 10 points for Donald Trump that same year.
While Florida Republicans believe redrawing the district to make it much more GOP-leaning should guarantee them the seat, not everyone looks at it that way. One of the nation’s most respected political analysis websites, Sabato’s Crystal Ball, last week moved the CD 14 race from leaning Republican to a “toss-up.”
Conservative true believer
Beltran is a hardline conservative who would prefer Florida banned all abortions, instead of the existing six-week ban. He says that if elected to Congress he’d push for a constitutional amendment “to end birth tourism and anchor babies.”
An attorney originally from New York City, Beltran was never afraid to challenge Gov. DeSantis or GOP leadership during his six years in Tallahassee. In 2023, he filed an amendment to push for the open carrying of firearms, but withdrew it after the House speaker and Senate president opposed it (that ban on open carry was found unconstitutional by a state appeals court in 2025).
He’s also emphasizing his bona fides as a true representative of the district, which has been torn up to remove all parts of Pinellas County and significant areas of Tampa, as well. It now encompasses parts of South Tampa, extends east to the Polk County line and south to the Manatee County line.
“We deserve somebody from East Hillsborough who’s represented East Hillsborough. Won elections in East Hillsborough. And with a track record of representing this community so that we can win in November,” Beltran told an audience at an event hosted by the Plant City Chamber of Commerce.
That was a dig at Steele, who has represented Pasco County for the past four years in the Florida House.
While Beltran has received several big endorsements, Steele is the preferred choice of the Republican Party of Florida establishment, including all three Cabinet members — Wilton Simpson, Blaise Ingoglia, and James Uthmeier.
He’s also one of the wealthiest members of the Florida Legislature. A former health care tech executive, he founded the software company DataLink in 2021 and retired after selling it to a private equity firm in 2022. He listed his net worth at more than $156 million at the end of 2025.
Pasco County state GOP Rep. Kevin Steele speaking in Plant City on Aug. 4, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)
Speaking in Plant City Tuesday, he said he was motivated to run for public office because he saw Gov. DeSantis “get beat up” during the COVID-19 crisis as “nobody stood by his side.” He added that during the pandemic, when the COVID vaccine was made available, “the feds” were going to provide it to his employees, with a mandate that they must be at his company’s office to receive it.
“And that day, every single one of my employees worked from home. Because I was not going to mandate that my employees take the COVID shot,” he said to scattered applause. ”You can either stand for something or stand for nothing at all.”
Emphasizing Hillsborough roots
Among the legislation Steele passed while in the House was a property rights bill creating a process for removal of squatters on real property.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.Steele has emphasized that he grew up as a Hillsborough County resident and attended Hillsborough Community College and the University of South Florida. But he has lived in Dade City and represented that portion of Pasco County in the Florida House since he was elected in 2022, prompting some of his opponents to emphasize their more direct connection to the community.
Steele told the Phoenix this week that he does own a residence in Hillsborough County and voter registration records show he is registered to vote there. Yet he continued to represent a part of Pasco in House District 56. Shortly after the Phoenix reported on his situation last Thursday, he stepped down from his House seat.
Another try
The only candidate in the race who’s run against Castor is Rocky Rochford, a retired U.S. Navy captain who served for more than 33 years.
“I’ve been there, done that,” he says of his 2024 race against the Tampa Democrat, which he lost by double digits. He jokes that Ron DeSantis is now on his Christmas Card list “forever” after the governor’s office drew up the district to make it a Trump +11 seat.
U.S. Navy veteran Rocky Rochford speaking in Plant City on August 4, 2026 (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix).
He says he’s totally prepared to take office and has drafted more than 40 bills he is prepared to file if elected. Those include separate “bill of rights” proposals for children and seniors.
And, he promises, “I came up with the solution to fix Social Security.”
Navy reservist
The only female in the race is Bea Valenti, a Navy reservist proud of her work as an intern and later staffer in the first Trump White House. She also has worked as a legislative assistant for Mississippi U.S. Rep Mike Ezell and North Florida U.S. Rep. Neal Dunn before becoming a senior domestic policy adviser for U.S. Sen. Ashley Moody.
She too, referenced the COVID pandemic in her comments in Plant City.
“I refused the vaccine as an active-duty person, because of what they were doing to our troops,” she said. “That was the beginning of my career, and I had a lot to lose, but not like our Iraq and Afghanistan veterans.”
Former Navy reservist Bea Valenti speaking in Plant City on Aug. 4, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)
She worked with Dunn on The TROOP Act, which would have required military departments to reinstate individuals removed from their ranks because they refused the COVID vaccine (the measure did not pass).
She referred to Dr. Anthony Fauci’s invocation of the Fifth Amendment more than 100 times during a Senate hearing on the origins and handling of the pandemic. Fauci led the country’s COVID response and headed President Trump’s White House Coronavirus Task Force.
“Y’all see [Anthony] Fauci this week?” she asked the crowd. “’I plead the Fifth. I plead the Fifth. I plead the Fifth.’ It’s treason what that man has done.”
Valenti referenced several policy items she worked on while serving on Capitol Hill, and said she was the only candidate who already has the “on-the-job training” to serve immediately if elected.
The other Republicans in the race include Michael Marcel, John Peters, Gavriel E. Soriano, and Ergin “Batman” Tek.

name: WyoFile
title: Hageman’s Senate campaign fund is eight times larger than Mead’s
description:
Wyoming’s lone congressperson amassed more than $2 million in receipts for the 2026 election cycle.
The post Hageman’s Senate campaign fund is eight times larger than Mead’s appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
U.S. Rep. Harriet Hageman listed $2 million in campaign committee receipts for her U.S. Senate race, eight times more than Sam Mead, her closest fundraising opponent in the Aug. 18 Republican Primary, new figures show.
Hageman, who’s backed by President Donald Trump and the Wyoming GOP, listed $2,023,907 in receipts for her Hageman For Wyoming committee in filings with the Federal Election Commission. She has spent $1.9 million, according to the federal agency.
Mead’s total receipts amount to $252,015, according to data posted Thursday and covering the 2025-2026 election cycle. He has spent $86,834, filings show.
Among other Wyoming Republican candidates for U.S. Senate, the FEC website lists information only for Jimmy Skovgard, who has received $10,379 in contributions from individuals, party committees and other committees, including political action committees.
The FEC had no posted information regarding fundraising and spending by candidates John Holtz or Jill M. Edwards.
Republicans U.S. Rep. Harriet Hageman, John Allan Holtz, Sam Mead and Jimmy Skovgard participate in a forum for U.S. Senate candidates hosted by the League of Women Voters of Wyoming on Wednesday, July 8, 2026, at Casper College. (Dan Cepeda for WyoFile)
Hageman’s receipts include $62,000 from the National Republican Senatorial Committee and $469,500 from other entities like the HF Sinclair Political Action Committee (Dino Pac) and the Devon Energy Corporation PAC, which are both associated with the oil and gas industry,   and the Council of Insurance Agents and Brokers PAC.
She also received $221,365 from other committees such as Keep the Senate Red, which pitched in $52,679. The Hageman Victory Fund donated $38,939. Both of those contributions were earmarked for the primary.
Mead received no party contributions and $500 from other committees. He loaned his campaign $100,000.
Skovgard loaned $5,388 to his campaign and raised $4,991.
On the Democratic side, James Byrd raised $19,575 and has spent $18,376. The FEC had no information on fundraising or expenditures by Democrat Billy Benavediz.
It’s inflation, stupid
The filings come as a survey commissioned by the group Keep it Public Wyoming shows that inflation/cost of living is the top issue in the GOP primary. More than 21% of respondents selected that issue as their most important.
Taxes and government spending were listed by 14% of respondents, illegal immigration by 13%, jobs and the economy by 11% and public lands by 11%.
The survey by Cygnal sampled more than 400 respondents in late July and has an error factor of about 4.5%, Cygnal said in a press conference Thursday
“We value the role that public lands play in Wyoming’s economy, our way of life, our outdoor heritage.”Lauren Heerschap
Brunton, a Riverton company that manufactures navigational tools like compasses, is a leader of the Keep It Public Wyoming campaign, company owner Lauren Heerschap said. “We value the role that public lands play in Wyoming’s economy, our way of life, our outdoor heritage,” she said.
The poll was commissioned “to see where Wyoming voters stand on the issues and to share those insights,” she said.
When asked whether public lands should be kept public and managed for multiple uses, or sold, 91% of GOP primary voters said the property definitely or probably should be kept in public hands.
Mead touts grassroots funding
Mead on Friday criticized Hageman’s war chest, saying her fundraising relied on out-of-state donors, Beltway special interests and entrenched political forces, not Wyoming residents. 
Hageman rejected his criticism.
“More than 29,000 individual donors have expressed their emphatic support for Rep. Hageman by donating to her campaign since she announced she was running for the U.S. Senate in December, campaign advisor Tim Murtaugh said in a statement. “She is running a campaign based on her record of representing Wyoming’s values in Congress, staying connected and hearing directly from people, and being as accessible as any elected representative has ever been.” 
Twenty-seven percent of Hageman’s campaign committee’s funds came “directly from PACs” Mead said of his analysis of fundraising data. He highlighted more than $300,000 in identifiable individual contributions from Florida, Texas and California.
Wyoming accounted for less than 5% of the money donated to Hageman’s principal campaign committee, Mead said in a statement.
“It’s no surprise the Washington machine is lining up behind the incumbent,” his statement reads. “The system is designed to preserve monied interests, not to elect candidates interested in improving the lives of Wyomingites.”
In contrast, Mead said, nearly all of the contributions to his campaign listed in his July quarterly filing came from individual supporters.
Hageman’s campaign said she remains closely linked to Wyoming residents.“No one will ever ‘out grassroots’ Harriet Hageman,” Murtaugh stated.

title: Judge orders Pentagon to resume wind energy project reviews
description: A federal judge has ordered the Department of Defense to lift its blockade of wind energy projects and resume the permitting process that has ground to a halt during President Donald Trump’s second term.  Under Trump, the Pentagon has stopped conducting the national security reviews that are required for wind turbines over 200 feet tall. […]
text:
Wind turbines built near power lines are pictured near Enid, Oklahoma. A federal judge ruled Thursday that the Department of Defense must resume national security reviews for onshore wind projects. (Photo by Janelle Stecklein/Oklahoma Voice)A federal judge has ordered the Department of Defense to lift its blockade of wind energy projects and resume the permitting process that has ground to a halt during President Donald Trump’s second term. 
Under Trump, the Pentagon has stopped conducting the national security reviews that are required for wind turbines over 200 feet tall. Renewable energy companies and Democratic attorneys general sued the administration, saying the refusal to conduct the once-routine reviews has stalled more than 155 onshore wind projects. 
On Thursday, Judge Karin Immergut of the U.S. District Court for the District of Oregon issued a preliminary injunction, ordering the Pentagon to resume the review process while the case proceeds. 
State AGs join legal fight against Trump’s wind farm freeze

In her ruling, Immergut said the agency had not complied with regulatory deadlines to review permits. 
“(The Department of Defense) cannot pick and choose which parts of this legal regime to follow,” she wrote.  
Environmental groups praised the decision.
“For months, wind projects capable of supplying millions of homes and businesses with low-cost power have been needlessly obstructed, as electricity costs and demand soar,” Phelps Turner, senior attorney for U.S. clean energy at the Environmental Defense Fund said in a statement. 
In a statement to Stateline last month, the Defense Department said it was “actively evaluating” projects in a complex process “to balance renewable energy development with the protection and preservation of testing, training, and operational readiness.”
Stateline reporter Alex Brown can be reached at abrown@stateline.org.

title: As Trump pushes for a massive $1.5T in defense spending, a few states brace for a windfall
text:
WASHINGTON — Congress is considering a hike of hundreds of billions in dollars in defense spending, which would represent a surge in military funding not seen since World War II. Whatever the exact level of spending ultimately flows to military installations and defense contractors, some states will likely benefit far more than others, a States Newsroom analysis of federal defense data shows. Just a handful of states makes up a core of military production, topping the lists of federal defense spending, the data shows. President Donald Trump has requested a total Pentagon budget of $1.5 trillion, an unprecedented increase of 42% over the previous year. While that full sum is unlikely to pass Congress, it lays out his vision for defense.The House and Senate are considering their own versions of the National Defense Authorization Act, which sets national defense policy. Both chambers propose boosting total base spending to $1.15 trillion, with Trump’s even bigger increases potentially targeted to come through the budget reconciliation process. Here’s where in the country a new round of defense funding may end up, and where it won’t, given historic spending patterns.Where is defense spending typically concentrated? According to Defense Department data from fiscal years 2020 through 2024, three states have consistently reaped the most federal funding: Texas, California and Virginia. Each has received nearly $50 billion or more annually since the 2020 fiscal year. While other states such as Florida, Maryland and Connecticut rank in the top states by funding, none has cracked more than 10% of total Pentagon spending — which Texas, California and Virginia regularly reach. Matt Borron, executive director of the Association of Defense Communities, said that many communities with military installations will stand to benefit from a spending increase. But he said that funding often doesn’t prioritize infrastructure or maintenance issues, which he described as “low on the totem pole.” “A lot of times our communities are worried about the infrastructure that supports the mission, and even the installation itself,” he said. “The facilities on base, are they up to speed? Are they being maintained? Is the housing still adequate?” He said that, with the defense bill’s focus on building up the military’s industrial capabilities and workforce, many communities will likely see benefits from the funding. Borron, whose organization lobbies for communities with defense installations, said that it is important to invest in the right places. More money doesn’t necessarily mean a better product or faster product, he said. “National security starts at home,” he said. “You need these communities to be this innovation hub. You need it to have great quality of life, so servicemembers and their families want to live there.” Virginia, Connecticut lead per capitaWhen accounting for population, a handful of states receive a bigger share than others. Virginia, which neighbors the nation’s capital and is home to the Pentagon, and Connecticut, which houses several large shipbuilding and Navy facilities, received the most defense spending per resident in both 2020 and 2024, along with sitting near the top of the pile when it comes to overall DOD funding.Maryland, which also neighbors the capital, Alaska and Hawaii also ranked highly in per capita spending. Even within states, spending is often concentrated in specific counties that contain major installations. In Texas, Tarrant County — home to Fort Worth — alone received more than $120 billion in defense spending from fiscal years 2020 through 2024, nearly 50% higher than the next highest amount.  Some states often don’t come out on top, however. Many Pacific Northwest and Northern states, including Idaho, Oregon, Montana and Minnesota, routinely rank toward the bottom of both per capita and total military spending. In the 2024 fiscal year, defense spending made up just a half percent of total GDP in both Oregon and Minnesota. The economic impactFor many communities with military installations or manufacturing facilities, national defense is their primary industry. Military installations can spur hundreds of millions or even billions of dollars to flow to local economies. According to a recent report from the Texas state comptroller, defense installations in 2025 added almost $150 billion to the Texas economy and supported about 628,000 jobs. Many states have embraced their identity as centers of military activity. In a 2023 op-ed in the Richmond Times-Dispatch, U.S. Rep. Rob Wittman, R-Va., wrote that a strong defense industry and reliable state economy “come as a package deal.” Texas Gov. Greg Abbott said on July 10 that military installations each provide “tremendous value” to communities across his state. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., despite voting against the defense policy bill in committee due to its overall size, said provisions of the bill that would support the state’s defense manufacturers and installations enhance “Connecticut’s vital role as an arsenal of democracy.” 

 







U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth signs a panel of the Dive-LD autonomous submarine made by employees at Anduril Industries at Quonset Point during his tour of the factory floor on Feb. 9, 2026. (Photo by Laura Paton/Rhode Island Current)

But some experts say the economic benefits can often be overstated. Julia Gledhill, an analyst at the Stimson Center, a nonprofit think tank that studies global peace and international security issues, said federal defense spending should not be used as a tool for economic development. In fiscal year 2024, according to DOD data, defense spending made up less than 2% of gross domestic product in a majority of states. Just eight states relied on defense spending for more than 5% of their GDP. While defense spending has a significant impact for many communities, she said, if an economic boost is the goal, there’s better places to put the money. Sectors like education or healthcare both have higher returns on investment, she added. “The purpose of the military is not job creation,” she said. “The purpose of military spending is not economic development.”Instead, Gledhill said the defense budget should reflect only what is needed. Military readiness Speaking to reporters during a cabinet meeting at Camp David in July, Trump described the increasing spending as an “unprecedented investment in the United States armed forces.” Buying more for the sake of buying more is not necessarily going to improve the military’s overall operational readiness, Gledhil added.“We're spending more and more, and we're buying more and more, and it's actually hurting military readiness rates, in direct contrast to what we're hearing from the likes of Secretary Hegseth,” she said, referring to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. She pointed to a recent report from the U.S. Government Accountability Office, a federal agency watchdog, that found that the F-35 fighter jet, the Defense Department’s most expensive weapons system, has increased in sustainment costs while declining in performance. 

 







F-35B Lighting II’s prepare to take off from the flight deck of Wasp-class amphibious assault ship USS Makin Island (LHD 8) in the Pacific Ocean on July 28, 2026. The F-35 is the Defense Department's most expensive weapons system. (Photo by Mass Communication Specialist Seaman Apprentice Tomas Zuelke/U.S. Navy)

That report found that the F-35’s mission capable rate — which is the percentage of the time it is able to carry out an assigned mission — decreased from 67% to 44% from fiscal years 2021 to 2025. The percentage of time that it is capable of completing all assigned missions, or the full mission capable rate, similarly decreased from 38% to just 25%, according to the GAO. In the president’s 2027 defense budget request, the number of desired F-35s increased from 47 purchased in 2026 to 85  — a total spending increase of more than $8 billion. And increasing military spending at such a significant rate, without a clear reason, Gledhill said, will have an impact on the rest of the federal government, citing cuts in Republicans’ 2025 tax and spending cut law to Medicaid and nutrition programs like the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. She added that, despite continually rising defense spending, veterans and military families continue to struggle and face high food insecurity. “I think that we can take care of people if we were a bit more judicious about the weapons that we procured,” she said. “That would actually strengthen the military.”Reporting for this project was supported by the Dow Jones News Fund.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: No political saviors: The Tennessee primary election cycle and the politics of maturity
description: One of the greatest misconceptions in American politics is that elections produce saviors. They do not. They reveal who “we” are. Every election exposes the character of a community. Its hopes, fears, priorities, and perhaps most importantly, its level of political maturity. The recent Shelby County election revealed something many of us would rather avoid:[...]
text:
Rep. Justin J. Pearson, photographed at a June 6, 2026 event in a Williamson County church, had nearly every objective measure for political success in his Democratic primary for the 9th Congressional District, writes Rev. Earle Fisher. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
One of the greatest misconceptions in American politics is that elections produce saviors.
They do not. They reveal who “we” are.
Every election exposes the character of a community. Its hopes, fears, priorities, and perhaps most importantly, its level of political maturity. The recent Shelby County election revealed something many of us would rather avoid: our greatest challenge is not simply increasing voter turnout. It is becoming mature enough to build and sustain collective political power.
For generations, Black communities marched, organized, litigated and sacrificed for the right to participate in democracy. Some gave their lives so future generations could exercise a vote that far too many now treat as optional or transactional. That legacy deserves more than our participation. It deserves our discipline.
Democracy has never been about getting everything we want. It has always been about securing enough collective power to improve the quality of life for the people we serve. That requires something increasingly rare in our political culture — the willingness to subordinate personal ambition to the common good.
Memphis has seen the consequences of failing to do so.
In the 2023 mayoral election, seventeen candidates sought the city’s highest office. Every one of them had the legal right to run. The question was never about rights. It was about responsibility. In a nonpartisan plurality election, every additional candidacy diluted an already fractured electorate. The eventual winner, Paul Young, received roughly 27 percent of the vote in an election where turnout hovered around 24 percent.
Before that election, UPTheVote901 organized the Memphis People’s Convention to help citizens and candidates engage one another beyond campaign slogans. The goal was not to crown a winner but to encourage discernment. Democracy depends upon informed voters, not simply ambitious candidates.
This year’s congressional primary presented many of the same challenges.
State Sen. London Lamar had every right to seek Tennessee’s 9th Congressional District seat. U.S. Rep.  Steve Cohen had every right to endorse her candidacy. Rights, however, are not the issue. Responsibilities are.
Neither Lamar nor Cohen had to spend valuable time and political capital campaigning negatively against Rep. Justin J. Pearson, the eventual winner of the Democratic primary. They could have made the case for their preferred candidate without diminishing another Democrat who, by nearly every objective political measure — national and statewide name recognition, fundraising prowess, charisma  — entered the race with the broadest coalition and the strongest path forward. More importantly, they could have preserved relationships that our community will now need if Democrats hope to reclaim and hold political power in November.
This is not about Lamar or Cohen alone. They are simply the latest illustration of a political culture that too often rewards personal preference over political principle and individual ambition over collective strategy.
Leadership sometimes requires the courage to run.
It also requires the wisdom to recognize that every campaign leaves a residue. The words spoken during a primary often become the obstacles that must be overcome in the general election. The strongest leaders understand that today’s opponent may be tomorrow’s governing partner.
The same immaturity appears among voters.
Too many Americans continue searching for political perfection. If a candidate fails to satisfy 100% of their preferences, they disengage altogether. Others dismiss every election as a choice between “the lesser of two evils” while refusing to acknowledge meaningful differences in healthcare, education, environmental protection, labor rights, voting rights and economic opportunity. In practice, many people surrender 80% of what they could gain because they refuse to accept the imperfect t20%t of progress available today.
Politics was never intended to produce saviors. It was intended to produce accountability.
Voting is not the end of democratic participation. It is the beginning. Every conversation, every registration drive, every candidate forum, every neighborhood canvass and every ride to the polls expands the possibilities of democracy. 
But turnout alone cannot save us if our political culture remains captive to personality, impulse and ego.
As a pastor, I cannot separate this conversation from my spiritual formation. Freedom requires responsibility. Love requires sacrifice. Justice requires community. Those virtues do not emerge naturally from self-interest, and neither does democracy.
The consequences of our political immaturity are no longer theoretical. While we divide our coalitions and search for perfect candidates, others are patiently redrawing districts, reshaping courts, weakening labor protections, privatizing public institutions, eroding environmental safeguards and rolling back civil and human rights. They are playing the long game. If we continue substituting personality for strategy and impulse for discipline, we should not be surprised if it takes a generation to recover what we surrendered in a single election cycle.
There is still time to choose a different path before November.
Candidates can repair relationships. Elected officials can unite rather than divide. Organizations can collaborate instead of competing. Pastors can educate, organize and mobilize. Citizens can reject cynicism and recommit themselves to the long work of democracy.
Most importantly, we can stop looking for political saviors.
There are none.
There never have been.
Democracy does not require perfect candidates. It requires mature citizens willing to place the common good above personal preference and political strategy above political ego.
The question before us is whether we are finally ready to become those people.

title: Central Iowa nurse with a history of licensing issues faces new charges from board
description: A central Iowa nurse with a history of disciplinary sanctions related to alleged sexual misconduct and the misappropriation of drugs is again facing charges from state regulators. The Iowa Board of Nursing has charged Rachel L. Blair, 35, of Ankeny with failing to comply with an order of the board, and with violating an agreement […]
text:
(Photo courtesy of the Iowa Board of Nursing)A central Iowa nurse with a history of disciplinary sanctions related to alleged sexual misconduct and the misappropriation of drugs is again facing charges from state regulators.
The Iowa Board of Nursing has charged Rachel L. Blair, 35, of Ankeny with failing to comply with an order of the board, and with violating an agreement or contract with the Iowa Professional Health Program.
The board has not disclosed the alleged conduct that gave rise to the charges, except to say that it occurred while Blair was working as a nurse in Urbandale. A board hearing on the matter is scheduled for Jan. 27, 2027.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Blair for comment.
State records show that in 2025, the board charged Blair with misappropriating medications or supplies from a patient or clinic.
In that case, the board alleged that on Dec. 3, 2024, the medication count was off during Blair’s shift at an unspecified care facility, with one fentanyl patch reported to be missing. During that same shift, the board alleged, Blair “fell to her hands and knees and struggled to stand.” Paramedics were called and administered Narcan, a drug that’s often used to quickly reverse a life-threatening opioid overdose.
In response to that situation, the board issued Blair a warning and she agreed to enroll in the Iowa Professional Health Program, which is designed to help healthcare providers who have substance-abuse issues. As part of her settlement agreement with the board, Blair agreed to fully comply with all requirements of the program.
State records also show that in 2020, the board charged Blair with initiating, or attempting to initiate a sexual, emotional or business relationship with a patient. The board alleged while working at the Polk County Jail from January 2019 through July 2019, Blair participated in personal, sexual phone calls with an inmate of the jail.
According to the board, Blair was fired for, on multiple occasions, providing the inmate with some unspecified form of treatment for which there was no order, and for admitting that she had personal feelings for the inmate.
In that case, the board suspended Blair’s license until she completed a six-week teleconference course on professional boundaries. Her license was then placed on probation for two years.
Court records show that a Polk County Jail inmate had told jail officials that a nurse, later identified as Blair, had been providing tobacco, drugs and sex to another inmate, who was known as “Casper.” According to a search warrant application filed by the sheriff’s department, Blair admitted to providing “Casper” with unordered, undocumented “massaging treatments,” approximately 15 times over four to six weeks, in a private treatment room.
According to the warrant application, a subsequent review of the jail’s recorded telephone calls uncovered communications between Blair and the inmate that included “sexual content and comments referencing a personal relationship.”
A review of text messages then uncovered 199 written exchanges between Blair and the inmate, according to the warrant application. The messages also included 21 photos of Blair, the sheriff’s department alleged. In addition, the warrant application alleged that money had been deposited into the inmate’s account three separate times by depositor “Clare Loren” — Loren being Blair’s middle name and the name associated with the text messages attributed to Blair.
According to the warrant application, Blair admitted destroying potential evidence in the case during the initial stages of the sheriff’s investigation of the matter.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Establishment frustrations, calls for local representation fueled McKinney’s primary win
description: Shri Thanedar, the second-term Democratic U.S. representative for Michigan’s 13th Congressional District, will not be up for reelection come fall, following a successful primary challenge from state Rep. Donavan McKinney, a native Detroiter who has promised to fight for a Democratic Party that represents the interests of working people.  Following his primar[...]
text:
Michigan state Rep. Donavan McKinney (D-Detroit) speaks at a rally advocating against a proposed 24% wholesale tax on marijuana for the next fiscal year. Sept. 30, 2025 | Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan AdvanceShri Thanedar, the second-term Democratic U.S. representative for Michigan’s 13th Congressional District, will not be up for reelection come fall, following a successful primary challenge from state Rep. Donavan McKinney, a native Detroiter who has promised to fight for a Democratic Party that represents the interests of working people. 
Following his primary success in the deep blue Democratic district, which includes portions of Detroit, as well as Grosse Pointe and the Downriver region, McKinney is heavily favored to win against Republican T.P. Nykoriak, who ran uncontested.
In 2016, Nykoriak was sentenced to 16 months in federal prison for stealing U.S. savings bonds from a church.
Heading into election night, McKinney was at a significant funding disadvantage with $142,853 in cash on hand compared to Thanedar’s approximately $5 million. Despite that financial advantage, Thanedar had long faced criticism from residents and public officials in his district over his constituent services, with then-Detroit Mayor Mike Duggan telling reporters in 2024 “He’s not a bad person; he’s just not helping.”
At the end of the race, unofficial results show McKinney defeating his opponent with 51.9% of the vote. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In an interview with Michigan Advance, Democratic political consultant Michael Radtke, who also is a Sterling Heights councilman, pointed to two major dividing factors in the race: Black representation for Detroit and the willingness to directly address constituent concerns. 
From 1955 to 2022, Detroit’s congressional delegation included at least one Black member of Congress. Since 2023 the majority Black city has been represented by Thanedar, who immigrated to the U.S. from India, and Rep. Rashida Tlaib, who is Palestinian American. 
McKinney’s grassroots approach to campaigning and anti-corporate politics were also essential, Radtke said. 
Denzel McCampbell, the city councilmember for Detroit’s 7th District and one of the local officials who endorsed McKinney, noted the state representative’s background, growing up poor in northeast Detroit, where he was raised by his mother and grandmother.
Understanding what brings those challenges, their solutions, and that there are folks living in the district who share similar stories is what leads to representation that can relate to residents’ experiences, McCampbell said, whether that’s having a representative who is from Detroit, or who shares experiences with Black residents in a district where they are the plurality.
McCampbell said McKinney provides that representation and understands that bold solutions are needed to address the issues that residents of the 13th are facing. 
During a press conference following McKinney’s victory, Rev. James Michael Curenton of Mayflower Congregational United Church of Christ said “We know that Donavan is one of us. Donavan is accessible to us. And Donavan will be accessible to us once he gets into Congress. We have someone that we know that will be there to represent our interests.”
During his campaign, McKinney took a stance against corporate influence in politics, emphasizing that “We didn’t take a dime of corporate PAC money,” and speaking out against corporations like DTE Energy, which provides electricity for much of southeast Michigan. For years the company has faced criticism from customers over high rates, poor reliability and lengthy power outages.
Michigan State Rep. Donavan McKinney (D-Detroit) speaks at a news conference detailing a Democrat-led effort to create a utility ratepayer’s bill of rights. Sept. 9, 2025 | Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance
That type of messaging was essential in pulling off the win, Radtke said, noting that the 13th Congressional District is among the poorest districts in the nation. 
“I think that in the coming days we’re going to start to realize that people are very frustrated that their needs are not being met,” Radtke said, pointing to the rising costs of basic needs like food, gas and energy.
People are tired of the status quo, McCampbell told Michigan Advance, explaining that when you have a candidate like McKinney, who pledges to hold corporations accountable, and is not taking their money, that makes a difference.
While national media outlets have counted McKinney’s win among a trend of Democratic socialist victories both in the state and across the U.S., Radtke argued McKinney’s success was rooted more in the candidate than in the ideology. 
“Donavan is someone who could live on your block. He’s got a young family. He understands the travails of the current world, you know, he’s not a millionaire,” Radtke said, drawing contrast with Thanedar.
“I think the people of this district don’t care what you call yourself if you show up to work for them every day in Detroit and in Washington D.C.,” Radtke said.
However, McCampbell, who ran for city council as a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, said you can’t separate the candidate and the ideology. 
“When I was talking to people on the doors, it wasn’t about what tag or ideology that I had,” McCampbell said. “It was about: Are you going to deliver on our needs? Are you going to have a responsive city council office? Are we going to be someone that you’re going to push bold policies to stand up for us in the neighborhoods against you know corporations and folks that just want to build playgrounds downtown. That was what resonated with folks.”
Democratic socialists and the DSA are presenting a vision that seeks to address issues like affordability, economic justice and the influence of corporations as a way of doing things differently, McCampbell said, arguing people should embrace that idea, rather than looking at Democratic socialist candidates as a negative.
“We should be listening to our electorate. We should be listening to our constituents. We should be listening to our community,” McCampbell said, noting that people are resoundingly pointing to the influence corporations are having on politics and demanding a change.
What’s next for Thanedar
On Wednesday morning, Thanedar called McKinney to congratulate him on his victory, offering him his full cooperation for a smooth transition between offices.
In a text message to Michigan Advance Thursday, Thanedar said he was honored to serve the 13th District and that he would continue to fight to bring home dollars for the district during his remaining time in office.
U.S. Rep. Shri Thanedar (D-Detroit) speaks at a rally to oppose plans to convert an industrial warehouse into an ICE detention center in Romulus. April 25, 2026 | Photo by Erick Díaz Veliz
While speaking to the Advance later Thursday afternoon, Thanedar carried a gracious tone, noting he had received almost 10,000 additional votes this year compared to the 2024 primary election.
In 2024, 80,000 people turned out to vote, while 110,000 came out in 2026, with Thanedar attributing the rise in turnout to frustration with President Donald Trump’s administration or the pull of Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, who he says may have inspired people to come out that previously wouldn’t have voted.
“I think they kind of bought into the narrative that Abdul and the Democratic Socialists are putting forward,” Thanedar said.
Ultimately, Thanedar said he was feeling good heading toward the end of his tenure in office and was grateful to the people for giving him the opportunity to serve in Congress to begin with. 
By the time his term is over, Thanedar noted that he will be 72 years old, and that Tuesday’s results had given him an opportunity to say “What else can I do?”
While he didn’t rule out another run for public office, Thanedar said he’s not looking to grab the next position he can find.
“I feel I’ve been blessed, and I’m going out with a lot of gratitude towards my constituents,” Thanedar said.

name: National
title: Education Department hands more states flexibility with federal dollars
description: The Trump administration is increasing its efforts to turn more control of federal education money to the states as it continues working to dismantle the Education Department. Six states have received waivers allowing them to consolidate more than $109 million in federal education funding and bypass certain requirements for local education agencies, Kirsten[...]
text:
Students walk down the hall at a public elementary school. The Trump administration has given states more flexibility in spending some federal dollars. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)The Trump administration is increasing its efforts to turn more control of federal education money to the states as it continues working to dismantle the Education Department.
Six states have received waivers allowing them to consolidate more than $109 million in federal education funding and bypass certain requirements for local education agencies, Kirsten Baesler, assistant secretary for the department’s Office of Elementary and Secondary Education, told Stateline in an interview.
The consolidation of four funding streams into one means the money can be used more flexibly by the states with Returning Education to the States waivers — Arkansas, Indiana, Iowa, Louisiana, South Dakota and Vermont. Some states chose to put that money toward statewide literacy or math improvement efforts. Indiana will run a pilot program allowing up to 15% of its districts to combine two funding streams that had been focused separately on teachers and students and to alter requirements for all schools on college and career readiness measures when calculating a high school’s performance rating. 
It’s a part of a growing push by the Trump administration to turn federal education measures to state control. Beyond the six states that received these waivers, 22 states have received Education Flexibility Partnership, or Ed-Flex authority, which allows states to waive certain federal education requirements for school districts without seeking separate permission from the Department of Education each time. 
That’s the highest number of states in the program’s 32-year history, Baesler said. 
Those states are: Arkansas, Colorado, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Maine, Massachusetts, Montana, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Vermont, Virginia and Wisconsin. 
While many public school district staff welcome the waivers, some state education groups have opposed them. Some have argued that consolidating federal funding weakens guardrails that ensure money goes to the specific populations and programs they were meant to serve. In Arkansas, for example, the Arkansas Education Association warned that greater flexibility would reduce transparency and possibly shift money away from formula-based funding for high-need districts, the Arkansas Advocate reported. 
A state must request such a waiver. Baesler said department officials are working with states before they submit applications to determine whether their goals require a waiver, an amended state plan or could already be done under existing federal law.
Baesler also said state officials should take greater responsibility for identifying and pursuing their own education needs and priorities rather than waiting for direction from the feds.
“Don’t wait for the signal to come because what students in North Dakota need are going to be completely different than what Texas needs or Louisiana or Oregon or Washington,” Baesler said.
In September, the department will convene with state representatives to discuss results from a Learning Agenda Initiative which includes eight states: Arkansas, Georgia, Idaho, Kansas, New Hampshire, Tennessee, Utah and Wisconsin, officials told Stateline. The program paired state education agencies with federally funded research and technical-assistance centers to examine state data and develop multi-year learning agendas identifying needs and ways to measure a state’s progress on its education priorities.
The department is also giving states additional points on some competitive grant applications when they design or help lead “Returning Education to the States” projects.
The future of the Department of Education has been a hot topic since President Donald Trump signed a March 2025 executive order directing Secretary Linda McMahon to take steps to close the department and push more control of education to the states. Congress, which created the department through a 1979 federal law, retains the authority to eliminate it.
But the department has begun to hand off some administrative duties to other federal agencies. 
Carissa Moffatt Miller, CEO of the Council of Chief State School Officers, said at an National Conference of State Legislatures conference earlier this month that transferring federal programs between agencies could disrupt grant payments because the Education and Labor departments, for example, use different grant management systems. Those delays could lead districts to hold back spending or pull teacher contracts even if Congress appropriated the money, she said.
Moffatt Miller said that federal funding accounts for about 12% of education funding, with the remaining 88% coming from state and local sources. Analysis from Education Week estimated that at least $12 billion in previously awarded federal education funds have been disrupted by administrative actions over the past year.
