name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Five individuals arrested for suspected fraud in ongoing Lincoln petition investigation
description: Lancaster County officials announced the arrest of five out-of-state individuals for suspected fraud on three Lincoln petitions.
text:
Lancaster County Attorney Pat Condon, left, and Lancaster County Sheriff Chief Deputy Ben Houchin announce criminal charges and arrests of five out-of-state individuals who helped circulate petitions for three petitions in Nebraska's capital city at a news briefing Aug. 7, 2026, in Lincoln, Nebraska. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Lancaster County officials announced Friday the arrest of five out-of-state individuals who helped circulate petitions for three Lincoln-focused petitions this summer.
However, more arrests could be on the way as the investigation continues.
Chief Deputy Ben Houchin of the Lancaster County Sheriff’s Office announced the arrests Friday morning in a 10-minute news briefing. He said five people have so far been arrested in Missouri, Nevada, Florida and Washington, D.C. None are Nebraska residents.
“Nothing in our investigation makes us believe any political entity is working or affiliated with this,” Houchin said. “These are people out doing crimes. Period.”
Lancaster County Sheriff Chief Deputy Ben Houchin. (Courtesy of Lancaster County Sheriff’s Office)
Lancaster County Attorney Pat Condon and the Nebraska Attorney General’s Office were among law enforcement helping with the investigation. Houchin said the U.S. Marshals Service has also “done us a huge favor” helping with arrests in other states.
“This investigation is early. We are going to continue the investigation,” Houchin said. “The system worked on catching these.”
Names under seal, extradition in progress
Houchin could not yet name the individuals charged, as the arrest warrants were kept under seal, but he expected that information to be released later Friday.
“We know people are concerned about this, and that’s the reason why, one, I wanted to keep it mum for a little bit till we could get these individuals arrested and stopped,” Houchin said. “I know you guys are interested in this and things, but I did not want to have our investigation interfered with and we lose these people and they can continue to harm.”
Lancaster County Attorney Pat Condon. Aug. 5, 2024. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Those charged will face at least one count each of falsifying a circulator’s affidavit. The Class IV felony could carry a maximum sentence of two years’ imprisonment and 12 months’ post-release supervision or a $10,000 fine, or both. However, each falsified petition page — which includes up to 20 signatures per page — could be a separate charge.
Condon and Houchin said they are in the process of extradition to get the individuals returned to Nebraska to face charges. If the individuals fight the charges, that could require governors to get involved to smooth the process.
“We’ll also continue to look at the information that we obtain from the investigation to see if further charges, either individuals or additional charges on the ones that we have already filed on,” Condon said.
Investigation began July 23
The investigation began July 23, three days after leaders for the Good Government Lincoln petition campaign turned in more than 30,0000 signatures on three proposed city charter amendments. The efforts failed to qualify under the initial batch of signatures, though supporters said this week they are restarting signature gathering efforts.
The petitions seek to move the dates of city elections to align with statewide elections, allow certain residents within a few miles of city limits to vote in municipal elections, and place term limits on Lincoln City Council members.
More than 13,300 Lincoln petition signatures flagged as fraudulent

Houchin said the sponsors hired the arrested individuals and turned in the petitions. Of the signatures, more than 65% were rejected. Of those 19,000 signatures, the Lancaster County Election Commission said two-thirds, or more than 13,300, are suspected to be fraudulent.
Local election officials are tasked with validating petition signatures for proposed local and statewide measures. Officials review signatures and check the voter’s name, address and date of birth. At least two of the three personally identifying forms of information must match.
Whether the sponsors face any legal trouble, Houchin said, is still under investigation.
“There’s a lot of unanswered questions that we need some more time to investigate,” Houchin said. “We’re just starting.”
Campaign supports criminal referral
Former state Sen. Tony Fulton, one such sponsor, said Thursday that the campaign takes citizen-led petitions very seriously and appreciates local election officials’ flagging irregularities. Fulton said the campaign supports the criminal referrals and the prosecution of “fraudsters.”
“We look forward to getting answers and in the meantime remain committed to giving voters a voice on these issues for the November ballot,” said Fulton, a former state tax commissioner under former Gov. Pete Ricketts.
Joining Mayor Leiron Gaylor Baird (at podium) at a news conference announcing the Co-Responder Program in 2024 were, from the left, Malone Center Executive Director John Goodwin, City Councilwoman Sändra Washington, CenterPointe Executive Vice President and Chief Operating Officer Tami Lewis-Ahrendt, Lincoln Police Chief Michon Morrow and Lincoln Police Captain Ben Kopsa. (Courtesy of City of Lincoln)
Lincoln Mayor Leirion Gaylor Baird has been a chief opponent of the measures. In a Friday statement, she thanked Lancaster County Election Commissioner Todd Wiltgen and his office for working to uphold election laws. She also thanked Lancaster County Sheriff Terry Wagner, Condon, the U.S. Marshals Service and others for working to ensure perpetrators are held accountable.
“Their dedication and professionalism have prevented bad actors from manipulating the ballot initiative process,” Gaylor Baird said of Wiltgen’s team.
‘Wasn’t real hard’ to spot wrongdoing
Houchin said that of the irregular signatures, it “wasn’t real hard to figure out they weren’t right” and that somebody had signed for other people. He said law enforcement contacted some signers and asked whether they signed. Many said they didn’t. Dates of birth were also wrong. 
So far, the investigation has involved only the three Good Government Lincoln petitions, but Houchin said the investigation is continuing. 
In this election cycle, three nonpartisan candidates submitted signatures seeking to qualify for the November ballot, and leaders for four statewide ballot measures submitted petitions seeking a vote of the people. Two groups seeking to create new political parties also submitted signatures. One candidate so far has qualified, but all other petitions are still under review.
Pillen, AG’s Office weigh in
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, in a statement Friday, said he is “deeply troubled” by the reports of “historic fraud” from paid signature gathering, and he called for the Legislature to reverse a 2015 decision allowing it. Ricketts, an ally of those running Good Government Lincoln, signed that 2015 bill into law.
“I’m grateful to the law enforcement who are protecting our election system and investigating this election fraud, and expect those responsible at every level to be held accountable to the fullest extent under the law,” Pillen said.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, left, and Attorney General Mike Hilgers. May 13, 2024. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers did not issue a statement, but his spokesperson, Suzanne Gage, said the office “takes petition fraud allegations seriously and will work with partnered agencies to root it out wherever it may be found and bring those who commit it to justice.”
The Nebraskans for Medical Marijuana group has been among those to criticize Hilgers for not taking a more public approach in this investigation since Wednesday afternoon, when questions about the petition signatures first arose. In 2024, Hilgers announced multiple legal investigations into the medical cannabis petition campaigns, which voters overwhelmingly approved.
Those investigations led to two arrests and two convictions with suspected circulator fraud and notary malfeasance. Prosecutors named other campaign members in court filings, but they were not ultimately charged. A Lancaster County District Court judge affirmed that the petition had enough valid signatures, a decision Hilgers is fighting at the Nebraska Supreme Court.
“We are committed to protecting the integrity of the petition process and maintaining public trust,” Gage said. “When credible information arises, we dedicate the resources needed to examine each situation thoroughly. Our office enforces election laws without bias, fear or favor.”
The 2024 investigation began in Hall County, where local election officials flagged irregularities. At least 200 signatures were flagged as fraudulent before the first charge was brought.
Condon and Houchin both said this is a first for Lancaster County. Houchin has been with the Lancaster County Sheriff’s Office his entire 33-year career, dating back to June 1993.
“We know who they are contacting and what they are doing,” Houchin said. “This is a crime, and these people are criminals. Doesn’t have anything to do with local government or anything like that.”

text:
The Heflin-Torbert Judicial Building in downtown Montgomery, Alabama, seen on Aug. 7, 2026. Justices on Thursday extended the deadline for the plaintiffs' brief to Monday. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)The Alabama Supreme Court on Thursday extended a briefing deadline for plaintiffs challenging Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville’s eligibility to run for the office.
Briefs for the plaintiffs, who argued that Tuberville has not met residency requirements under the Alabama Constitution, were due Friday on an expedited schedule. Barry Ragsdale, one of the plaintiffs’ attorneys, has been in Tuscaloosa for an administrative hearing for three weeks for a different case, according to court filings. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“While the undersigned anticipated being able to work on the appellants’ brief while also participating in the three-week hearing, the Administrative Law Judge’s rigorous schedule and the complex nature of the proceedings have prevented appellants’ counsel from working on and completing the brief by the current Aug. 7, 2026 deadline,” attorneys wrote on Tuesday. 
The brief is now due on Monday. According to the plaintiffs’ motion, Tuberville’s lawyers had no objection to the extension. 
Messages seeking comment from Ragsdale and Tuberville’s team were left on Thursday and Friday, respectively. 
The lawsuit made its way to the Alabama Supreme Court after a Montgomery County judge dismissed the case in July due to a lack of jurisdiction after an hourslong hearing, but not the merits. 
Plaintiffs allege that Tuberville does not meet the state’s residency requirements to run for governor, and echoes many accusations reported by Alabama media outlets. Tuberville maintains that he meets the seven-year residency requirement.

name: National
title: US employers shed 23K jobs in July
description: US employers shed  23,000 jobs in July, and the employment count for earlier months was revised downward by 103,000 jobs as labor shortages begin to weigh on hiring, according to new statistics released Friday by the federal Bureau of Labor Statistics. “There’s no sugarcoating the overarching message in the July jobs report,” Mark Zandi, the […]
text:
McKenna Melby of the North Dakota State College of Science speaks with a job fair attendee in Fargo, North Dakota, on July 28, 2026. Melby  was recruiting potential students for the certified nursing assistant program.(Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)	US employers shed  23,000 jobs in July, and the employment count for earlier months was revised downward by 103,000 jobs as labor shortages begin to weigh on hiring, according to new statistics released Friday by the federal Bureau of Labor Statistics.
“There’s no sugarcoating the overarching message in the July jobs report,” Mark Zandi, the chief economist at Moody’s Analytics, wrote in a social media post. “The economy is struggling. Job growth is at a virtual standstill.”
Inflation could be taking a toll as employment in general merchandise retailing declined by 21,000 jobs and gas stations cut 5,000 jobs.  Employment in finance also dropped by 14,000, continuing a slide of 121,000 jobs since a recent peak in May 2025.
The number of health care jobs grew by 22,000 in July, but that was lower than the monthly average gain of 36,000 in the past  year.
The federal government also revised the job numbers for May and June, subtracting 66,000 from the May total and 37,000 from June, even though the World Cup boosted employment during those months.  The adjusted job growth numbers for May and June are 63,000 and 20,000, respectively.
Today’s children could prosper in tomorrow’s shortage of young workers

Small businesses saw “a surprising and substantial tightening of the labor market” in July, according to a report from the National Federation of Independent Business (NFIB), which represents  300,000 small and independent business owners. In a survey, 27% of members cited labor supply and quality as their single most important problem, up from 19% in June and the 12% historical average.
The cost of health insurance also stood out as a top concern. That was especially true in Texas, one of 10 states that has not  expanded Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act to provide coverage for a broader population of lower-income people. In Texas, almost 15% of NFIB members said health insurance costs were their single most important problem, the highest of any state, compared to about 10% nationally.
“I have yet to have a conversation with anyone who doesn’t think this is a problem and in most cases it’s their biggest problem,” NFIB State Director Jeff Burdett said.
State jobless rates remain stable in June as men’s World Cup helps in some areas

Nationally, most small businesses can’t afford to provide health insurance at all, according to NFIB surveys, he said.
“They want to provide health insurance, they need to provide it to be competitive, it’s just cost prohibitive,” Burdett said. “What that means is that talented workers are bypassing small businesses entirely in favor of large employers.”
Another recent employment report from ADP, a payroll processor, also pointed to a sudden tightening of the labor market: The pay for job changers rose at the fastest pace in a year.
“Job changers are highly sensitive to real-time economic conditions, and their rapid pay growth implies supply constraints in parts of the labor market,” Nela Richardson, ADP’s chief economist, said in a statement.

name: Mississippi Today
title: On Mississippi’s death row, ‘Humans Remain,’ advocate says
description: Liz McCann is co-founder of Humans Remain, a nonprofit organization that focuses on advocacy and education for Mississippi death row inmates and serves as a platform for them to share first hand experiences of awaiting execution. McCann, based outside of London, runs the organization with several men on death row, including Joesph Patri Brown.
text:
Thirty-four men and one woman in Mississippi await a death sentence handed down years ago, sometimes decades ago. Some people know their names, their victims and details of their crimes. Few probably know who they are or how they spend their days. 
Abdur Rahim Ambrose Sr. enjoys fixing broken things for a challenge. Kelvin Lashaun Jordan works on puzzles, draws and writes poetry. Tim Ronk, nicknamed Jersey because he is from the Garden State, likes to read fantasy.
These self-written introductions are possible through a nonprofit organization called Humans Remain, an online platform for Mississippi’s death row prisoners to talk directly to the public by sharing their stories, academic achievements and writing. 
“The guys have a platform to talk … and for people to try and understand that, perhaps, they’re not their worst 15 minutes,” said Liz McCann, a co-founder of the group based outside of London, England. “There’s a whole lot more of a story to these people.”
Mississippi is among the few Southern states where she has connected with death row prisoners. McCann began talking with some of the death row men about four years ago, and last year she partnered with some of them to create the organization, which celebrates its first anniversary this weekend. 
“It’s an honor to be able to be a voice and to give a voice to so many men and women. We are no longer voiceless and faceless with this inhumane system which seeks to execute us,” Joesph Patri Brown, a co-founder of the group, said in a message shared by McCann. 
Joesph Patri Brown, who has been on incarcerated in Mississippi for over 30 years, is the author of “The Image They Had Painted.” The cover is a person emerging from a whirlpool, which he uses to describe the criminal justice system. The book gives a glimpse into his life and the lives of the men around him and critiques the death penalty.  Credit: Publication Studio Guelph
Brown has been on death row for over 30 years for his conviction in the shooting death of a convenience store clerk in Adams County during an armed robbery but has maintained his innocence. He is a published author who has used his writing as a form of advocacy for himself and on behalf of others on death row in Mississippi. 
He said he is proud Humans Remain has become a national and world-recognized group opposing the death penalty. 
McCann has built relationships with the people on death row through consistent phone contact, video calls and exchanging messages on tablets. 
She said the organization’s name came from conversations with the men about gruesome headlines used to write about crime.  
“We read a lot about human remains, and I thought, ‘Well, yes, but what about the people behind that?’” she said. “ ‘Humans Remain’ became our working title, and we all agreed it was visceral and hit the note that we were looking for.”
McCann, who has previously campaigned for human rights issues, said she has been interested in death penalty abolition since reading a book about it when she was 19. 
After finishing her education, having a career and raising children, she focused on meeting people on death row, starting with pen pal correspondence with one man in Florida and another in North Carolina. 
Her interest in Mississippi came from reading about the American South and watching the 1987 BBC documentary “Fourteen Days in May,” which was about the days leading up to the execution of Edward Earl Johnson. It featured attorney Clive Stafford Smith, who unsuccessfully tried to stop the execution.
McCann said some of the men who remain on Mississippi’s death row remember Smith, who went on to challenge death sentences across the South and advocate against the death penalty and human rights abuses internationally. In recent years, he has represented detainees at Guantanamo Bay. 
“Personally, I am proudest of the things I have done that help to humanize those who society tells us to demonize, so it’s great to see Liz doing just that,” Smith said in a testimonial about Humans Remain that is featured on its website.
The men on death row at the Mississippi State Penitentiary at Parchman meet weekly with McCann over a video call to give updates about Humans Remain, work on projects for the organization and plan for future ones. She said a core group of about nine men play an active role in the nonprofit. 
McCann helps maintain the organization’s website featuring journal entries by the men and Lisa Jo Chamberlin, who is the only woman on death row in Mississippi, and occasional blog posts from McCann’s perspective as an advocate. There are also educational sections about developments in the death row prisoners’ cases, writings about ending the death penalty and information about death row exonerees. 
She also helps them create videos to share on social media. 
Caleb Corrothers, who received two death sentences in 2011, is an artist and one of the over 30 men Humans Remain co-founder Liz McCann has gotten to know through phone and video calls over the past four years. Humans Remain, founded in August 2025, is a platform where death row inmates like Corrothers have been able to share their first hand experience on death row through writing, art, journals and advocacy. Credit: Courtesy of Liz McCann, Humans Remain
McCann said people are curious about death row and the prisoners’ lives there. People can submit questions on the Humans Remain website for the men to answer. 
A common question is about what they eat because people have seen horror stories about prison food, McCann said. 
Since moving to Parchman’s Unit 17 late last year, they have a dedicated kitchen team and they are getting good meals using fresh produce from their garden, which is under the watch of Blayde Grayson, she said. 
The dedicated kitchen team, garden and self-contained unit where the men live are a stark contrast to the living conditions for Chamberlin, who is in segregated housing and has experienced restrictions, including access to phone calls and enrollment in classes.  
On Friday, Chamberlin’s location was listed at the Delta Correctional Facility, the second women’s prison located in Greenwood. It’s over 100 miles away from the women’s section at the Central Mississippi Correctional Facility in Pearl, where she had been housed since her 2006 conviction for the murder of two people in Hattiesburg. 
McCann said people are also inquisitive about the executions and some have asked for commentary about states adding execution methods. Mississippi uses lethal injection. In 2022, it added toxic gas, firing squad and electrocution as execution methods, although those options have not been used
McCann said the death row men have also found it bizarre to be living in the “death house” where the execution chamber resides, and they find it baffling when people have come to visit the chamber.

title: Some Haitians targeted for ankle monitors by ICE as they face threat of mass deportation
text: WASHINGTON — Even before Haitian immigrants in Ohio officially lost their Temporary Protected Status, the Department of Homeland Security required dozens of them to report to immigration appointments and accept ankle monitors, according to their attorneys and local advocates.The practice of using electronic monitoring appears to only be happening in Springfield, Ohio, according to a half dozen advocates and immigration attorneys representing Haitians. Additionally, community leaders and lawyers from other cities with large Haitian immigrant populations such as Boston, Chicago and Miami have not seen the same tactic. One advocate has seen an increased presence of federal immigration agents in Brooklyn, New York, but so far no check-ins. The advocates and lawyers from Springfield said they do not know the exact number of Haitians under electronic monitoring. “It's really just theater,” said Lynn Tramonte, the executive director of the Ohio Immigrant Alliance, an advocacy group. “They're putting ankle monitors on people to make it look like they're doing something, but it's devastating for the people who are getting these placed on their ankle. They're a constant reminder that you're not free.”U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement did not respond to a detailed list of questions from States Newsroom regarding the use of ankle monitors. The use of ankle monitors for immigrants who have no criminal background and previously held legal status is a departure from standard practice. Typically an ankle monitor is used for immigrants with a criminal record, an order for deportation, or a missed appearance in immigration court. Springfield is home to 15,000 Haitian immigrants. The community became a focus of President Donald Trump’s campaign promise to conduct mass deportations in September 2024 when he falsely accused them of eating house pets and vowed to terminate their legal protections in order to deport them. The Supreme Court in June cleared the way for the Trump administration to end TPS for up to 350,000 Haitians. The case is now back at a lower court in the District of Columbia, which is litigating whether the government’s decision to end protections for Haitians was based on racial animus. Deportation or monitoringFollowing the ruling, the DHS sent letters to Haitians in Springfield as early as July 22, said Guerline Jozef, executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance. States Newsroom has reviewed a copy of the letter that dozens of Haitians in Springfield received directing them to bring all their immigration documents to an appointment at an ICE office.Then, on July 31, about 50 Haitians had check-in appointments at the Cincinnati ICE field office. At the appointments, they were pressured to accept $2,600 to self-deport or alternatively to wear an ankle monitor. All of them rejected the money, Jozef said. “Being deported to Haiti right now is a death sentence,” she said. Two days later, on Aug. 2, a dozen Haitians with TPS were summoned to check-ins and left with ankle monitors, said Katie Kersh, the managing attorney for Advocates for Basic Legal Equality, a nonprofit that provides legal representation to immigrants in Ohio.“The people getting the ankle monitors are the people who are complying ... and they're getting this thing that we connote with criminality, which is an ankle monitor, when they've literally gotten that because they followed the orders of the call-in letter,” Kersh said.The practice could ramp up following Wednesday’s order from a federal judge that lifted a stay in place since February that prevented the Trump administration from ending temporary protections for as many as 350,000 Haitians. On the same day the stay was lifted, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in an interview with NewsNation that the department was “going after (Haitians) right now.”“We are giving them an opportunity to either leave on their own and we'll help you, or we'll arrest you and send you back,” he said. “Either way, you don't have status inside this country anymore.”Chaotic rolloutImmigration attorneys and advocates for Haitians in Ohio described to States Newsroom a disorganized scene at the ICE check-in appointments on July 31 and Aug. 2.Kersh said she witnessed ICE officers taking out brand-new ankle monitors that weren’t charged. Instructions were only provided in English and Spanish, when the first language for many Haitians is usually Creole. A translator was nowhere to be found, she added, so she brought one along.ICE personnel appeared unable to be flexible when issues arose. A Haitian woman who worked a night shift wouldn’t have time to charge the ankle monitor given to her Aug. 2, Kersh said.An ICE officer told the woman “to just charge it while you’re sleeping,” and the woman, whom Kersh represented, again told the officer that she worked nights, Kersh said. Kersh said she tried to find other options for electronic monitoring for her clients, such as a daily facial recognition check-in or a wrist monitor, but said the immigration officials would not deviate.She said an ICE officer told her that “we are being told from headquarters that we have to ankle monitor them specifically.” Permission to travel to courtAnother issue is the ankle monitor’s 75-mile radius, Kersh said. Ohio’s only immigration court is located in Cleveland, 188 miles from Springfield. So a Haitian with an ankle monitor would first have to get permission from an ICE officer to travel to their court hearing. “It just sort of feels like the wheels are off the bus,” she said.Getting to the appointments was its own hurdle. When Haitians received a letter directing them to attend ICE check-ins, many of them had to scramble to find a way to attend because of recently expired driver’s licenses. Ohio legislators passed a law that ties a valid driver’s license to immigration status.Jozef said the Haitians fitted with ankle monitors last week were told by ICE officers that they would need to return several weeks later and were given no other information on what would happen at future check-ins.“We are not sure what will happen to the people, but as of right now, the tactic that is being used is to have those call-ins to be able to control the movement of the people, and to be able to target them more easily,” Jozef said.Longtime Trump goalRevoking legal status for Haitians to open them up for removal has been a goal of Trump’s since his first administration, but he has ramped up the effort in his second term that began after he made mass deportations a central campaign theme. “They really, really, really, really want to target these people,” said Geoffrey Pipoly, the attorney who represented the Haitian TPS holders before the Supreme Court. During the first Trump administration, the government tried to end TPS for Haiti with an 18-month wind-down period, but courts blocked the termination. “We went from the first Trump administration giving these folks 18 months to get their affairs in order to now, their position is: We're not even going to give you 32 days from the final judgment of the Supreme Court … as soon as the earliest possible time that we are legally allowed to start deporting people, that's what we're going to start doing,” Pipoly said.After the Supreme Court’s decision in June, lower courts typically have a 32-day deadline to implement the high court's ruling, meaning that the estimated date for the 6-3 decision regarding Haitians would go into effect July 27. But Haitians were already receiving letters from ICE dated July 22 to report for a check-in. 16 years of protectionsCongress created TPS in the 1990s as a way for nationals who hail from countries deemed too dangerous to return to due to violence, natural disasters or other destabilizing factors, to remain safely in the U.S. The status allows them to remain and work in the United States anywhere from six to 18 months. In order to qualify for the program, immigrants must go through a background check and pay application fees each renewal cycle. TPS does not provide a pathway to citizenship, but recipients can apply for another immigration status, such as asylum. Of the roughly 350,000 Haitians with TPS, about 200,000 of them are in the workforce, according to the immigration advocacy group FWD.us. Of that group, they work in industries like healthcare, retail, agriculture and manufacturing. Haiti was first granted TPS in 2010 after a devastating earthquake. In 2021, President Joe Biden extended the protections after the assassination of Haitian President Jovenel Moïse. The State Department currently has a “Do Not Travel” advisory for Haiti “due to the risk of crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest, and limited health care.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Cyclosporiasis continues to rise as state says most lettuce, salad greens safe to eat
description: Michigan has documented 12,485 cases of cyclosporiasis, according to the state’s Department of Health and Human Services, up from the 10,773 cases reported last Friday. The department is issuing weekly updates on the number of documented cases with weekly updates on hospitalizations, as well as cases recorded in each of Michigan’s 83 counties. A total […]
text:
Vegetables and lettuces at a grocery store in Michigan. Michigan health officials say lettuces and salad greens are emerging as a likely source in the nationwide cyclosporiasis outbreak, which has sickened thousands of people across the country. (Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance)Michigan has documented 12,485 cases of cyclosporiasis, according to the state’s Department of Health and Human Services, up from the 10,773 cases reported last Friday.
The department is issuing weekly updates on the number of documented cases with weekly updates on hospitalizations, as well as cases recorded in each of Michigan’s 83 counties.
A total of 279 people have been hospitalized with cyclosporiasis, up from 193 reported last Thursday.
Earlier in the week, the department reported that two individuals had died from cyclosporiasis.
“Both individuals had significant underlying health conditions that may have been impacted by cyclosporiasis and dehydration,” the department said, noting that the parasitic infection is not typically life threatening.
Cyclosporiasis has been detected in 72 counties. Wayne, Oakland, Washtenaw, Ingham and Genesee counties have the highest number of reported cases.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The state health department announced on July 1 that it was investigating the outbreak, which is caused by the microscopic Cyclospora parasite and spreads through contaminated food or water. Symptoms can emerge two days to two weeks after exposure and include watery diarrhea, loss of appetite, weight loss, cramping, bloating, increased gas, nausea and fatigue.
On Thursday, the state dropped its recommendations for residents to purchase whole heads of lettuce rather than bagged salad greens, and to remove their outer layers, wash the inner leaves and cook them when possible. 
As new case reports slow and emergency department visits decline, the state is returning to its recommendation that residents observe basic food safety practices such as handwashing, separating foods that could contain harmful germs like raw meat or unwashed fruits and vegetables during preparation, and cooking food to the proper temperature to kill germs.
On July 17, Taylor Farms de Mexico issued a voluntary recall of iceberg lettuce products sourced from central Mexico. On July 24, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration said it is continuing its investigation into infections linked to iceberg lettuce from the region along with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and state and local health departments.
The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services says its data suggests that the majority of contaminated produce is likely no longer available for consumption, though it advises residents to continue to avoid recalled lettuce.
The CDC is issuing weekly updates on cyclosporiasis cases, documenting 10,468 cases as of Aug. 4, with 12,255 cases – mostly from Michigan – yet to be confirmed through laboratory testing.
The federal agency notes its reports do not include probable cases, which may result in lower case counts than those reported by state health departments. 
The CDC is investigating multiple clusters of Cyclospora cases including a multistate outbreak tied to iceberg lettuce affecting 15 states: Arkansas,  Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Michigan, Missouri, Nebraska, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania and West Virginia.
Michigan remains the hardest hit state, with the CDC recording more than 4,000 cases.

Rain is moving “Lions, Sea Serpents & Mermaids, Oh My!” inside the Copeland Maritime Center, where families can explore the creatures and legends that once filled sailors’ imaginations.
WILMINGTON, Del. — Mermaids, sea serpents and other legendary creatures will be taking shelter from the rain Saturday.
Because of expected rain and potentially poor weather, the Kalmar Nyckel Foundation is moving its Aug. 8 Second Saturday program from Fort Christina Park indoors to the Copeland Maritime Center at the Kalmar Nyckel Shipyard in Wilmington.
The free family program, “Lions, Sea Serpents & Mermaids, Oh My!,” runs from 1 to 4 p.m. and explores the monsters, mythical creatures and maritime folklore that accompanied sailors across largely unknown oceans for centuries.
Visitors will learn about mermaids, sea serpents, lions and other creatures that appeared in sailors’ stories and as decorations aboard sailing ships. Children also can create their own sea serpents as part of the hands-on program.
Sea Monsters Filled an Unknown World
Long before satellites, sonar and modern ocean science, sailors ventured into waters they could barely understand.
Enormous whales, giant squid, unusual fish, violent currents, strange sounds and sudden storms could all become the foundation for stories about something more frightening lurking below.
Across different cultures, those fears produced an extraordinary collection of sea monsters.
Greek mythology told of Scylla, a multiheaded monster that attacked passing sailors, and Charybdis, a deadly whirlpool capable of swallowing ships.
Norse and Scandinavian stories helped create the legend of the kraken, an enormous tentacled creature said to be capable of pulling ships beneath the waves.
Sea serpents appeared repeatedly in sailors’ accounts, with mariners describing enormous snake-like creatures rising from the water or swimming alongside their vessels.
Some sightings may have been whales, giant squid, oarfish or other real animals viewed under difficult conditions.
But when sailors could not explain what they saw, folklore could.
Mermaids Brought Beauty to the Danger
Mermaids became especially enduring because they represented something different from the traditional monster.
They were mysterious and potentially dangerous, but also beautiful and human.
Stories of beings combining human and aquatic features date back thousands of years. Over time, the familiar image emerged of a woman above the waist and a fish below.
For sailors months from home, the mermaid became a powerful combination of attraction and danger — much like the sea itself.
Even explorers reported seeing them. Christopher Columbus recorded a mermaid sighting in the Caribbean in 1493, although historians generally believe he probably saw manatees.
The account shows how sailors often interpreted unfamiliar things through stories they already knew.
When Monsters Appeared on Maps and Ships
Maritime monsters were not limited to stories.
Historic maps sometimes filled unknown waters with enormous fish, serpents and fantastic creatures, visually warning travelers that they were entering places humans did not fully understand.
Mythical creatures also appeared aboard ships as carvings and figureheads.
Lions might symbolize strength and courage, while women, gods and fantastic creatures could represent protection, identity or good fortune.
Saturday’s program uses those traditions to introduce families to a time when superstition and seamanship frequently traveled together.
Why Sea Monsters Still Fascinate Us
Science has explained many of the creatures and natural forces that once frightened sailors, but sea monsters never disappeared.
The kraken, sea serpent and mermaid remain familiar characters in books, movies, television and popular culture.
Part of their appeal may come from the same mystery that fascinated sailors centuries ago.
Humans know far more about the oceans today, but the deepest waters remain difficult to explore and new marine species continue to be identified.
We know legendary krakens probably were not pulling sailing ships underwater, but giant squid are real.
There is no evidence mermaids exist, but sailors genuinely reported seeing them.
And some ancient stories about frightening waters appear to have been inspired by very real maritime hazards.
That mixture of fact, fear and imagination is what keeps sea-monster folklore alive.
A Delaware Maritime Connection
The setting adds another layer to Saturday’s program.
Today’s Kalmar Nyckel is a full-scale replica of the Swedish colonial ship associated with the establishment of New Sweden in the Delaware Valley in 1638.
The replica was built at the Wilmington shipyard and today serves as a floating classroom and ambassador for Delaware maritime history.
Saturday’s event explores another part of that history — not simply how sailors crossed the ocean, but what they imagined might be traveling beneath them.
And while mermaids may still get much of the attention, they were only one creature in a much larger and stranger world of maritime folklore.

Where: Copeland Maritime Center at the Kalmar Nyckel Shipyard, 1124 E. Seventh St., Wilmington.
What to expect: Sea monsters, mermaids, sea serpents, maritime folklore, ship symbolism and hands-on family activities.
Cost: Free.
Who: Families and visitors of all ages interested in maritime history and folklore.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico environment department updates public comment portal following fraud reports
description: The New Mexico Environment Department on Friday announced a change to its public comment portal, following reports of fraudulent submissions in support of a controversial data center's air quality permits.
text:
A rendering of Project Jupiter with public comments alleging that canvassers falsely signed a resident’s name to a pro-Project Jupiter letter without his knowledge or consent. (Courtesy of STACK Infrastructure)The New Mexico Environment Department on Friday announced a change to its public comment portal, following reports of fraudulent submissions in support of a controversial data center’s air quality permits.
Source New Mexico reported in June that residents from three New Mexico cities said their names falsely appeared on letters urging state environment officials to approve air quality permits for the Project Jupiter data center after they were approached by canvassers for the project.
An environment department news release on Friday said the department thus far had been notified that approximately 42 of the more than 17,500 comments submitted through the Department’s public comment portal on the air quality permit application for project developer Yucca Growth Infrastructure may have been fraudulent, including ones submitted for public officials.
New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez in July opened an investigation the allegations of fraudulent submissions. In its news release Friday, NMED said it had shared information from the public comment portal with NMDOJ for its investigation and, depending on the outcome, “may pursue appropriate civil or criminal action against those responsible.”
Under the new protocol, people submitting public comments with an email address will receive an automated confirmation email that will give them the opportunity to confirm their comments or notify the Department if they did not submit or authorize them.
“The new process will allow individuals to quickly identify and report potentially fraudulent comments while preserving a simple and accessible process for legitimate public participation,” the news release stated.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Flock cameras are causing an uproar in CT — and everywhere else
authors: Davis Dunavin | WSHU and Ava Keogh | WSHU
description: The CT town of Milford has become a front line for opposition to Flock cameras after a raucous town meeting.
text:
They’re meant to see everything. But in the past few weeks, Flock cameras have been seen seemingly everywhere, and not for good reason.
A Florida man staged a solo protest by blocking one camera with a pool skimmer. In one Minnesota town, someone cut down every Flock camera overnight. And comedian John Oliver devoted his show this week to privacy and civil rights concerns around the cameras.
The cameras are motion-activated and use AI to log license plates and other vehicle identifiers. Supporters say they crack down on stolen vehicles and investigate crimes. Opponents say they’re a violation of privacy and civil rights — and that there’s no way to know who’s watching or why.
Now the town of Milford, Connecticut has become a front line for opposition to the cameras after a raucous town meeting.
“All these Flock cameras have nothing to do with safety! They have to do with control!” said resident Tony de Blasio, who said he was a former Marine, at the meeting.
“This isn’t a partisan issue. I don’t care who’s in this room. There are Democrats and Republicans. We all want this done.”
The list of speakers that night bore him out. Local candidates from both major parties spoke against the cameras.
“Benjamin Franklin once said those who would give up essential liberty to purchase a temporary safety deserve neither liberty nor safety,” Democrat Andrew Rice said. “If you want safety, then give the people resources that they need to live decent lives.”
Republican Chris Lancia, who spoke immediately after Rice, said he’s worked in telecommunications for decades building cameras like Flock.
“What can’t a police officer do that these cameras don’t?” Lancia said. “You want the speeding to stop? Put a police cruiser there. Let our officers do their job. Stop being soft on crime. These cameras need to go.”
Milford police chief Keith Mello’s the one who proposed them in the first place. He said he still thinks they’re a good idea, especially because he doesn’t have enough cops as it is.
“I’ll say now, if you don’t trust police or you don’t trust the government, you don’t trust big business, there’s probably not a lot that I can do to convince you other than tell you this is the best information that we have,” Mello said.
Milford officials voted to consider a moratorium on the cameras next month.
But in the meantime, state leaders — including Milford’s own representative in Hartford — are already speaking out.
Senate Majority Leader Bob Duff and State Senator James Maroney of Milford said the cameras are an invasive technology. They said residents have a right to be concerned, and deserve answers about who’s watching and why.
The state of Connecticut will conduct a survey on the number of cameras and how they are used to strengthen protection acts and technology regulations in 2027.
This story was first published Aug. 7, 2026 by WSHU.

title: Conservative group’s ‘right to natural gas’ initiative makes Colorado’s 2026 ballot
description: Amid a historic drought, record heat and a deadly wildfire season, Coloradans will be asked by a right-wing “dark money” group this year to enshrine a “right” to a major source of climate pollution in the state constitution. Backers of Initiative 177, led by the group Advance Colorado, submitted enough petition signatures to qualify for […]
text:
A flare stack burns at a natural gas facility in Garfield County on May 16, 2023. (Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)Amid a historic drought, record heat and a deadly wildfire season, Coloradans will be asked by a right-wing “dark money” group this year to enshrine a “right” to a major source of climate pollution in the state constitution.
Backers of Initiative 177, led by the group Advance Colorado, submitted enough petition signatures to qualify for the November ballot, the Colorado secretary of state’s office said Thursday. Sponsors submitted 189,508 total signatures, 146,165 of which were deemed to be valid, and as a constitutional measure, it cleared the required 2% support in each of the 35 state Senate districts.
Initiative 177 proposes a two-sentence constitutional amendment that would give consumers the right to buy natural gas for cooking and heating, as well as producers the right to sell it.
“Consumers have the right to purchase natural gas for cooking or heating in homes or businesses throughout the state,” the measure reads. “Distributors and utilities have the right to sell natural gas for homes or businesses.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The use of natural gas as a fuel for appliances in homes and businesses accounts for roughly 15% of Colorado’s annual greenhouse gas emissions. State policymakers have set a goal of net-zero emissions by 2050, largely through incentives and investments encouraging a transition to electric appliances.
Advance Colorado, which does not disclose its donors, calls state policies “limiting the use of natural gas … economically incompatible with citizens’ energy needs.”
The group’s backing of Initiative 177 — which resembles previous measures floated by the oil and gas industry to establish constitutional protections for “energy choice” and bar state and local governments from restricting natural gas use — comes despite a mutual agreement between industry and environmental groups not to new pursue ballot measures until 2028. Advance Colorado has said it wasn’t a party to that deal.
Earlier this year, an effort by Democratic lawmakers to put unspecified “guardrails” around Initiative 177’s potential implementation was announced by legislative leaders but then dropped in the final days of the session. Environmental advocates, who initially argued the “truce” regarding oil and gas ballot measures had been broken by Advance Colorado, introduced two measures of their own in response, but did not move forward with signature gathering.
Initiative 177 is one of as many as 14 citizen initiatives that could appear on Colorado’s 2026 ballot. Seven measures have already qualified. The secretary of state’s office is required to determine the sufficiency of the remaining seven measures no later than Sept. 2.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Tennessee voters oust Trump-backed congressman and set matchup for redrawn Memphis-area US House seat
authors: David A. Lieb and Kristin M. Hall, Associated Press
description: People vote at a polling place in a primary election Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026, in Memphis, Tenn.
text:
MEMPHIS, Tenn. — Former Tennessee Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher defeated U.S. Rep. Andy Ogles in a Republican primary Thursday for a significantly reshaped congressional district — marking a rare rejection of a candidate endorsed by President Donald Trump.
Voters also picked a pair of Memphis-area lawmakers to square off in another vastly reconfigured U.S. House district. Trump-backed state Sen. Brent Taylor will face Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson, who gained national prominence when he was expelled from the Tennessee House for protesting in support of gun control measures and then reelected by voters.
The primaries provided the first test of a new U.S. House map that was redrawn in May by Republican state lawmakers after the U.S. Supreme Court weakened federal Voting Rights Act protections for minorities. Trump cheered along the redistricting as part of a broader national plan to try to hold on to a slim House majority in the midterm elections.
Republicans already hold eight of the state’s nine congressional seats and will be going for a clean sweep of the districts in November.
The previously compact 9th Congressional District, based in Memphis, had a majority Black population and is represented by a Democrat. But it was cracked apart by Republicans this year, causing a ripple of changes that also reconfigured Ogles’ 5th District.
A Trump-endorsed candidate is defeated
Ogles, a member of the conservative Freedom Caucus, had faced controversies related to his campaign finances and his resume, among other things. But Trump gave him an early endorsement last fall — and praised him on Election Day as “a Conservative Warrior” — as Ogles sought a third term.
Ogles capitalized on a previous redistricting in the 2022 elections, winning a formerly Democratic-held seat that was reshaped to Republicans’ advantage by splitting the Nashville area among three districts.
The new 5th District stretches from Ogles’ base in central Tennessee to the northwest corner of the state before snaking south along the Mississippi River to Memphis — with 82% of its voters new, according to an Associated Press estimate.
Although he lacked Trump’s endorsement, Hatcher was backed by Republican Gov. Bill Lee, under whom he served for seven years. Hatcher campaigned as pro-Trump while emphasizing his farming background.
“The message resonated, and the message was: Work like a farmer, get things done and serve others,” Hatcher told the AP after winning the primary.
Ogles’ campaign declined to comment. Ogles’ controversies have included the FBI seizing his cellphone in 2024 as part of an investigation into his campaign finance reporting. The Justice Department recently agreed to return the device, signaling that it was abandoning the probe, which began under the Biden administration.
In 2023, Ogles acknowledged that he had graduated with a liberal studies degree from Middle Tennessee State University, saying he was “mistaken” for previously describing it as an international relations degree.
Columbia Mayor Chaz Molder won the Democratic primary in the 5th District.
Democratic congressional candidate State Rep. Justin J. Pearson, D-Memphis, speaks to supporters at a primary election night party on Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026, in Memphis, Tenn. Credit: AP Photo/George Walker IV
Pearson and Taylor to face off in revamped Memphis district
The new 9th District stretches about 200 miles east from Memphis across rural areas before reaching north toward Nashville. It previously favored Democrats but now tilts Republican, with 71% of voters new to the district, according to an AP estimate.
After the redistricting, longtime Democratic Rep. Steve Cohen announced that he would no longer seek reelection.
Pearson noted to supporters Thursday night that it was 61 years ago to the day that the Voting Rights Act was signed. He said the Supreme Court and Tennessee lawmakers have effectively undone portions of it, leading to the redrawing of the formerly majority-Black district.
“The political dilution and degradation of our rights is happening,” Pearson said. But he added: “We’re one step closer to Washington, D.C.”
Taylor said in a statement to supporters that “Pearson is the face of the extreme left in this race — the same activist who has repeatedly put chaos over order.”
Republican congressional candidate State Sen. Brent Taylor, R-Memphis, speaks to a supporter outside an early voting polling place Friday, July 24, 2026, in Brentwood, Tenn.  Credit: AP Photo/George Walker IV
While Pearson opposed Trump’s deployment of National Guard troops to address crime in Memphis last year, Taylor joined other Republicans in supporting it, calling it “an investment.”
Taylor also sponsored a 2024 law that required law enforcement agencies to communicate with federal immigration authorities if they discover people are in the country illegally.
Memphis voters voice dismay over redistricting
For decades Memphis, the most populous city in Shelby County, formed the base of its own congressional district. Now the county is split among three districts that extend outward like spokes into rural areas.
Lonzo Taylor, a retired postal worker and military veteran, said Black voters like himself have had their voices diluted.
“We only had one district in the whole state of Tennessee, and you don’t even want that to be fair? It’s just terrible,” said Taylor, 72. “I love this state, but I am very disappointed in our governor,” who called lawmakers into a special session for the redistricting.
Terrice Thomas, 45, an educator who votes for Democrats, had to learn a lot more about the candidates when she got switched from District 9 to District 8. She is concerned Memphis constituents could get overlooked.
“Is everybody going to have an equal say on what’s happening in their communities or even the people that you’re voting for?” Thomas said. “Are they going to really take into account the different areas and what makes us unique?”
Garrett wins GOP primary for open seat in 6th District
Republican U.S. Rep. John Rose opted not to seek reelection in the 6th to run for governor instead. That created a contentious primary for the GOP-leaning district, which stretches east from Nashville.
State Rep. Johnny Garrett won a Republican contest that included Rose’s recent chief of staff, former U.S. Rep. Van Hilleary. Mike Croley won a five-way Democratic primary.
Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., speaks during a ceremony to rename a bridge after President Donald J. Trump, Thursday, July 9, 2026, in Dandridge, Tenn.  Credit: AP Photo/George Walker IV
Republican voters pick Blackburn for governor
U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who is a Mississippi native, defeated Rose in the GOP primary to succeed Gov. Lee, who is barred by term limits from seeking reelection. Memphis City Council member Jerri Green won for the Democrats.
Republicans have held the governor’s office since 2011 and won every U.S. Senate election since 1994.
Sen. Bill Hagerty won the Republican primary without opposition and will face Marquita Bradshaw, who won the Democratic nomination, in November.
___
Lieb reported from Jefferson City, Missouri. AP writer Geoff Mulvihill in Haddonfield, New Jersey, contributed.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: ISU researchers develop kits to help stoke the biomanufacturing industry
description: Researchers at Iowa State University are working to increase interest in biomanufacturing with bioreactor kits that can be used at community colleges or high schools.  Nigel Reuel, an associate professor and the Stanley Chair in interdisciplinary engineering at ISU, said students and parents understand more traditional career paths, like nursing or teaching,[...]
text:
Researchers at Iowa State University and Novonesis are developing classroom bioreactor kits to help boost interest in the burgeoning biomanufacturing field. Pictured is a commercial scale bioreactor. (Photo by Lance Cheung/USDA) Researchers at Iowa State University are working to increase interest in biomanufacturing with bioreactor kits that can be used at community colleges or high schools. 
Nigel Reuel, an associate professor and the Stanley Chair in interdisciplinary engineering at ISU, said students and parents understand more traditional career paths, like nursing or teaching, but usually are unfamiliar with the field of biomanufacturing. 
He said the idea is that the kits will introduce students to the “really cool industry in biomanufacturing.” 
“This gives students early on an ability to be really hands-on and see, like, ‘Oh, I get it!,’” Reuel said. “We grow the cells; it makes this thing, and that’s a product. It allows them to see that this could be a really kind of interesting career path.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Biomanufacturing uses fermentation and chemical processes to turn agricultural materials, like corn, soybeans or plant residues into everyday products. Common biomanufactured products include pharmaceuticals and vaccines, fuel, chemicals, plastics, textiles and other consumer products. 
Reuel said it’s likely the field will continue to grow as the manufacturing industry looks for alternatives to petroleum-based materials and the agriculture sector vies for additional domestic markets for corn and soybeans. 
“There’s huge facilities, high paying, great jobs, and honestly, they’re just kind of hurting for a pipeline because no one really thinks about it,” Reuel said. “It’s not something that a high school counselor is going to sit you down and talk about.”
The research team that came up with the Bioreactor Educational Activity Kits, called BREAKs, didn’t set out with the goal of making something for the classroom. 
An early version of the Bioreactor Educational Activity Kits, or BREAK. (Photo courtesy of ISU)
Reuel said the team was working on a grant funded project with the biosolutions company Novonesis to monitor and take control of bioreactors using artificial intelligence. Reuel said to track enzyme activity in a bioreactor and gather data that could be fed into the reinforcement learning AI model, ISU and Novonesis researchers needed access to a “small array of reactors.” 
Bioreactors are “fancy” tanks that can grow bacteria or cells rapidly, Reuel explained. Sometimes the cells themselves are the product, or other times, manufacturers want a product that is secreted by certain types of cells, like a specific enzyme. 
Reuel said there weren’t any solutions on the market for small, “open source” bioreactors that would meet the goals of the team working to inform the AI model, so they used common parts and made their own small bioreactors for around $300 a piece. 
He later pitched the idea to the nonprofit Schmidt Futures and BioMADE, the U.S. Department of Defense sponsored Manufacturing Innovation Institute, and secured funding to turn the reactors into a product for community colleges and advanced high school science classes. 
“You don’t really know how something works until you have something that you can take apart and break,” Reuel said. “The idea is that the bioreactor that comes in a box … students can play around with it, build it, grow their own bacteria … at a cost point where it’s not prohibitive.”
Reuel said it will probably take about a year before the kits are ready for orders, but already, the project has secured a partnership with Des Moines Area Community College to develop curriculum around the kits. 
The kits are also part of the RuralSTAMINA Biomanufacturing Engine, a U.S. National Science Foundation initiative to “turn agricultural resources into new high-value products, create competitive jobs, and unleash economic opportunities.” 
Reuel is chief technology officer of the engine, which received $160 million from NSF for 10 years to connect research, manufacturing, workforce and other resources across the biomanufacturing industries in Iowa and Nebraska.
He said a focus of the engine is training people for the biomanufacturing workforce and keeping the corn belt states “as the center of of the universe in terms of biomanufacturing”
“This is going to be a big deal,” Reuel said.

title: Todd Blanche confirmed by the US Senate as attorney general; Collins, Murkowski vote no
text: WASHINGTON — After a lengthy battle over the status of President Donald Trump’s nearly $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund, Todd Blanche was confirmed as attorney general by the U.S. Senate early Saturday.Blanche, the acting attorney general, won approval to take the role permanently after GOP Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana said he would back him, a turning point for Blanche’s nomination push. The vote at about 4:30 a.m. Eastern was 50-49, with Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., absent due to health issues.Republican Sens. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Susan Collins of Maine joined all Democrats in opposing the confirmation of Blanche, Trump’s personal defense attorney before joining the government at the start of Trump’s second term. “I am deeply honored by the trust and confidence President Trump has placed in me to lead the Department of Justice as our great nation’s 88th Attorney General.  I am grateful to the Senate for staying late to complete this process. To the dedicated public servants of the Department of Justice, thank you for your work each day to uphold the law and keep our country safe,” Blanche said in a statement on social media following the vote. “God bless America.”Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., blasted Blanche’s confirmation.“Senate Republicans have handed Trump an excuse on a silver platter to keep up his pervasive, breathtaking corruption,” he said in a statement.  “If you want to wipe out corruption, you can’t have the president’s personal attorney as the Attorney General. You don’t need a PhD in political science to know that.“Todd Blanche has no intention of stopping Trump’s corruption. He advanced his career enabling it. Every senator who voted to confirm him has now branded themselves as an enabler, too.”The Senate adjourned for its summer recess about an hour after the vote and will not return to regular session until Sept. 14.Cassidy explanationCassidy, who has long clashed with Trump, said in a Friday floor speech his vote was not a reflection of that relationship, but about the importance of having a Senate-confirmed attorney general who had the backing of U.S. attorneys in Louisiana and former Attorney General Bill Barr.“Mr. Blanche is not perfect, and he will tell you this, but the choice is not between perfection and Mr. Blanche,” he said. “It is between Mr. Blanche and another acting attorney general who may not run the department effectively under President Trump… All considered, I will vote for Mr. Blanche.”Cassidy held the determinative vote on Blanche following Murkowski’s announcement earlier Friday she would oppose his confirmation. Collins had said earlier in the week she would vote against confirmation. Trump announced Blanche in June as his pick for the top role at the Justice Department, replacing Pam Bondi.Cassidy alluded to his strained relationship with Trump. He voted to convict in Trump’s second impeachment trial that covered Trump’s conduct leading to the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol. Cassidy lost his primary race to a Trump-backed challenger this year.“I have a history with Mr. Trump,” he said. “But that history does not matter one bit.”Murkowski oppositionIn a social media post, Murkowski — another Republican at whom Trump has leveled strong criticism, including as recently as a podcast interview published early Friday morning — said the country needed an attorney general able to “check the worst impulses of this administration,” and that she lacked confidence in Blanche to do that.Cassidy seemed to hold a similar objective, but reached a different conclusion about Blanche’s ability.Trump is often unwilling to take advice, Cassidy said, but a competent, Senate-confirmed attorney general with whom Trump has a close relationship might be better equipped than whoever else Trump would choose to run the department.Cassidy said that in a recent conversation with Barr, who had his own clashes with the president during and after his time as attorney general in Trump’s first term, the former attorney general endorsed Blanche as someone who could “run the department as effectively as anyone can under President Trump.” “Some have called that faint praise,” Cassidy said. “I don't think that it is. I think it is a reality.”Trump has expanded presidential decision-making at the Department of Justice, which, at least since the Watergate scandal of the 1970s, has been viewed as operating independently from the White House.Ultimately, the attorney general answers to the president, Cassidy said.‘Slush fund’ concernsCassidy criticized Blanche’s role in creating a fund for “victims of lawfare,” including those convicted of Jan. 6-related charges, and in approving a settlement with the IRS that gave Trump and his family broad immunity from tax prosecution.“Mr. Blanche showed poor judgment in approving the anti-weaponization slush fund and exempting the president from IRS audits,” Cassidy said.Blanche acknowledged those “mistakes” and “made efforts to kill the slush fund,” Cassidy said.Blanche wrote a memo this week that said the fund would not move forward and that the IRS agreement only applied retroactively, not to future prosecutions. That move was enough to win over Republican holdouts on the Senate Judiciary Committee, Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Cornyn of Texas.Murkowski on Friday raised doubts that the fund would be dissolved if the Senate voted to confirm Blanche and loses leverage with the administration, but again, Cassidy appeared to reach a different conclusion.Senate Judiciary Chairman Chuck Grassley, an Iowa Republican, praised the confirmation vote and spoke in favor of Blanche’s nomination on the Senate floor.“Beyond his obvious qualifications and successful track record, Blanche has demonstrated extraordinary patience, compassion and tenacity as he’s made his way through the gauntlet of the Senate’s advice and consent process,” Grassley said in a statement. “He’s been forthcoming and responsive to my colleagues and has proven himself to be a steadfast advocate for the rule of law. Today, the United States Senate voted to confirm Todd Blanche’s nomination and advance the safety and security of Americans nationwide.”  Confirmation bestows legitimacy Cassidy noted that Blanche did not need Senate approval, and that he could continue doing the job in an acting capacity.But a major factor in voting to confirm Blanche was that people within the department viewed Senate confirmation as crucial to an attorney general’s influence.“I am told that Senate confirmation is important in interactions with the president, with others in the Cabinet and is important to DOJ employees in general,” Cassidy said. “Being Senate-confirmed gives him greater leverage to push for things that should be pushed for.”Cassidy also said he spoke to Louisiana U.S. Attorneys David Courcelle and Kurt Wall, who told him having a Senate-confirmed attorney general was important and that Blanche was more than capable. They praised Blanche for quickly providing resources when they asked, Cassidy said.“I cannot overstate Mr. Walls’ and Mr. Courcelle’s support for Mr. Blanche,” he said.
