name: North Carolina Newsline
title: North Carolina high schoolers show improvements in mental health
description: One of the most vexing problems caused by the pandemic was the toll it took on the mental health of young people. Students struggled with school closures, isolation from their friends, and the difficulties of remote learning. But after years of focus on behavioral health, it appears that North Carolina high school students are doing […]
text:
A new survey shows the mental health of North Carolina's high school students is improving, but experts say more investments are needed in school psychologists and social workers. (Photo: iStock/Getty Photo) One of the most vexing problems caused by the pandemic was the toll it took on the mental health of young people. Students struggled with school closures, isolation from their friends, and the difficulties of remote learning.
But after years of focus on behavioral health, it appears that North Carolina high school students are doing better. That’s according to the 2025 North Carolina High School Youth Risk Behavior Survey, which was presented to the State Board of Education this week.
Researchers examined the responses from 1,692 students from 25 traditional public and charter high schools who voluntarily participated in the survey during the spring of 2025.
Dr. Ellen Essick, section chief for N.C. Healthy Schools in the state Department of Public Instruction, said the percentage of high schoolers who said they felt so sad or hopeless they stopped doing their normal activities for at least two weeks dropped to 29.7%.
“We’ve still got work to do, but it was good to see that drop from that high of 43% in 2021,” said Essick.
Dr. Ellen Essick, Section Chief for NC Healthy Schools, Department of Public Instruction (Photo: NCDPI)
North Carolina also saw a double-digit decline in the percent of high schoolers who said they had seriously considered attempting suicide. In 2021, 22.3% of students said they had considered ending their life. In 2025, that number fell to 11.4%.
“This is the lowest it’s been in a 20-year period,” said Essick. “If we can address some of the needs before they get to a place of contemplating suicide, then I think that totally helps us in terms of how we support students.”
Fourteen percent of the students in this latest survey acknowledged needing mental health counseling, but did not get it.
Taking a deeper dive into the data, 56% of high schoolers who self-reported making Ds and Fs in school felt sad or hopeless, compared to 22% of their counterparts who said they made mostly As in school.
“We don’t know if poor grades came first and then the mental health issues came, or mental health issues contributed to poor grades,” said Essick.
Jill Camnitz, who represents northeastern North Carolina on the State Board of Education, said it was “heartbreaking” that almost two in 10 high-school students say they have poor mental health most of the time, with one in 10 considering suicide.
One in four NC teens experience depression. Can peer-to-peer support improve their mental health? 

 Social media and addictive substance use decline 
“But I also put a lot of hope in the fact that we’re seeing a decrease in the use of social media, because we know that those are very deeply connected,” said Camnitz.
In the behavioral survey, the share of students who said they used social media more than once an hour or several times a day declined 4.5% over the last two years.
In January, a new law took effect restricting cell phones in the classroom. Educators say it has had a positive impact in reducing social media use during the school day and improving emotional well-being.
Alcohol use among North Carolina high schoolers who self-reported declined more than 26% since 2005. Marijuana use also declined more than 10% in the same period.
The state has also made headway in discouraging teen tobacco use and vaping. Only 3.5% say they currently smoke cigarettes. Nearly 13% of high schoolers routinely used vaping products, down from 21% in 2023.
 Improving school-based mental health services 
On the whole, students who were surveyed reported lower substance use and lower rates of fighting and safety-related absences than in the past. But Essick said the state must continue to invest in training support personnel, who may be the first to identify a problem and then serve as a bridge in making a referral.
School psychologists and psychiatrists have been in short supply in North Carolina for years. According to the N.C. School Psychology Association, 23 school districts in North Carolina have zero full-time school psychologists.
Essick is hopeful that will change.
In the past two years, North Carolina has received four mental health grants from the U.S. Department of Education totaling $29 million to help recruit more school social workers and counselors.
Earlier this year, the Department of Public Instruction announced a $4.8 million grant to fund salary and housing stipends for school psychologist interns to serve in high-need and rural districts. The grant supports supervision for those interns and practicing school psychologists.
“We have 10 interns already placed for this coming year. Some of those are from out of state, which is what we need because we don’t have enough [psychologists] produced in North Carolina,” said Essick. “If we can get somebody to come from out of state, then that’s one more professional we get in our schools.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: No silver bullet, no single fuel: What Texas can teach the Carolinas about energy resilience
description: What do record-setting heat waves, hurricane season, and severe droughts all have in common? They all create strain on the power grid, threaten reliability, and drive up costs. Duke Energy, which serves customers throughout the Carolinas, forecasts a demand increase eight times the pace of the prior 15 years due to economic development, population growth, […[...]
text:
Solar panels and wind turbines. (Photo: Marga Buschbell-Steeger/Getty Images)What do record-setting heat waves, hurricane season, and severe droughts all have in common? They all create strain on the power grid, threaten reliability, and drive up costs.
Duke Energy, which serves customers throughout the Carolinas, forecasts a demand increase eight times the pace of the prior 15 years due to economic development, population growth, and electrification. Managing energy affordability and reliability will be a balancing act, and energy experts across the political spectrum recognize that no single resource will be a silver bullet. What we do need is an “all of the above” energy approach.
A state that has fully embraced that approach is one you may not at first expect, yet it should get a gold (lone) star for its balanced generation mix. Texas has always been a major energy producer, but over the last decade it has invested in enough renewable energy to produce almost half of its total energy supply. This growth in renewable energy is not attributed to climate goals. It is driven by lower costs and long-term planning.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Wind and solar are among the cheapest and fastest forms of new energy generation. Texas has taken advantage of these low-cost resources and emerged as a clean energy leader by adding roughly 14,000 MW of wind and 19,000 MW of solar in five years. As a result, renewables generate 30% of the state’s electricity — enough to power nearly 10 million homes.
In North Carolina, renewables provide about 15% of electricity generation, while South Carolina remains closer to 8%. While both states have made progress in solar expansion in recent years, and North Carolina has two utility-scale wind projects online, the pace of development is much slower.
When it comes to energy, Texas and the Carolinas do have a few things in common. First, they both need affordable energy that is not affected by fluctuating fuel prices, and second, they need a reliable system during times of peak demand. Wind and solar check both of these boxes. They are quick-to-deploy resources that prove valuable during extreme weather and peak demand periods. They also apply downward pressure on energy costs by allowing utilities to use free renewable energy first, reducing the need to run more expensive resources.
History shows us that natural gas prices spike dramatically during severe weather events, which ultimately impacts ratepayers. By investing in fuel-free resources like wind and solar, Texas has built a more diversified resource mix that protects customers from sudden swings in fuel costs. During extreme conditions, such as hurricanes and winter storms, wind, solar, and battery storage help keep electricity affordable by stabilizing prices and reducing reliance on expensive fuel purchases.
People often criticize wind and solar because they aren’t considered baseload generation, but this overlooks the fact that grid operators can predict how much energy they will produce days in advance. Fossil fuels have reliability challenges too. Fuel supplies and prices can be disrupted by extreme weather or global events, often with little warning. Extreme weather can compromise gas infrastructure just as demand peaks, creating reliability challenges and price spikes. Unlike renewable variability, these problems are hard to predict and difficult for grid operators to control.
The July 4th weekend was one of the hottest stretch of the summer so far, and electricity demand climbed with the heat. Off the coast of New York, South Fork Wind ran at an average capacity factor of 74.7%. That included a capacity factor of nearly 90% on July 2, the day that the New York Independent System Operator issued an energy watch due to a decline in operating margins.
While summer loads remain critical, planning forecasts project that the combined winter peak demand for Duke Energy Carolinas and Duke Energy Progress will grow by more than 6,000 megawatts over the next 25 years—an increase of more than 20% over today’s system. Wind energy tends to produce strongly during winter peak periods, making it well-positioned to help meet growing winter demand, strengthen grid resilience, and diversify the Carolinas’ energy mix against future extreme weather events.
The Carolinas are staring at a future of growth and pressure on an aging system. As we plan for tomorrow’s energy needs, we can’t pretend that every resource does the same job. Texas has recognized the economic and energy security benefits of an “all of the above” strategy. It’s time for the Carolinas to build a portfolio that is less fragile, less exposed to fuel shocks, and more predictable over time. A resilient grid.
Jocelyn Juliano is program manager at the Southeastern Wind Coalition in Chapel Hill, N.C.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: July heat produces ‘flash drought’ with more than half of North Dakota affected
description: More than half of North Dakota is now in a drought, with blistering July heat shriveling crops and taking a toll on pastures.  The U.S. Drought Monitor, which is updated weekly on Thursdays, shows a third of the state in moderate drought and more than 23% in extreme drought. The extreme drought area increased dramatically […]
text:
A soybean plant suffers from a lack of moisture in a sandy area of field in Griggs County, North Dakota, on July 31, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Jeff Stachler/NDSU Extension)More than half of North Dakota is now in a drought, with blistering July heat shriveling crops and taking a toll on pastures. 
The U.S. Drought Monitor, which is updated weekly on Thursdays, shows a third of the state in moderate drought and more than 23% in extreme drought. The extreme drought area increased dramatically from the previous week, when less than 9% of the state was in that category. 
“July was one of the warmest and driest on record, and so in turn we had some very rapid shift into dry conditions across the state,” Daryl Ritchison, state climatologist for North Dakota, said Thursday. 
The severe drought areas include a pocket in central North Dakota, much of the southwest corner and Cass, Traill and Steele counties in the east. 
The U.S. Drought Monitor map updated on Aug. 6, 2026, with more than half of North Dakota in a drought stage. (Screenshot from U.S. Drought Monitor)
Ritchison helps prepare weekly recommendations for changes in the U.S. Drought Monitor, and this week recommend the Sheridan County area in central North Dakota jump up two categories, from abnormally dry to severe drought. 
Miranda Meehan of North Dakota State University Extension helps facilitate reporting of pasture and crop conditions around the state. Unlike some years of prolonged dry weather, she said conditions have changed quickly this year, with several days of 100-plus degree heat in July. 
“This is almost like a flash drought,” Meehan said. “It was dry, but then with the heat, it just really intensified things.”
None of North Dakota is in the extreme or exceptional drought categories, which can be found in other areas of the western United States
Ritchison submits recommendations for which areas of the state fall into drought categories. He relies in part on a system called CMOR — Condition Monitoring Observations and Reports. People can submit photos, comments and anecdotal information through the nationwide system. 
There has been a spike in the number of comments submitted from North Dakota in the last week, with reports of lost crop yields, dried up watering holes for livestock and pastures that can’t be grazed. 
“Our alfalfa dried up, as we could not take a second cutting and our first cutting was only 40 bales compared to 60 last year,” Angie Johnson reported from northern Cass and southern Traill and Steele counties. “In many areas, the corn crop is completely fried and will have no yield. Soybeans and edible beans have aborted pods.”  
Cattle kick up dust in a dry pasture in Golden Valley County in western North Dakota in July 2026. (Photo courtesy of NDSU Extension)
Ranchers are having to pull livestock off of pastures early, instead using what feed they may have on hand. Some producers are baling crops to use as livestock feed instead of trying to sell  poor quality grain at the elevator. 
Ed Kessel farms near Dickinson in western North Dakota. He said farmers bale crops every year in his area where more producers also have livestock to feed, but he is seeing more of it this year. He is concerned that his wheat crop yield will be down and that it won’t meet milling quality standards, which could mean a steep price discount when he sells. 
An annual mid-July wheat tour to estimate yields put the North Dakota crop at a respectable 48 bushels per acre. But Kessel said the prolonged hot and dry weather means the yields will not be as good as projected.
“The heat took a lot of bushels away from us,” Kessel said. 
NDSU Extension provides recommendations to producers for managing a drought. 
Meehan said producers need to be careful about alternative feed sources. She said some baled crops can be high in nitrates and can be potentially fatal to an animal or an unborn calf. Similarly, shrunken watering holes can have poor water quality and should be tested. 
Meehan encouraged people to keep submitting reports through CMOR to create an accurate drought picture. Some U.S. Department of Agriculture drought relief programs are triggered by an area being in a severe drought and the reports can be helpful when applying for federal disaster assistance. 
Ritchison said he tries to read every comment. “Citizen science can very much help,” he said.
Reach North Dakota Monitor deputy editor Jeff Beach at jbeach@northdakotamonitor.com

title: Nebraska education commissioner says 5% spending cut won’t apply to school funding formula
description: LINCOLN — Nebraska’s education commissioner said a 5% spending cut Gov. Jim Pillen requested from all state agencies won’t apply to the state’s school funding formula. Commissioner Brian Maher provided an update on the Nebraska Department of Education’s response to the governor’s spending memo at a State Board of Education meeting Thursday. While portions of[...]
text:
Nebraska Education Commissioner Brian Maher of Lincoln talks to reporters after the first meeting of the School Financing Review Commission. Aug. 12, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Nebraska’s education commissioner said a 5% spending cut Gov. Jim Pillen requested from all state agencies won’t apply to the state’s school funding formula.
Commissioner Brian Maher provided an update on the Nebraska Department of Education’s response to the governor’s spending memo at a State Board of Education meeting Thursday. While portions of the memo will not impact the department, he said, it will require them to cut roughly $2.3 million in the agency’s current budget.
Pillen issued the memo in July, asking state agencies to immediately cut spending by a minimum of 5% on a month-to-month basis, which is expected to be in effect for both the current budget and the next biennium starting July 1, 2027. Maher noted the memo does not have the enforcement power that a statute or executive order holds, but it does signal the state’s long-term budget woes with multiple projected deficits on the horizon.
After meeting with members of the governor’s office, Maher said department officials learned that the 5% cut would not apply to the more than $2 billion in state aid going to schools, including Tax Equity and Educational Opportunities Support Act (TEEOSA) funds. It also would not apply to roughly $93 million in federal funding allocated to the department.
What’s left over is about $46.5 million in general fund dollars going to the department. Finance Officer Bryce Wilson said about $21 million of that amount is fixed costs that cannot be pulled, and parts of the remaining $25 million are also earmarked for specific purposes.
“Once we start throwing all those things together, it is not an easy task to come up with a 5% reduction for the department,” Wilson said.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
There are five different “buckets” of legislative funding that could be pulled from, Wilson said. The largest is administrative costs, which was appropriated roughly $36.5 million between the state’s general fund and various cash funds. Others include the state’s vocational rehabilitation program and services for the deaf, blind and visually impaired.
No decisions about the cuts were made at the meeting. Maher said in addition to examining the funding buckets, department officials are following the governor’s advice to increase scrutiny on travel expenses and eliminate “nonessential activities.”
“I would tell you I don’t have any (activities) to say,” Maher told the board. “But we’re having some conversations on some things that we’re looking at, saying ‘Does that really help further the cause of the Nebraska Department of Education?’ And I think that’s probably a good conversation that you should have.”
Pillen’s memo also requested a hiring freeze across state agencies, but Maher said the governor’s representatives told them that order likely doesn’t apply to the Education Department. However, Maher said he intends to follow the request through a “measured approach.”
This means department officials will be looking at every vacant position and determining whether it should be filled or whether positions could be combined.
“While we may not have to do those things right now, I think it’s more a matter of should we do those things right now,” Maher said.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: The lost art of disagreeing well: In Idaho, we need these ground rules to truly solve conflicts.
description: Less than two weeks after the senseless killing of Jordan Harbst on the Boise Greenbelt, the finger-pointing had begun. State lawmakers claimed a lack of compliance by city officials was to blame. Boise’s mayor struck back arguing that legislators were turning a tragedy into political theater. Before the family had finished mourning the death of […]
text:
We should challenge claims, not character; ask questions before assigning motives; and begin with a shared goal, writes guest columnist Andrew Ellestad. (Photo by Getty Image)Less than two weeks after the senseless killing of Jordan Harbst on the Boise Greenbelt, the finger-pointing had begun. 
State lawmakers claimed a lack of compliance by city officials was to blame. Boise’s mayor struck back arguing that legislators were turning a tragedy into political theater. 
Before the family had finished mourning the death of their son, the public conversation had become about who deserved the blame. I couldn’t help but wonder, was anyone actually trying to solve the problem?
This issue isn’t something unique to the Treasure Valley or Idaho alone. We see it play out across the United States over issues like immigration, education, national security or a myriad of other issues.
Pedestals concentrate power. They discourage dissent. What if we built Idaho community differently? 

The motivation isn’t to persuade. It’s to score points. Often the loudest voice gets the attention, but the difficult work of listening, negotiating and governing is set aside.
At the College of Idaho, I regularly teach on leadership, negotiation and organizational behavior. As I look at our nation, I’m convinced we don’t have a disagreement problem, we have a disagreement skills problem. Conflict or disagreement, when handled well, solves problems, improves organizations and allows democracies to function. 
In my classes, we talk about the difference between task conflict and relationship conflict. Task conflict is focused on the issue at hand. Relationship conflict attacks the person on the other side of the issue. 
Every organization, community or social group has conflict. The distinction between the two types is key. 
A recent review of over 100 studies which examined over 8,000 different groups found that disagreement over a task is most useful when it stays separate from personal conflict and is directed toward decision quality. Additionally, other research has shown that task conflict is more likely to improve performance when people feel psychologically safe enough to question one another without fear of ridicule or retaliation. 
Here in Idaho, it means disagreement needs ground rules. Challenge claims, not character; ask questions before assigning motives; and begin with a shared goal. Without this environment, debate generates passion but little improvement.
It seems that today, we have confused disagreement with disrespect. If we listen carefully, you will often hear a narrative by one party that assumes the other is ignorant, immoral, or corrupt. When such hyperbolic language is used, it becomes practically impossible to engage in a productive conversation focused on solving the issue at hand.
Idahoans have a long history of demonstrating charity and good-will toward our neighbors. As our state grows and more perspectives, influences and opinions emerge, it almost guarantees that we will see more conflict on the topics of taxes, public safety, education or homelessness. 
But that conflict does not have to result in relationship conflict. We should expect more from ourselves and the leaders we elect to serve our community. 
Democracy and relationships are messy. Our founding fathers understood that as they created the checks and balances that guide our nation. Democracy was never intended to eliminate disagreement. 
But it did set up processes and systems in which we can channel our disagreement into better outcomes. When we start treating our neighbors as enemies rather than partners in problem-solving, we’ve already lost something more valuable than the argument at hand.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: The financial dilemma that wound up helping US churches thrive
description: By many measures, Americans are growing less religious: Since 2007, for example, the percentage of people who pray daily has dropped, while the “unaffiliated” have grown to 29%. But those numbers can distract from just how much faith still matters in American public life – much more so than in Western Europe, despite its similar […]
text:
(Photo by Erica Shires/Getty Images)By many measures, Americans are growing less religious: Since 2007, for example, the percentage of people who pray daily has dropped, while the “unaffiliated” have grown to 29%. But those numbers can distract from just how much faith still matters in American public life – much more so than in Western Europe, despite its similar religious roots.
About two-thirds of Americans consider religion “somewhat” or “very” important, compared with 56% in Italy, 40% in Spain and 36% in Germany. While about two-thirds of American Christians pray every day, only 18% of European Christians do so.
Why such a stark divide? One reason, some scholars have argued, is the United States’ tradition of separating church and state, also called “disestablishment.” In other words, Americans’ freedom of religion helped faith to thrive in ways that the state-sponsored churches did not.

As my research into the history of philanthropy shows, disestablishment was not just a cornerstone of American democracy. It was also an engine for the extraordinary growth of philanthropy, which played an important role in fueling American churches’ growth and innovation.
Money from members
Prior to the American Revolution, most colonies sponsored particular churches and collected taxes to support them. New England governments tended to support Congregationalist churches, which grew out of Puritan traditions, while many Southern colonies supported the Church of England.
The First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution prohibits the government from establishing religion. The Supreme Court did not decide that that amendment applies to state governments until the 20th century. Within a few decades of independence, though, states’ support for established churches had disappeared. The last to disestablish was Massachusetts, which ended support for Congregational churches in 1833.



Let us know what you think...


 


After Christian churches were stripped of state funding, churches had to find new revenue sources. Ministers’ and teachers’ salaries had to be paid, church buildings constructed and maintained, and colleges and other religious institutions supported. The funding for all that had to come from voluntary contributions from members – meaning that ministers were turned into fundraisers, and believers into donors.
Donors weren’t just giving money to be charitable. They were getting services and community in return, which helped keep them emotionally and socially invested – and helped religion thrive. Members essentially became stakeholders of their denominations. In the 21st century, those networks of donors and services have included everything from schools and radio stations to children’s activities.
New generations
Religious colleges are a major example of this dynamic. On the eve of the Civil War, the country had 207 religious colleges, accounting for nearly 60% of all colleges and universities. Most had been founded after independence. Forty-nine were Presbyterian, 34 Methodist, 25 Baptist, 21 Congregational, 14 Catholic and 11 Episcopalian. The remaining 53 were founded by smaller religious groups, such as the Lutheran and Universalist churches.
Colleges took on a central role in many churches’ religious life. They trained ministers and teachers for the denominations that funded them.
Some American denominations built K-12 schools as well, which reached far more students than colleges could. The Presbyterian Church, for example, did not just build universities, such as Austin College in Texas and Lafayette College in Pennsylvania, but also established 59 academies in 20 states and numerous primary schools. These schools admitted and trained Presbyterians who, as adults, became the rank and file of their congregations – and, as alumni, donated to their alma maters.
Scholarship programs
Building and maintaining colleges is expensive.
And in the 19th century these American colleges could not necessarily rely on students paying the full cost of attendance: Many students were too poor to do so. In 1806, only six out of the 39 graduating students at Dartmouth College had paid their fees in full.
Lack of funding pushed many colleges into bankruptcy and closing. In fact, 68 of the 109 Presbyterian colleges established between 1794 and 1904 had shut down by 1940.
Colleges developed a new fundraising strategy: offering donors “scholarship certificates,” which were essentially tuition waivers that could be used by family and friends. They came with price tags, from a few hundred to a few thousand dollars.
Selling “scholarship certificates” mobilized believers who wanted to support their denomination. The fundraising campaign to create Southern Methodist University in Dallas in the early 1900s, for example, involved more than 29,000 donors from across Texas. SMU’s first bursar acknowledged that the university had largely been built by “poor people” who had submitted small donations. The university committed itself to admitting 50 students each year, free of charge, who would be nominated by the church’s 50 presiding elders in Texas.
Colleges thereby became instrumental in maintaining and growing the memberships of the denominations they served. More broadly, they played an important role upholding the religious diversity of American society.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama Department of Corrections could pay private attorney additional $38 million
description: A state representative Thursday blocked two contracts between the Alabama Department of Corrections and a private attorney that would pay the attorney an additional $33 million, saying ADOC needed to provide answers on how it plans to resolve lawsuits in the future. Rep. Chris England, D-Tuscaloosa, put holds on a $30 million increase in one […]
text:
Rep. Chris England, D-Tuscaloosa, speaks with reporters on Thursday, Aug. 8, 2026, after a meeting of the Alabama Legislature’s Contract Review Committee. England voted to delay two contracts to pay Bill Lunsford, a private attorney, an additional $33 million to defend the Alabama Department of Corrections. (Ralph Chapoco/Alabama Reflector)A state representative Thursday blocked two contracts between the Alabama Department of Corrections and a private attorney that would pay the attorney an additional $33 million, saying ADOC needed to provide answers on how it plans to resolve lawsuits in the future.
Rep. Chris England, D-Tuscaloosa, put holds on a $30 million increase in one contract defending the department in a lawsuit brought by the U.S. Department of Justice over violence in the state’s prisons, and a $3 million increase in another lawsuit alleging DOC provides inadequate mental health care to those in its custody.
Both went to Bill Lunsford, an attorney with Montgomery-based Butler Snow who received millions of dollars in legal contracts with the state, including one worth $4.68 million in Dec. 2024 and a $7.68 million one in June 2023. Lunsford stands to receive an additional $38 million from ADOC, according to Thursday’s  Contract Review Committee agenda.
“There is a direct correlation between how much you pay your lawyers and how bad of a client you are,” England said. “And the Department of Corrections is an awful client.”
A message was sent to Lunsford on Thursday seeking comment.
The contract with the $3 million increase —  from $1.65 million to $4.65 million – involves the Braggs v. Dunn litigation, alleging the state does not provide adequate mental health services to people who are incarcerated.
To date, the state has spent $17 million on the legal services contracts up for review on Thursday, according to England.
The DOJ contract rose from $3.6 million to $36.6 million, a $30 million increase. DOJ sued the state in 2020 after several reports finding widespread physical and sexual assault in Alabama’s men’s prisons. DOJ said the conditions violated inmates’ Eighth Amendment protections against cruel and unusual punishment.
No reason was given for either of the increases.
England decided to delay the contract awards for a maximum of 45 days until the agency gives him information about its plans for the lawsuits from this point forward.
“Has there been any sort of discussion about conflict, conflict resolution, and … I would be interested to also know if there were any settlement discussions in this case, what they looked like, and if we were ever offered a settlement in the Braggs case?” England said during the committee. “I want to get to a point where we analyze this from a position of trying the case and how much it costs us, and settling the case and how much it costs us.”
U.S. District Judge Myron Thompson, overseeing the Braggs case, has issued several directives to DOC to improve mental health treatment, including hiring additional corrections officers to adequately staff the prison so that people in custody can receive adequate mental health treatment;  having third-party experts monitor the condition of people suffering from mental illness within the prison facilities, and ordering that staff adequately screen and appropriately classify people with mental health conditions.
A three-judge panel of the U.S. 11th Circuit Court of Appeals in June upheld Thompson’s ruling but reversed him on some remedies, including one order for ADOC configure all its cells so that people in them do not have the means to commit suicide. A second is that the agency fills “all mandatory and essential posts” at all levels, and the panel exempted Julia Tutweiler Prison for Women from the relief ordered by Thompson.
England did allow two contracts awarded to Lunsford. One was for an increase of $4.5 million over the recently concluded litigation over physical and sexual abuse of women incarcerated at the Julia Tutwiler Prison for Women in Wetumpka.
A second contract that was also changed that will pay an additional $1.5 million for Lunsford to defend the agency in a lawsuit filed by people housed in St. Clair Correctional Facility in Springville alleging “mismanagement, poor leadership, overcrowding, inadequate security, and unsafe conditions, including broken and nonfunctioning locks on the majority of cell doors, have led to an extraordinarily high homicide rate, weekly stabbings and assaults, and a culture where violence is tolerated, creating conditions of confinement that violate the Eighth and Fourteenth Amendments to the United States Constitution.”
In August 2025, a district court judge in Birmingham removed Lunsford and two other attorneys from a DOC case after one of Lunsford’s colleagues  filed an AI-generated court brief that fabricated imaginary court citations.
Lawmakers on the committee said the state is trying to address the issues plaguing prisons.
“We are building one new facility, anticipating building another facility,” said Sen. Dan Roberts, R-Mountain Brook during the meeting. “Those are 4,000-bed, definitely state of the art. They are a little behind schedule, but we are working as a state on a plan.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Looking back on 60 years of Medicare and Medicaid
description: Last week marked the 61st anniversary of Medicare and Medicaid, and with so many dire threats to both health care programs, we would do well to reflect on their history and the promises delivered to millions of Americans since they were signed into law six decades ago in Independence, Missouri.   On July 30, 1965, President […]
text:
Medicaid sign at U.S. Senate Democrats’ press conference on Feb. 19, 2025. (Photo by Shauneen Miranda/States Newsroom)Last week marked the 61st anniversary of Medicare and Medicaid, and with so many dire threats to both health care programs, we would do well to reflect on their history and the promises delivered to millions of Americans since they were signed into law six decades ago in Independence, Missouri.  
On July 30, 1965, President Lyndon B. Johnson signed the Medicare and Medicaid Act, marking the beginning of Medicare, a health insurance program for people over 65, and Medicaid, a health insurance program for people with limited income. 
At the bill-signing ceremony, former President Harry Truman and his wife Bess were enrolled as Medicare’s first two beneficiaries and received the first Medicare cards.  President Johnson then recognized Truman for his 20-year effort in pushing for a national health insurance program. As far back as 1948, Truman, while campaigning for reelection, had said, “I put it to you, is it un-American to visit the sick, aid the afflicted or comfort the dying? I thought that was simple Christianity.” Truman won reelection, however he faced impossible opposition from Congress, and would have to wait 20 years to see his dream of a national health care program fully realized. Truman then remarked at the ceremony, “Mr. President, I am glad to have lived this long and to witness today the signing of the Medicare bill which puts this Nation right where it needs to be, to be right.”
Today’s Medicare program provides healthcare for 70 million senior Americans. Prior to President Donald Trump’s so-called “Big Beautiful Bill” passed in July of last year, nearly 81 million Americans received health care through Medicaid. But in passing that bill, the GOP controlled Congress, including our entire delegation, made the single largest cut to healthcare in U.S. history, with a $1 trillion cut to Medicaid alone. In only one year since that fateful vote, a staggering 8 million Americans have already lost healthcare coverage. And for what? To pay for tax breaks for billionaires and big corporations.  
And the hits from the Trump administration keep coming: last week the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced that it will end Medicare Part D, a subsidy program that stabilizes premiums of prescription drug plans, impacting nearly 25 million seniors and people with disabilities who afford prescriptions through that program.
The elimination of Affordable Care Act tax credits coupled with onerous eligibility restrictions have also led to skyrocketing premiums and a precipitous drop in the number of people with health care coverage. We can expect that healthcare enrollment will continue to deteriorate as people on Medicaid struggle to reckon with the mountains of paperwork now required around work reporting requirements and redeterminations — scheduled to go into effect in January 2027.  
According to Steve Davis, a professor in the department of health policy management at West Virginia University, “You will see less utilization of healthcare services because people no longer have insurance. So less utilization, less access to health care and more sickness, morbidity and potentially even mortality. And that is more costly for us all.”
The president and our members of Congress have turned their backs on the needs of West Virginians. This may come at a great political cost as the damage is felt by more and more people in terms of higher costs, loss of coverage, bankruptcies, hospital closures, preventable deaths and job loss.
President Johnson, in his praise of President Truman for his unwavering commitment to a national health care program, said, “And just think, Mr. President, because of [Medicare and Medicaid] — and the long years of struggle which so many have put into creating it — there are men and women in pain who will now find ease. There are those, alone in suffering who will now hear the sound of some approaching footsteps coming to help. There are those fearing the terrible darkness of despairing poverty — despite their long years of labor and expectation — who will now look up to see the light of hope and realization.”  
Instead of hope or help, today’s approaching footsteps are bringing misery to millions of Americans.  But at some point, hopefully soon, they will wake up a sleeping giant.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: It all comes back to sludge in House District 31
description: Editor’s note: This is the fifth in a six-part series on state legislative races, chosen based on expected competitiveness between candidates and relevant issues to the district. Of the 113 seats in the Rhode Island General Assembly, all of which are elected every two years, 22 have primaries in September. A high heat sewage processing […]
text:
From left to right: Democrats Jim Sheehan, Matthew McCoy and Thomas Menec all want to improve the transparency and communication required by the Quonset Development Corporation if elected to the Warwick House District 31 seat. (Courtesy photos)
Editor’s note: This is the fifth in a six-part series on state legislative races, chosen based on expected competitiveness between candidates and relevant issues to the district. Of the 113 seats in the Rhode Island General Assembly, all of which are elected every two years, 22 have primaries in September.
A high heat sewage processing plant initially in the works for Quonset Business Park is now paused, but the stench from perceived dishonesty about the project clings to North Kingstown. 



About House District 31
Open seat, represented by Julie Casimiro from 2016 to 2026
Geography: Northern and eastern sections of North Kingstown, part of Exeter
Population: 14,870 residents, 11,293 registered voters
Partisan breakdown: 57% independent, 27% Democrat, 16% Republican 
Demographics: Median age: 42;  86.6% white; $115,349 median household income (2024)


So much so that it launched campaigns by three Democrats all vying for the open seat to represent House District 31. Rep. Julie Casimiro, also a Democrat, is retiring after a decade representing the district spanning the eastern section of North Kingstown and part of Exeter.
“That made me leap out of my chair and say ‘I gotta run,’” said Jim Sheehan of the sludge plant. “Quonset needs to be reformed. I’ve done it before, I can do it again.”
A former state senator, Sheehan’s previous 20-year stint in the legislature was also prompted by a controversial project proposed for Quonset, which he helped defeat while sponsoring the 2004 legislation that created Quonset Development Corporation as a quasi-public state agency overseeing development in the industrial park.
Sheehan, 60, chose not to run for the Senate seat in 2020 because he wanted to spend more time with his family.
But he couldn’t resist the pull of politics after learning about the sludge pyrolysis plant this spring, more than 18 months after the developer received preliminary approval from Quonset’s governing board in a decision that even most town officials say they did not know about.



Quotation







Quonset needs to be reformed. I've done it before, I can do it again.


– Jim Sheehan, a Democrat for House District 31 


North Kingstown Town Councilor Matthew McCoy is one of few who did know; as one of two town representatives on Quonset’s board of directors, McCoy was in the room for the executive session presentation that laid out the details of the $225 million project. He was in the minority of board members who voted against the lease agreement, but believed he could not share any information with his fellow councilors or town administrators because the project was discussed in a closed-door session. McCoy resigned from the Quonset board in March, apologizing to the standing room-only crowd of incensed residents who packed the high school auditorium for a town council meeting about the project. But he still felt powerless to make the changes he wanted, an influence he thinks can be gained via a seat on Smith Hill.
“We can write resolutions and write letters, but the real changes need to occur at the General Assembly,” McCoy, 65, said. 



Quotation







We can write resolutions and write letters, but the real changes need to occur at the General Assembly.


– Matthew McCoy, a North Kingstown town councilor running in the House District 31 Democratic primary 


Thomas Menec has no experience in politics, but he too felt frustrated by the lack of communication between Quonset’s governing board and town officials. A North Kingstown police officer who also works as a school resource officer at North Kingstown High School, Menec, 47, says that never having held elected office — except for as president of the police union — is a plus.
“They’ve had their bites at the apple,” Menec said of McCoy and Sheehan. “I bring fresh ideas, I suppose.”
All three candidates named changes to the Quonset bylaws to require more communication with and input from its host community as a priority if elected. Sludge may be the top issue, but it’s not the only topic on the table.
Menec, who also serves as a chief warrant officer for the U.S. Coast Guard, named restoring the cost-of-living increases frozen under then-Treasurer Gina Raimondo’s 2011 pension reforms as a top item on his to-do list. 
“I’m big on promises,” said Menec, who as a member of the North Kingstown Police Department was also hurt by the retirement benefits cuts for state workers and teachers. “If you make a promise, you have to keep them.”



Quotation







I’m big on promises. If you make a promise, you have to keep them.


– Thomas Menec, a Democratic candidate for House District 31


Sheehan, a history teacher at Toll Gate High School in Warwick, wants to focus on affordability, proposing more state funding to help first-time homeowners on their mortgage payments and parents in need of childcare as potential policy solutions. 
McCoy is also focused on “kitchen table issues” like energy costs, healthcare and housing. A U.S. Navy veteran who works part-time as a certified mental health first aid instructor, he’s spent years advocating for veterans protections and funding with state lawmakers and Rhode Island’s congressional delegation.
Though all Democrats, the three candidates showcase the range of ideologies within the party. McCoy identifies as a progressive, a vocal advocate with local gun safety groups. He supported the assault weapons sale ban approved by lawmakers in 2025, and the millionaire’s tax included in the fiscal 2027 budget.
Sheehan, who received endorsements from Casimiro and the District 31 Democratic Committee, considers himself a moderate. He also supported the ban on assault-style weapons, having pushed for similar legislation during his time in the Senate, although it didn’t pass. But Sheehan was hesitant to throw his weight behind a millionaire’s tax without more information.
Menec has spent most of his life as a registered independent voter, in part because of his position as police union president. He changed his affiliation just before filing his candidacy paperwork in June, he said. 
While Menec also said he is a centrist candidate, he opposed the ban on sale of assault-style weapons because “I’m a strong supporter of the Constitution.” And he did not like the millionaire’s tax, either. 
The winner of the Sept. 9 primary is unopposed in the Nov. 3 general election.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Campaign to enshrine voting rights in Virginia Constitution kicks off in Norfolk
description: Portsmouth school board member Quniana Futrell appeared somber behind the podium in Norfolk’s Slover event space as she spoke in support of a proposal to amend Virginia’s constitution to automatically restore voting rights for people who complete felony sentences.  She recalled her experience growing up with both of her parents incarcerated and said her moth[...]
text:
Jamel Ridgenal speaks in Norfolk on Aug. 6, 2026 about his support for a Virginia constitutional amendment to allow automatic restoration of voting rights to people with felony convictions who have completed their sentences. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)Portsmouth school board member Quniana Futrell appeared somber behind the podium in Norfolk’s Slover event space as she spoke in support of a proposal to amend Virginia’s constitution to automatically restore voting rights for people who complete felony sentences. 
She recalled her experience growing up with both of her parents incarcerated and said her mother died the day after her release from prison. 
“Standing as an elected official, being the dream and hope of my ancestors, I never got my mother’s vote,” she said. “That one vote would have been the one that meant everything to me — but Question Three fixes that.”
Question Three is among a trio of pending constitutional amendments to protect reproductive rights, marriage equality and voting rights in Virginia’s constitution. 
The measures would make the protections less subject to turnover in the state legislature and instill state-level protections should federal laws change. 
The proposals have passed the state legislature two years in a row and will  appear on ballots for voters statewide to approve or reject in November.
Amid passionate debate, civil rights resolutions clear Virginia legislature

“Vote yes,” Futrell implored the crowd, which responded with cheers. 
Futrell was one of several local, state and federal lawmakers, activists and people whose lives include incarceration who laid out the reasons they support the amendment and encouraged others to, as well.
“Some of you understand this work here because you have experience behind bars and there are some of you in this room who have the luxury to not know this personally — so please take our word for it,” Del. Cia Price, D-Newport News, told the crowd. 
As chair of the House’s Privileges and Elections committee, Price helped push the advancement of the amendment. She and other speakers encouraged attendees to not only plan to vote for the amendment, but to spread the word about it in their communities.
Virginia’s current constitution bans people with felony convictions from voting unless they successfully petition a governor or receive a pardon from them.
While three of Virginia’s four previous governors had streamlined the process to ensure people who have finished their sentences can once again vote, former Gov. Glenn Youngkin changed the process to a petition-based one, with little clarity on criteria. Approvals slowed during his tenure.
The proposed constitutional amendment seeks to allow people who have finished serving their time to become automatically eligible to vote again. 
The event was held on the 61st anniversary of the federal Voting Rights Act of 1965, an observance several speakers tied to the amendment. 
The federal policy prohibits racial discrimination in voting by eliminating various tactics that had been used to keep Black people from the polls. Though white women gained the right to vote in 1920, the VRA extended that right to Black women and others of color, as well. 
Enshrining new voting rights into Virginia’s constitution is even more timely, U.S. Rep. Bobby Scott, D-Newport News, said, because  the U.S. Supreme Court earlier this year “just about knocked (the VRA) out.” 
A decision by the court weakened a section of the legislation that led to Louisiana eliminating one of its Black-majority congressional districts. 
“We have to make voting a voting issue,” Scott said. 
Various organizations including New Virginia Majority, League of Women Voters and Nolef Turns were present Thursday and shared information and resources with attendees. 
Jamel Ridgenal and Sergio Hayes, two men whose past incarceration has shaped their present passion for civic engagement, spoke of the amendment from a personal perspective.
Ridgenal said formerly incarcerated people work and pay taxes and deserve to weigh in on how elected officials use public resources “just like everybody else.”
Hayes said depending on a governor to restore rights is “not restoration, that’s permission.” 
“It depends on who that person is sitting in that office,” he said. 
Gov. Abigail Spanberger has restored more than 60,000 people’s rights since taking office earlier this year, but Hayes said restorations have fluctuated governor by governor.
“We will make it no longer a favor from a governor, but a guarantee,” he said.

title: ACLU of Virginia lawsuit alleges King George School Board blocked LGBTQ+ student club
description: A leading civil rights defense firm has lodged a lawsuit against King George County School Board for allegedly blocking middle school students from creating a student organization supporting LGBTQ+ students. According to the lawsuit, filed Tuesday in federal court by the ACLU of Virginia and the Potomac Law Group, two students proposed the Gay-Straight Allia[...]
text:
The ACLU of Virginia and the Potomac Law Group have filed a lawsuit against Prince George County's school board for allegedly blocking middle school students from forming a LGBTQ+ advocacy club. (Photo by Parker Michels-Boyce for The Virginia Mercury)A leading civil rights defense firm has lodged a lawsuit against King George County School Board for allegedly blocking middle school students from creating a student organization supporting LGBTQ+ students.
According to the lawsuit, filed Tuesday in federal court by the ACLU of Virginia and the Potomac Law Group, two students proposed the Gay-Straight Alliance (GSA) club last August, but faced pushback from the wider community that said the club was not an “age-appropriate” group and that the GSA would “not be a safe space, but a dangerous place.” 
The case comes after the U.S. Department of Education recently stopped collecting data on bullying against transgender and non-binary students, and could shape how Virginia schools weigh student club policies against First Amendment protections.
“Student clubs help students build community, find belonging, and thrive, and when schools offer those opportunities, the law requires that they be available on equal terms to all students,” Mary Rohmiller, partner at Potomac Law Group, said in a statement on Tuesday. 
“But King George County Schools appears to be applying a double standard to the GSA at its middle schools. The students at the heart of this case are not asking for special treatment – they’re asking for equal treatment,” Rohmiller continued.
King George School Board Chair Colleen Davis and Superintendent Jesse Boyd did not comment on the case or respond to questions about the board’s policy and process for new student clubs or whether the board will revise them to align with community feedback. The board will hold an event to kick off the upcoming school year Friday afternoon, followed by a regular meeting on Aug. 17. 
The suit, representing the families of the two students, names Boyd, Davis, and the other four board members. 
According to the lawsuit, last fall, 17 students expressed interest in the club after a student, unnamed in the complaint, completed the administrative process for starting the GSA club at their middle school, which serves nearly 1,100 students in grades 6-8.
School officials paused the creation amid community backlash against a teacher who agreed to serve as the club sponsor, and threats to school officials surfaced.
Ultimately, the board’s action led to revised policies that, according to the lawsuit, effectively prohibit noncurricular groups at the middle school, including the proposed GSA. 
The policy changes limited noncurricular student groups to King George High School and set requirements and procedures for noncurricular student organizations for high school students.
“King George County Schools cannot move the goalposts to prevent an organization that promotes respect and equality for LGBTQ+ students from existing just because school board members disagree with its message,” ACLU-VA Staff Attorney Julia Kahn said in a statement. “The First Amendment and Equal Access Act protect all students, and the school board cannot pick and choose who the rules apply to. Why this club, and not others?”
According to the suit, school administrators proposed replacing the GSA with more general clubs, such as “Safe Space Group,” since the board would be unlikely to approve it if it were explicitly identified with LGBTQ+ students.
But the students rejected the alternatives.
The lawsuit also alleges that the students received different treatment from the administration compared to other student groups, including the Fellowship of Christian Athletes, a Christian nonprofit organization that focuses on combining sports and faith, and elementary school clubs. 
The administration accommodated the FCA when it was proposed by amending the curriculum of a leadership class to make the FCA curricular rather than extracurricular, according to the lawsuit. The families said this effort undercuts the board’s stated justification for eliminating noncurricular groups.
The families of the two students said they continue to suffer irreparable harm from being unable to establish and participate in the GSA.
Although the lawsuit details the case at King George schools, it does not mention the Genders and Sexualities Alliance Network, which has a similar acronym and supports LGBTQ+ youth and their allies in becoming leaders and advocates for safer, more inclusive schools and communities.
The GSA Network encourages those interested to register their school-based and community alliances.
A trial date has not been set yet in the case.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: FOIA FRIDAY: Data center debate sparks Franklin resident’s transparency concerns
description: One of the less noticed features of the Virginia Way is the long-running tendency of the commonwealth’s leaders to conduct their decision-making behind closed doors. While the Virginia Freedom of Information Act presumes all government business is by default public and requires officials to justify why exceptions should be made, too many Virginia leaders in[...]
text:
(Photo by Getty Images)One of the less noticed features of the Virginia Way is the long-running tendency of the commonwealth’s leaders to conduct their decision-making behind closed doors. While the Virginia Freedom of Information Act presumes all government business is by default public and requires officials to justify why exceptions should be made, too many Virginia leaders in practice take the opposite stance, acting as if records are by default private and the public must prove they should be handled otherwise.
In this feature, we aim to highlight the frequency with which officials around Virginia are resisting public access to records on issues large and small — and note instances when the release of information under FOIA gave the public insight into how government bodies are operating.
 Franklin County officials have privacy agreements while deliberating a data center, resident FOIA shows

A Freedom of Information Act request by Franklin County residents revealed county officials entered into confidentiality agreements with an unnamed company related to a proposed data center project the local government is currently weighing.
WFXR reported that local residents said they felt left out of the approval process because it appears substantial discussion about the 150-acre project has happened behind the scenes, rather than at public meetings. 
The response to the FOIA, obtained by resident Danae Crosby, shows a confidentiality agreement with participating parties’ names redacted except for Economic Development Director Danielle Poe. 
The documents reference “Project Flash” and Summit View Business Park, where the data center would be housed if approved. 
The large plot of land the project would require has prompted residents’ concerns  over local infrastructure and the development’s utility needs. 
Transparency in approval processes is the latest issue to emerge in local debates about data centers. The data center industry and its proponents say the projects generate millions in tax revenue for localities. 
While Franklin’s data center is not yet reality, county Supervisor Dan Quinn explained that leaders’ behind-the-scenes discussion over projects is sometimes necessary. 
“We have closed meetings when companies come to the county and they want to discuss business arrangements, commercial terms,” he told WFXR. “Those meetings are necessarily closed.”
 Mineral town council members sue, alleging FOIA law violation

Town Council members Rebecca McGhee and Michelle Covert filed a suit in Louisa County General District Court seeking enforcement of FOIA law over alleged violations by Mineral town staff, The Central Virginian reported. 
The suit said Mineral Mayor Pam Harlowe and FOIA Officer Teresa Newton did not abide by transparency standards, including “providing public notice of meetings, adopting and following agendas, complying with rules for electronic participation, and ensuring the committee meetings are open to the public.” 
Covert and McGhee argued that the officials’ failure to take these steps prevented them from rightfully and fully participating in their own town government. 
Town officials held a vote earlier this year to terminate the contract of the town manager on a vote of 4-3. 



The Mercury’s efforts to track FOIA and other transparency cases in Virginia are indebted to the work of the Virginia Coalition for Open Government, a nonprofit alliance dedicated to expanding access to government records, meetings and other state and local proceedings.



Covert and McGhee questioned whether that vote was legitimate, due to the council’s alleged lack of adherence to the town’s electronic meeting attendance policy. The termination was also not listed on the public agenda, the plaintiffs argue. 
A special meeting between the council and planning commission concerning zoning is another issue named in the suit.
Covert and McGhee alleged that there was no agenda for the meeting prepared, adopted or published. During this meeting, the mayor accepted a resolution to declare that Mineral formally opposed the Valley Link Transmission Line project. 
McGhee and Covert said leaders’ failure to operate transparently invalidated the resolution.
An allegation that a council member refused to share documents with local journalist Tammy Purcell of the Engage Louisa newsletter is also included in the lawsuit.  
 FOIA reveals Richmond uses people’s cell phone data to determine staffing, planning for public parks 

A FOIA request by the Richmond Times-Dispatch revealed that Richmond’s Parks and Recreation department is engaged in a three-year agreement dating to 2024 with Placer.ai, a locational analytics platform that gathers cellphone geolocation data and sells it to governments, small businesses and large corporations. 
City spokeswoman Tamara Jenkins said that the city uses the data to help determine how to best allocate public resources. 
By exploring how often people are frequenting public parks and correlations between events that might be driving them there, Jenkins said the data informs the city’s choices on “planning, staffing, grant writing, maintenance and capital maintenance forecasting purposes.”
“Responsive records show that, between July 2025 and June 2026, William Byrd Park saw 1.4 million visitors. Joseph Bryan Park saw nearly 670,000, while Forest Hill Park saw around 385,000,” the newspaper reported. 
While the data can also point to people’s demographics and where they may have gone after visiting a park, the newspaper said Jenkins stressed that  information is for Parks and Recreation use only and not shared with Richmond police or other investigative entities. 
Placer.ai staffer R.J Hottovy told the newspaper that the platform can track how many people access certain areas over given periods of time and track movement profiles, but it can’t determine exactly who people are because the platform doesn’t collect personal information. 
Without legal standards, Christopher Newport University professor Steven Keener warned The Times-Dispatch, people can only take private companies’ word on how their data may or may not be protected. 
“Once you start integrating locations with the profile data, your ‘anonymous data’ is becoming far less anonymous,” he said. “And these companies … make promises all the time. They say, ‘We won’t use it this way, we won’t use it to track women into Planned Parenthood clinics.’” 
“But in reality,” Keener said, “if you don’t have strong legislative guardrails to prevent that from happening, the company can and will change that at any time that makes sense for them.”
Have you experienced local or state officials denying or delaying your FOIA request? Tell us about it: info@virginiamercury.com

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana’s Medicaid rolls shed people and costs. But what is the price?
description: We saw both sides of the Medicaid coin this week. First, Senior Reporter Casey Smith delivered a three-part series digging into exactly why so many Hoosiers have dropped off the rolls for the state’s low-income health insurance program. The stories were, at times, heartbreaking. Parents spending hours, days and weeks to ensure their disabled children […]
text:
Pins urge people to “Protect Medicaid” at an April 1, 2025 rally. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Indiana Capital Chronicle)We saw both sides of the Medicaid coin this week.
First, Senior Reporter Casey Smith delivered a three-part series digging into exactly why so many Hoosiers have dropped off the rolls for the state’s low-income health insurance program.
The stories were, at times, heartbreaking.
Parents spending hours, days and weeks to ensure their disabled children can go to the doctor, receive medications and other supports.
Other Hoosiers making appointments to take paperwork to a state office only to have no one around to help.
Missed mail. Losing benefits before the deadline to provide necessary verification.
Data from Indiana’s Family and Social Services Administration shows that, between March 2025 and June 2026, about 44.5% of those cases reviewed were renewed, 31.9% were closed for noncompliance and 7.7% were closed after a finding of ineligibility. The rest fell into a broad category, including pending. 
And those kicked off for noncompliance often regain benefits a few weeks or months later, after resolving the paperwork issue. That’s called churn — and there is a cost to it.
The state, and therefore taxpayers, pay in administrative hours and salaries.
But our neighbors on Medicaid also miss doctor’s appointments, fall behind on prescriptions, and backslide on chronic illnesses while they wait for coverage to be reinstated.
Hospitals too feel the brunt of the situation, with many uninsured Hoosiers — including those removed from Medicaid — flooding the emergency rooms.
State officials have said they are tightening Medicaid rules and requirements to ensure it’s there for those who really need it. But these are people who really need it.
The savings
FSSA revealed the other side of the coin Wednesday, when the agency announced it had saved $300 million in Medicaid costs, sending it back to the General Fund for other purposes (or to collect interest in the state reserve accounts.)
It’s clear that Medicaid growth in certain areas, such as autism therapy, had grown faster than is sustainable. And, of course, it’s the responsibility of a participant to follow the rules, provide documentation and ensure their eligibility.
But the fact that compliance denials are occurring at three times the rate of actual ineligibility is a big problem.
It’s a bit reminiscent of the failed welfare modernization contract with IBM from 2009. The plan was to revamp case management and significantly reduce face-to-face meeting requirements via more computerized processes. But incomplete applications and delayed benefits ultimately doomed the project.
Beneficiaries are already struggling to keep up with the renewals, program changes and interim checks. And it’s going to get worse for up to 470,000 Hoosiers on the Healthy Indiana Plan who must start proving in 2027 that they’ve been meeting work or education requirements.
State officials need to ensure the system can bear the new load. One thing that could help is to use texting to reach families. Lower-income families move more often and some of the notices are simply not reaching them. Plus, the postal service isn’t as reliable as it used to be.
Software improvements and more staff are also clearly needed.
But all that comes at a cost. The question is, are we going to spend so much time and resources ensuring eligibility that we are costing the state and society as a whole?
