During a stop on a state fly-around Thursday, U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, a leading Republican gubernatorial candidate, said she will halt alleged efforts to spread Communism if elected. 
Blackburn made the remarks in Mt. Juliet as part of her swing on Tennessee’s primary Election Day, in which Republican and Democratic candidates will be selected in the gubernatorial, U.S. Senate, all nine congressional seats and state House and Senate districts. 
She was joined by state Rep. Johnny Garrett, who is running for the 6th Congressional District, Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs, Blackburn’s campaign treasurer, state Rep. Clark Boyd of Lebanon and anti-transgender activist Riley Gaines of Sumner County. 
When asked by the Lookout if she would continue to support keeping Tennessee National Guard troops in Memphis as part of the Memphis Safe Task Force, Blackburn didn’t answer but did express her continued support for the collaboration of federal and state agencies created in September by President Donald Trump with the backing of Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee. 
Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs, with state Rep. Johnny Garrett to the left and anti-transgender activist Riley Gaines, speaks to supporters at an Election Day event for Blackburn and Garrett. Jacobs is thought to be a leading contender to replace Blackburn int he U.S Senate should she win her race for governor. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
“We started our morning in Memphis and people in Memphis are thrilled the city is safe,” Blackburn said. 
Lee told reporters this week crime in Memphis has dropped to its lowest point in decades, though he gave no specifics. 
Since May, agents with the task force have shot and killed four men in the city. All of the cases remain under investigation, but in at least one instance, the Drug Enforcement Agency officer involved in the shooting will not be prosecuted. 
Both Blackburn and Garrett mentioned Communism and threats to women’s sports by transgender athletes as their main concerns.
“We are truly sending a message that Tennessee is a conservative state and that all of these woke policies, all this move towards Communism, that ends at the Tennessee state line,” Blackburn said.

Karen Harding, a gospel singer from Sumner County, said she believes Blackburn has been great as a senator and that she would do a “phenomenal job” as governor.
“And it’s pretty cool that she’s the first woman, too,” said Harding. “I got an invitation and thought, I have to be here and support her.”
If Blackburn wins the Republican nomination, she will be the first woman to do so. A win by Democrat Jerri Green, a Memphis City councilmember thought to be the leading Democratic candidate in the gubernatorial race, would give Tennessee its first all-woman state election.

Ogles accompanies RFK, Jr. for proposed Head Start rule change announcement


By Cassandra Stephenson -  1:48 pm





U.S. Rep. Andy Ogles stands alongside U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. at Susan Gray Head Start in Nashville, Tennessee on Aug. 6, 2026. The secretary addressed proposed rule changes that would strip federal regulations for the Head Start program back to statutory requirements, putting further regulatory responsibilities on states. (Photo: Cassandra Stephenson/Tennessee Lookout)
U.S. Rep. Andy Ogles stood alongside U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. and Administration for Children and Families Assistant Secretary Alex Adams Thursday morning as the pair discussed the proposed rollback of federal regulations for Head Start, a program that provides education, nutrition and other supports for children from low-income families.
Ogles, who is on Tennessee’s ballot and faces a challenge in the Republican 5th Congressional District primary from former state agriculture commissioner Charlie Hatcher, did not take any election-related questions, but spoke briefly in support of the proposed changes.
Kennedy’s proposal would eliminate federal standards for the program beyond what is required by law, shifting regulatory decisions for things like staff-to-child ratios and education requirements to states. It would also reduce the amount of funding that Head Start programs can spend on administrative costs from 15% of the program’s total cost to 5%. Adams said the change could save around $2.2 billion, which could then be used to create more program spots for children.
Administrative costs can include everything from payroll to special support staff for children with disabilities. HHS later clarified in an email to the Lookout that teacher salaries and expenses related to educational facilities are not included in the administrative services category. ACF would continue to allow grantee agencies to apply for temporary waivers for the administrative cost cap.
Asked about stripping back mandates on salaries for Head Start employees, Kennedy asked if every Head Start should reflect the salary that someone may receive in New York, even if that program is located in Arkansas, Tennessee, or another state with an overall lower cost of living.
U.S. Rep. Andy Ogles, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., and Administration for Children and Families Assistant Secretary Alex Adams deliver remarks on a proposed federal rule change for Head Start at Susan Gray Head Start in Nashville, Tennessee on Aug. 6, 2026. (Photo: Cassandra Stephenson/Tennessee Lookout)
Kennedy and Adams pitched the regulation reduction as “cutting red tape” and opening “flexibility” for states and parents.
The proposed rule change would also require Head Start programs to provide nutrition in line with the Make America Healthy Again guidelines and establish a baseline requirement for physical activity. 
The Notice of Proposed Rulemaking will be published in the Federal Register on Friday and will accept public comments for 60 days.

title: Florida’s primary races for commissioner of agriculture

text:
Florida Commissioner of Agriculture Wilton Simpson in Lakeland on July 17, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)One of the three Florida Cabinet positions on the ballot this year is commissioner of agriculture, which oversees the state’s $13 billion ag sector — which is worth more than $213 billion considering multiplier effects.
The Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services (FDACS) includes 12 divisions and seven offices involved in regulation and promotion of farm products, establishing rules for the state’s animal, aquaculture, forestry, and produce industries, and licensing producers.  It oversees state forests, wildfire response, concealed weapons licensing, and the hemp industry.
The commissioner sits on the Florida Cabinet, which with the governor oversees a range of public agencies.
Republican primary: Wilton Simpson vs. Matt Taylor
Wilton Simpson has held the position four years. At one point, he was considered a potential candidate to succeed Ron DeSantis as governor, and his fundraising haul shows that a lot of other people thought he might be a leading contender.
Simpson has raised more than $30 million from (count them) four political committees, including contributions from some of the state’s biggest corporations and lobbyist groups, such as Florida Crystals Corp., Associated Industries of Florida, and NextEra Energy Capital Holding, a subsidiary of NextEra Energy, parent company of Florida Power & Light.
Simpson, 60, has been endorsed by President Donald Trump, who called him a “true America First Patriot” in a Truth Social post in October. As a teenager, he began working on his father’s egg farm in Trilby, a small rural community in east Pasco County. He later began managing the operation. The farm houses about 1 million chickens, and their eggs are mostly distributed within a 100-mile radius of the farm, Simpson said at The Economic Club of Florida in 2023. He also operates an environmental remediation company.
Simpson had a net worth of $31.5 million as of Dec. 31, according to state disclosure forms.
He did not respond to the Phoenix’s request for an interview about his candidacy.
Simpson’s lone Republican challenger in the Aug. 18 primary is Matt Taylor, also known as “Matt the Welder,” a Plant City native who has been active making social media posts to boost his campaign. Taylor has more than 474,000 followers on Instagram.
Matt the Welder, a/k/a Matt Taylor is running for the GOP nomination for commissioner of agriculture. (Photo from his campaign website)
He is in fact a welder and tractor mechanic who says the Department of Agriculture has become a “giant bureaucracy” to which he wants to bring accountability.
A strong part of his candidacy is based on concerns about development in the Sunshine State.
He complains Florida Republicans have shifted direct funding away from Florida Forever, the state’s main program for buying land for conservation, and instead have directed taxpayer funds towards the Department of Agriculture’s Rural and Family Lands Protection Program. That program allows agricultural landowners to permanently preserve their land from development but doesn’t require them to allow public access. Under a conservation easement, a private landowner can manage his or her property for timber production, sod, row crops, cattle grazing, hunting or private recreation.
“These easements, when we buy them or when the state buys them, they’re not setting up, like, a park,” Taylor told the Phoenix in phone conversation. “Like 4G Ranch, I think, was just purchased in June of this year up in Pasco. I can’t take my family up there to do any kind of recreation, whether it be hunting, biking, hiking, whatever.”
In that case, 4G Ranch was jointly purchased by the state and Pasco County (as part of its Environmental Lands and Acquisition and Management Program) for $68 million, but the result is that while the 1,893 acres cannot be used for development, it won’t become a recreational park.
Floridians have proven in recent years, he said, that public pressure can stop overreach by developers or, in some cases, state or local government support for proposals that appear to benefit developers.
As examples he cited “Blue Ribbon” legislation that stalled this year in the Florida Legislature; the uprising about placing golf courses and other amenities in state parks during the summer of 2024; and the moratoriums popping up around the state to halt construction of data centers.
One place where public pressure didn’t work was in the City of Fort Meade in Polk County, where local officials recently approved a massive data center. As Taylor notes, now some of those officials are being targeted in a citizen recall effort.
“We’ve hit a time in growth to where folks are starting to realize we don’t have the infrastructure, we don’t have the water, we don’t have all of the things necessary to support the growth, so why are we approving it?” he asked.
Taylor is critical of Simpson’s declaration on his campaign website that he is “Defending the Second Amendment,” noting his support while a state senator in 2018 for the Marjory Stoneman Douglas Public High School Safety Act, which among other matters raised the age to purchase a long gun from 18 to 21 years.
“Whatever is politically convenient at the time, that’s what he’s going to go with,” Taylor said. “Why is he saying he’s pro-gun now? Well, he did get about $50,000 from [gun manufacturer] Sig Sauer, so maybe that changed his mind.”
Taylor has raised nearly $269,000 in the race.
Democratic primary: Joey Mendoza Atkins vs. Don Prichard
Don Prichard says he filed to run for the Democratic nomination for agriculture commissioner when he realized no one else had done so, just weeks ahead of the qualifying deadline. He considers the office one of the most important in the state because of the powers vested in it.
The 45-year-old native Floridian’s spent his career in law enforcement, working for the Broward County Sheriff’s Office from age 19 until last year, when he left to become a captain with the Pembroke Park Police Department — a job he still attends to every day while working nights and weekends to get his message out to voters.
When asked why he thinks he should succeed Simpson, he replies that he wouldn’t be a “rubber stamp for the governor.”
“I want to make sure that we represent Floridians, and I believe that the current administration is representing special interests and large corporate groups over Floridians that we have a duty to be responsible for, to protect and to look after,” he said.
Democratic agriculture commission candidate Don Prichard. (Don Prichard campaign)
One of his top concerns, Prichard said, is regulation of AI data centers, one of the most contentious issues in Florida this year. The Legislature this past session passed a bill (SB 484) that would ensure data center companies pay for their own utilities, and not nearby ratepayers.
The law authorizes water management districts or the Department of Environmental Protection to require large-scale data centers to use reclaimed water as part of any consumptive-use permit approval.
“They’re not looking at long-term effects,” he complained about the Legislature.
“Ensuring that the water that they’re going to have to use — and they’re already in droughts in Central Florida. They’re not coming up with systems that are going to be self-sufficient and that will protect our environment and Floridians, and looking at long-term issues that need to get addressed, and our water table is one of them.
“So, if they’re continuing to use more water or we continue to develop, we have to look at alternatives in how we can preserve our natural aquifers and waterways and still accomplish what we need to accomplish. And I don’t think that legislation really addressed the long-term effects of a data center. It only addressed that they’re not going to pass over the electrical costs to the consumer when they do these data centers.”
Prichard has raised $28,135 in the contest.
Miami trial attorney and former sports agent Joey Mendoza Atkins believes government should be about protecting people over powerful interests, and that’s a major reason why he’s entered the Democratic primary, he said.
Atkins knew the odds against him would be formidable. His campaign website declares his candidacy as “David vs. Goliath.”
He considers his experience working at a legal aid foundation representing migrant farm workers has been essential.
“I think it gave me a first-hand understanding that agriculture isn’t just about crops, it’s about people, it’s about the families who harvest our food,” he said in a phone interview.
“It’s about farmers just trying to stay in business. And I think every Floridian ultimately depends on a safe and affordable food supply. And so, while somebody might have taken that experience from a purely immigration sort of perspective … I take a more holistic approach. So, how … does that actually impact food prices? How does that impact the ability of farmers to stay in business and operate and live the American dream?”
As for the Florida Forever-to-Rural and Family Lands Protection Program shift, on his website Simpson boasts that the program has produced a 243% increase in farmland preserved.
Joey Mendoza Atkins (from his website)
Like Matt the Welder, Atkins isn’t supportive of that change.
“Conservation easements are an important tool in that space in the toolbox,” Atkins said.
“But conservation shouldn’t be measured by the number of acres put into easement. It should be measured by the public benefit that those easements provide. Too often, we celebrate acreage without asking about whether we’re protecting the right lands, improving water quality, supporting family farms, expanding wildlife habitat, or even providing appropriate public access when it makes sense.”
One of the items Simpson advocated for in an agriculture package in 2024 made Florida the first state in the nation to ban lab-grown or “cultivated meat” in 2024.
“I support Florida’s farmers and ranchers, and I understand why many of them are concerned about lab-grown meat,” Atkins said. “It’s quite obvious about cutting into what they do. Agriculture is a foundation of the state’s economy, and we should never put family farmers at a competitive disadvantage. My philosophy is finding creative and dynamic single ways to support them.”
Atkins loaned himself $8,480 for his campaign. From outside sources, he has raised just $1,290.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: As a new school year begins, let’s put children’s mental health first
description: The need to pay attention to our children's emotional well-being has never been greater.
text:
As another school year begins, parents across our community are busy checking supply lists, buying backpacks, adjusting sleep schedules, and preparing children for the excitement and sometimes the anxiety that comes with returning to school.
While these routines matter, there is another question that deserves equal attention: Is my child emotionally ready for the school year ahead?

Giselle Acevedo

The need to pay attention to our children’s emotional well-being has never been greater. Across Connecticut, families are experiencing a growing youth mental health crisis.  Mental health-related visits to emergency departments and urgent crisis centers consistently increase as children return to school each fall, when academic, social, and emotional pressures converge.
The numbers are sobering. Nationally, nearly one in five children has been diagnosed with a mental, emotional, or behavioral health condition, with anxiety and depression among the most common concerns.  And so many struggle silently.
Yet behind every statistic is a child—a son or daughter, a student, a teammate, or a friend who needs someone to notice, to listen, and to believe in them.
For many children, the return to school is filled with anticipation and opportunity. For others, it can bring uncertainty, loneliness, fear, academic pressure, social challenges, or the resurfacing of emotional struggles that may have gone unnoticed during the summer months.
Children experience the world differently than adults. They do not always have the language to tell us they are anxious, depressed, overwhelmed, or afraid. Instead, they communicate through changes in behavior, mood, relationships, and even physical symptoms.
As both a therapist and the President and CEO of the Child & Family Guidance Center, I have learned one truth that guides everything we do: 
Every child deserves a champion — someone who believes in them. Someone who sees their strengths before their struggles. Someone who advocates for them when they cannot advocate for themselves.
Most often, that champion is a parent, grandparent, caregiver, or trusted adult. No one knows your child better than you.
Schools play an essential role in educating our children, but a child’s deepest sense of identity, belonging, and unconditional love begins at home. Values are nurtured within families. Confidence is built through relationships. Emotional security grows from knowing there is someone who will always be in your corner.
That does not mean parents have all the answers.  In fact, one of the greatest strengths a parent can have is the willingness to ask questions and seek support.
What should parents watch for?
As children return to school, pay attention to changes that seem unusual for your child, particularly if they continue for several weeks.
These may include:

Persistent sadness or irritability.
Increased anxiety about school or separating from caregivers.
Withdrawal from friends or family.
Changes in sleeping or eating habits.
Frequent headaches or stomachaches without a medical explanation.
A sudden decline in grades or motivation.
Loss of interest in activities they once enjoyed.
Difficulty concentrating.
Increased anger or emotional outbursts.
Talking about feeling hopeless, worthless, or that they do not belong.

None of these signs automatically mean a child has a mental health disorder. They are signals that your child may need additional attention, understanding, and support.
What about friendships?
One of the greatest sources of both joy and stress during childhood and adolescence is peer relationships.
Parents should pay attention to whether their child has friends they enjoy spending time with, whether they are increasingly isolated, whether they are experiencing bullying, or whether social media is affecting their confidence and emotional well-being.
Ask questions that invite conversation rather than interrogation. Instead of asking: “How was school?” Try asking: “Who made you smile today?” “Who did you sit with at lunch?” “What was the best part of your day?” “Was there anything today that felt difficult?”
Small conversations every day often reveal much more than one serious conversation after a problem develops.
Partner with your child’s teachers
Teachers spend many hours with our children and often notice changes parents cannot see. Likewise, parents understand their child’s personality, history, and behavior in ways teachers cannot.
The strongest support for a child comes when families and schools work together not as critics of one another, but as partners. If something feels different, trust your instincts. Reach out early. You do not need certainty before asking for help.
Parenting without becoming overbearing. 
Many parents worry about striking the right balance. We all want to protect our children.
Yet children also need opportunities to solve problems, make mistakes, develop resilience, and build confidence. Healthy parenting is not about removing every obstacle.
It is about remaining emotionally available while allowing children to develop independence.

Listen more than you lecture.
Be curious before becoming critical.
Correct behavior without diminishing the child.
Celebrate effort as much as achievement.
Let your child know that your love is never dependent upon grades, athletic performance, or perfection.

Children who know they are loved without conditions are better equipped to navigate life’s inevitable challenges.
You are not alone.
Connecticut has responded by expanding children’s behavioral health resources, including Urgent Crisis Centers designed to help families receive immediate care before a crisis requires hospitalization. But no system can replace the role of caring adults. Parents, teachers, coaches, relatives, neighbors, and communities remain the first line of support for our children.
Perhaps this is the most important message I can offer.  If your child is struggling, you have not failed.  Children face enormous pressures today—academic expectations, social media, loneliness, family stress, world events, and the ordinary challenges of growing up.
Many families experience moments when they need additional support.  Seeking help is not a sign of weakness. It is an act of love.
At the Child & Family Guidance Center, we have the privilege of walking alongside families every day. We do not simply treat symptoms. We partner with parents, caregivers, schools, and communities to better understand each child as a whole person with unique strengths, dreams, and possibilities.  Every day we see that when children receive support early and when families are equipped with the tools they need young lives can change dramatically. After 35 years of working with children and families I know a few things to be true:

Every child deserves to feel safe.
Every child deserves to be heard.
Every child deserves hope.
And every child deserves a champion.

As this new school year begins, may each of us commit to being that champion for the children in our lives.
Together, we can ensure that every child has the opportunity not only to succeed in school but to thrive in life.  Isn’t this all you ever wanted for your child?
Gisselle Acevedo is President and CEO of the Child & Family Guidance Center.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: A reality check for CT’s housing market
description: State and municipal officials control the real answer to CT housing shortage: allowing higher density zoning and cutting local red tape.
text:
The vital value of a home goes well beyond the roof and walls that protect us from the cold. Maya Angelou knew: “The ache for home is in all of us, the safe place where we can go as we are and not be questioned.”
But finding that special home — that “safe place” — is very hard to do in Connecticut, where the short supply and huge demand has raised prices and limited, or eliminated, choices for so many.
In fact, it’s so hard to find an affordable and appropriate home in many states that a rancorous, partisan Congress of virtually-never-agreeing Republicans and Democrats just – hold onto your hats – agreed on a new housing law that will ease, though not solve, the nation’s high-price-low-supply plague.
